Tech Report: Behind the Scenes of the Inaugural Bon Appétit LIVE

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1507 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This past weekend the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen in Latest York City opened its doors to the public for Bon Appétit Live, an immersive day of cooking demos and classes, talks with chefs and recipe experts, Test Kitchen tours, games, prizes, and plenty to eat and drink.
  • The day kicked off with a warm welcome from Bon Appétit’s editor-in-chief Jamila Robinson, who exclaimed that “the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen is the heart of our brand.” Robinson also shared that Bon Appétit just rolled out a latest cooking app containing tens of thousands of recipes from the Test Kitchen archives.
  • Guests fueled up with an impressive array of curated breakfast treats alongside refreshing beverages from S.Pellegrino, before moving on to interactive experiences.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This past weekend the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen in Latest York City opened its doors to the public for Bon Appétit Live, an immersive day of cooking demos and classes, talks with chefs and recipe experts, Test Kitchen tours, games, prizes, and plenty to eat and drink.

The day kicked off with a warm welcome from Bon Appétit’s editor-in-chief Jamila Robinson, who exclaimed that “the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen is the heart of our brand.” Robinson also shared that Bon Appétit just rolled out a latest cooking app containing tens of thousands of recipes from the Test Kitchen archives.

Guests fueled up with an impressive array of curated breakfast treats alongside refreshing beverages from S.Pellegrino, before moving on to interactive experiences.

In the first class of the day, baking novices and aficionados alike joined senior Test Kitchen editor and BA Bake Club expert Jesse Szewczyk in the Test Kitchen for Pie Crust Fundamentals, presented by East Fork. The hands-on class featured guest Keia Mastrianni, brand storyteller and “unofficial pie lady” of East Fork. Mastrianni proclaimed her enthusiasm for pie making: “I love preaching the gospel of pie. My favorite thing is teaching people to make pie dough with their hands.” Szewczyk agreed, emphasizing the tactile nature of the process: “It’s a very physical thing to do…a recipe can be written, but teaching someone to make pie dough requires demonstration.” Participants were in luck as Szewczyk and Mastrianni demonstrated a buttery pie crust fortified with cream cheese, a recipe ideal for Thanksgiving developed by former senior Test Kitchen editor Shilpa Uskokovic. After Mastrianni shared crimping tips, participants made their own pie dough at stations throughout the kitchen, with Test Kitchen editors on hand to offer guidance. One participant, James, was particularly excited to be working with director of cooking Emma Laperruque. He enthused, “Before Emma’s and Chris [Morocco’s] recipes, I would burn water. [Bon Appétit] has made cooking really accessible, and I built a lot of confidence. I love the simplicity of Emma’s recipes…they are all so flavorful and so good.”.

Sources indicate that each guest left ready for holiday baking season with new pie-making skills, and a ceramic pie dish from East Fork’s new bakeware collection, featuring clay and glaze made in-house with materials sourced in the Southeast. Before moving on to their next experience, Mastrianni encouraged everyone to keep honing their skills, emphasizing, “Practice makes pie. Progress, not perfection.”.

Meanwhile, in the neighboring Demo Kitchen, a Pasta Boot Camp was underway with Bon Appétit senior cooking editor Kelsey Jane Youngman and chef Stefano Secchi. Secchi, chef and partner of Newly introduced York City’s Rezdôra (recipient of one Michelin star) and Massara, honed his craft in Modena, Italy, under legendary chef Massimo Bottura.

Industry observers note that after walking guests through the fundamentals of making and shaping fresh pasta by hand, Secchi demonstrated a filled ravioli dish aptly named Holiday in Parma. Made with 00 flour and egg dough, the ravioli was piped with a chestnut and Parmesan filling and served with a rich reduction of chicken broth, butter, and saba (a traditional Italian syrup made from slowly simmered grape must).

In a recent development, while guests savored their pasta in the Demo Kitchen, a lively panel discussion was underway on the 34th floor. Moderated by editor-in-chief Jamila Robinson, the Bringing Culture to Cooking panel featured chefs Fariyal Abdullahi (executive chef, Hav & Mar, NYC), Nicholas Bazik (chef and owner, Provenance, Philadelphia, a Bon Appétit Best New Restaurant of 2025), and Vijay Kumar (executive chef and partner, Semma, NYC, a Best New Restaurant of 2022). The conversation explored how culture, identity, and personal experience inform each chef’s cooking. The chefs shared some of their favorite home-cooking ingredients, such as Chef Bazik’s fermented lime juice, a versatile seasoning made by combining fresh lime juice with salt at a 2% ratio by weight. Chef Abdullahi championed berbere, the Ethiopian spice blend she likened to “Ethiopian salt” for its ubiquity in the country’s cooking. Abdullahi cautioned that store-bought blends are convenient but not necessarily of the highest-possible quality. “You should make it at home!” she encouraged.

Recent findings suggest that back in the Test Kitchen, Visit Maine hosted Lobster 101, a hands-on lobster class and oyster tasting with Bon Appétit’s manager of audience strategy Carly Westerfield and Krista Tripp, founder of Aphrodite Oysters in South Thomaston, Maine. Each participant received a whole, steamed Maine lobster and the ingredients and tools needed to transform it into a creamy, decadent lobster dip. Under Westerfield’s guidance, the class learned how to break down their lobsters, extract the meat, and assemble a dip made with cream cheese, mayonnaise, celery, chives, and lemon juice. The approachable demonstration demystified the process and highlighted guests how easily they could prepare a luxurious appetizer at home, just in time for the holidays.

Industry observers note that participants worked with hard-shell lobsters, but Tripp encouraged them to visit Maine and sample both hard-shell and soft-shell varieties. She explained that soft-shell lobsters, typically in season from July through August, have a sweeter, more tender meat. The two are actually the same animal at different stages of its molting cycle: a soft-shell lobster has recently shed its old shell, leaving a newer, more pliable one that is easier to crack. The class concluded with a tasting of Aphrodite Oysters, grown in the waters off South Thomaston, Maine. The medium-size oysters were briny and subtly sweet, reflecting the cold, brackish waters of the Lower Weskeag River where they were grown. A small squeeze of lemon was all that was needed to enhance their flavor as guests tilted their heads back, slurped, and allowed themselves to be transported to the rugged coast of Maine.

Meanwhile, in the Demo Kitchen, Bon Appétit director of culture Joseph Hernandez was joined by Matt Conroy, chef at Washington, DC’s Maison Bar à Vins, for a live cooking demonstration of one of Chef Conroy’s favorite dishes. Named one of Bon Appétit’s Best Upcoming Restaurants of 2026, the restaurant pairs French-inspired cooking with an eclectic wine list and seasonal cocktails. Chef Conroy prepared a new fall salad made of chicory, pear, and smoked blue cheese, finished with a Banyuls vinaigrette.

In the cafeteria, guests gathered for a live version of the Dear Bon Appétit advice column. Bon Appétit director of cooking Emma Laperruque presented questions about home cooking and holiday entertaining to chef Amanda Freitag. One attendee asked Freitag how to handle undercooked turkey legs and thighs each year. Freitag recommended removing the legs and cooking them separately, as in this BA recipe for Gravy-Braised Turkey from Jesse Szewczyk.

Next, food stylist Thu Buser showcased her exceptional culinary artistry by decorating an elaborate “snake cake” with vibrant green swirls and flowers. Then, a break for lunch with BA’s Best Mozzarella Sticks, a variety of salads and skewers, hot honey salmon, smoothies, and a cranberry maple mule.

Industry observers note that while attendees grazed and mingled, Jamila Robinson joined legendary chef and restaurateur Marcus Samuelsson to discuss Back to Green: Rediscovering a World of Delicious, Healthy Eating, his newly introduced global plant-forward cookbook coauthored by Robinson. Samuelsson captured the atmosphere of the event, remarking, “What a party we are having here…the energy is amazing!”.

In a recent development, the final demonstration of the day featured Cornmeal Shortcakes with Blueberry Compote presented by Visit Maine with Jesse Szewczyk and Ron Howard of Brodis Blueberries. Featuring a recipe from Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firsker, the shortcakes showcased farm-fresh wild blueberries grown on a ninth-generation family farm. As Szewczyk prepared the recipe, Howard discussed the importance of wild blueberries to Maine’s agricultural heritage. A native crop, they can be traced back to the end of the last Ice Age, predating lobster as a symbol of the state. “Everyone should think of wild blueberries as the ultimate Maine crop,” Howard explained. After tasting the shortcakes, attendees would be hard-pressed to disagree. Szewczyk noted that compared with conventional blueberries, the wild blueberries produced a more saturated color and tasted more distinctly of blueberry.

According to recent reports, the day ended on a sweet note with pastry chef Eunji Lee, winner of North America’s Best Pastry Chef Award from The 50. Attendees had a chance to meet Lee and sample pastries from Lysée, her pastry boutique influenced by Korean and French culture and inspired by Fresh York City.

Bon Appétit Live brought together chefs, culinary personalities, and food editors for a day of conversations, cooking, tasting, and learning. Attendees experienced the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen firsthand, learned directly from chefs and editors, and engaged with the people and products behind the food. As editor-in-chief Jamila Robinson stated, “Food is always an invitation…we are so happy to give everyone access to the same experiences we have.”.

Bon Appétit LIVE 2026 was sponsored by East Fork, Visit Maine, and S.Pellegrino® Sparkling Natural Mineral Water with thanks to All-Clad, As Ever, Bachan’s, Better Sour, Field Company, Floura, Gimme Seaweed, GOODLES, Graza, Hedley & Bennett, Kann Coffee, Material Kitchen, Misen, Owala®, Rip Van, SharkNinja, and Staub.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Though Polo by Ralph Lauren may conjure up images of days spent in the countryside, the brand celebrated the launch of its newly introduced Blaze bag in quintessential California fashion on Wednesday afternoon, with a poolside lunch at Sunset Tower Hotel.

On a refreshingly cool day, the likes of Chloe Bennet, Charlotte Lawrence, Laura Harrier, Diana Silvers, and Justine Lupe descended upon the storied hotel with the new purses slung over their shoulders.

It has been revealed that named after the white marking on a horse’s face, the Blaze, which debuted as part of Fall 2026, has already become a staple in Lawrence’s rotation. “It’s been my number-one bag. I’ve been using it for three months now,” the “Sleep Talking” singer told Vogue. “It’s so cute, and it’s also way bigger than it looks. It’s even been my carry-on when I’m traveling.”.

It has been revealed that though most attendees arrived with the aforementioned bag in tow, each put their own spin on Ralph Lauren’s signature Western-inspired preppy aesthetic. Fringe was a recurring theme, with both Bennet and singer Scout Willis in leather and suede jackets. Harrier, meanwhile, leaned into her crisp style in a white button-up and straight-leg jeans, while podcaster Liz Perez opted for the same pared-back formula.

Lupe, best known lately for her role in Nobody Wants This, eschewed outerwear in favor of a long-sleeve navy-and-white striped polo top and fiery red sweater draped over her shoulders. “I love something that feels boyish and androgynous, but also feminine at the same time,” she explained. “And I think a polo does a really great job of marrying those two qualities.”.

It has been revealed that for Lupe, who lives across town in Eagle Rock, any visit to the Sunset Tower Hotel feels like a special occasion. “I feel like I'm doing something fancy, and it’s never a casual thing. It’s like my equivalent of when you’re a kid and you’re dressing up to go out with your grandparents,” the actress shared.

Recent findings suggest that for the first hour, the group socialized inside as servers strolled around with mini lobster rolls, watermelon and feta bites, and Champagne. When it came time for lunch, attendees were greeted by a long table adorned with burgundy floral arrangements. Before taking their seats, some stopped to snap photos of the picturesque white-and-maroon umbrellas overlooking the pool. A chopped salad with tomato, cucumber, fennel, chickpeas, haricots verts, and mozzarella kicked off lunch. For the main course, guests chose between chicken paillard and grilled salmon, both served atop a bed of arugula.

It has been revealed that willis and Lawrence settled in next to each other, facing Harrier and chef Eleonore Toulin. Farther down the table, writers Laurel Pantin, Amanda Alagem, and Alessandra Codinha caught up and swapped shopping recommendations. Sorbet with fresh berries gave guests an excuse to linger a little longer, soaking up the scenic views and mild afternoon air before heading back to their day.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that all our office talks about around the holidays are our melty, crispy cranberry brie bites, and I gotta tell you, I totally get why—they’re a superstar app. So, taking cranberry and brie and stuffing it into chicken breasts for a main meal was a no-brainer. This is my favorite way to shake up my weeknight chicken routine in the fall, and it's going to be my go-to dish to impress come Friendsgiving season.

Preparing the chicken:I wouldn’t typically recommend a larger chicken breast for searing, but it’s necessary for stuffing. Butterfly or cut the breast, starting at the top of the thickest point, and slowly create a slit about three-quarters of the way through. Season with salt on the inside and outside of the breast. Place a piece of brie and a spoonful of cranberry sauce toward the inner seam and close. Sear each stuffed breast until the outside is browned. Doing this in a heavy-bottom pan like a cast-iron will allow you to transfer right to the oven without removing the breast to a sheet pan. Finish cooking the breast until the internal temperature is 165°.

Storage:Store the chicken in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. To avoid the chicken from drying out, I suggest wrapping the pieces in foil and slowly heating them in a 350° oven.

Latest Update: I’m A Professional Cook & My Secret To Perfectly Smooth Gravy Is This $4 Pantry Staple

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (392 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that gravy is one of the most problematic dishes on the Thanksgiving table.
  • Making the gravy the day before is a surefire way to avoid the last-minute panic.
  • It has been revealed that the secret to perfectly smooth gravy is Wondra flour.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that gravy is one of the most problematic dishes on the Thanksgiving table. Every year, home cooks struggle and sweat over gravy that’s too thin, too greasy, or—worst of all—lumpy. All while your relatives watch and the turkey gets cold.

Making the gravy the day before is a surefire way to avoid the last-minute panic. But on holidays when prepping ahead just isn’t in the cards, one simple hack can solve your gravy woes: a $4 pantry staple that will thicken up any gravy in mere minutes—without any lumps.

It has been revealed that the secret to perfectly smooth gravy is Wondra flour. Known to chefs and home cooks alike for its bright blue cylindrical can, Wondra is wheat flour that has been pre-gelatinized, dried, and finely milled so it dissolves more easily and thickens sauces faster than regular flour. This means you can whisk it directly into any gravy (no matter the temperature!) without worry about clumping—and it will thicken that gravy almost immediately.

If you’re making gravy from scratch with no other thickener besides Wondra, I recommend starting with 1 tablespoon for every cup of stock and/or drippings. You can do this by heating the drippings or stock in a pot on the stove, then just whisking in the Wondra. It should thicken within a few minutes. If your drippings don’t have a ton of fat, I recommend whisking in a little butter too, to help with the flavor.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re using Wondra to troubleshoot a gravy that’s too thin, I recommend whisking in a few teaspoons at a time. The Wondra should do its thickening magic within a minute or two after it goes in, and then you can decide whether you need more.

While Wondra flour is great for thickening gravies and sauces, it’s far from a one-trick pony. I’ve used it to coat white fish (such as tilapia) before pan-searing to give it a beautifully thin, crispy crust—and help prevent the fish from sticking to the pan. It’s also a common ingredient in batters for fried foods, since its lower protein content helps form a lighter, crispier crust—and it’s also a magical way to get a flakier pastry dough. So even if you only make gravy once a year, that blue canister won’t go to waste.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Terence Young, the director of Dr. No, needed a suit for Sean Connery to wear for his debut as James Bond, he took him to see his personal Savile Row tailor, Anthony Sinclair.

Recent findings suggest that “Connery’s suits were considered relatively contemporary, because Anthony always had a very soft shoulder on his suits,” explains Elliot Mason, the director of business at Anthony Sinclair, which is no longer located on Savile Row, but still makes classic British suiting. “Anthony liked to nip in the waist, so it gave that real hourglass silhouette to the suit, which really is quite timeless. And as was the trend at the time, the Connery suits all had a relatively high rise, double-pleated with English forward pleats, and most of his trousers had Daks button-tab adjusters on the side.”.

Opting to dress James Bond in a Savile Row suit might seem like a no-brainer in hindsight, but the decision—and the cut of the suits themselves—still resonates more than 60 years later. Sinclair would make all of Connery’s suits during his nine-year run as James Bond, and his blend of classic British tailoring and of-the-moment influences would create a template for every Bond to come. With Robert Pattinson—a Dior ambassador and a guy with a reputation for adventurous style—chosen to take up the mantle in Bond 26, the question now becomes: what will he wear?

Tailor Anthony Sinclair fitting Sean Connery for one of the suits he wore in 1963’s From Russia With Love.

In a recent development, ian Fleming, the author who created James Bond, spent a lot of time talking about what Agent 007 drank (Wolfschmidt Vodka) what he drove (Bentley convertibles, for the most part) and how he made his coffee (he was a dedicated pour-over guy), but, surprisingly, he never specified where the spy bought his clothes. As a result, for the last six decades, it’s been up to the directors and costume designers of the 25 previous films to create a upcoming look for every successive Bond. In the Connery and Moore eras it was Savile Row suits. Timothy Dalton’s Bond wore Paul Smith. Brosnan was a bespoke Brioni guy, as was Daniel Craig, who also brought Tom Ford into the mix. At 6’1” to Craig’s 5’10”, with a leaner build, and a long track record of fashion-forward dressing, Pattinson has everything needed to reinvent Bond once again.

“I’m pretty sure we’re going to see something quite different from Pattinson's Bond,” says Matt Spaiser, the tailoring obsessive behind BondSuits.com and the author of From Tailors with Love: An Evolution of Menswear Through the Bond Films. “Pattinson is a different kind of actor, and he’s going to wear something that moves differently. Plus, he’s 18 years younger than Daniel Craig.”.

Sources indicate that the actor playing Bond has a major influence on how he dresses—Daniel Craig, an adventurous dresser himself, was very hands-on with the wardrobe in his films—but Pattinson’s ongoing contract with Dior could also factor in. “Some of his Dior looks look somewhat like James Bond—he wears a great tuxedo—but I don’t think it’s going to tell us what he’s going to wear as James Bond,” Spaiser says. “He’s worn suits from other brands in other roles—like in Tenet, he wasn’t wearing a Dior suit—so I don’t think he's necessarily obligated to be wearing Dior as James Bond.”.

Daniel Craig, seen here in 2019 with then-Prince Charles on the set of No Time to Die, mainly sported sharp Tom Ford suiting in his later Bond films.

Another crucial factor that contributes to a new Bond’s look is what’s happening in fashion whenever the film eventually gets made. “One thing that we've seen throughout most of the Bond eras is that he dresses in suits that are fairly traditional, but there's always some nod to the era that they’re in,” says Spaiser. “Sometimes they lean a little more into fashion, like when Roger Moore was wearing flares. That was something that I think they couldn't avoid without making Bond look too old-fashioned at the time.”.

Recent findings suggest that tone also plays an crucial role, and historically has ping-ponged between serious (Connery, Dalton, Craig) and more campy (Moore, Brosnan), but with Denis Villeneuve, the auteur behind Sicario, Blade Runner: 2049, and Dune in the director’s chair, the smart money isn’t on hovercraft gondolas and punny Bond girl names. A darker, more atmospheric milieu could make for an interesting complement to Pattinson’s taste for high-fashion.

According to recent reports, if Mason were dressing Pattinson for the role, he notes, he’d take a lead from his clientele, many of whom, like Bond, are well-heeled Londoners with a taste for expensive sports cars and well mixed cocktails. “The majority of our customers are reasonably conservative, and when it comes to fit, they’re sensitive to current trends,” Mason notes. As such, he’d opt for longer jackets, both single- and double-breasted, that are fuller through the body, and straight-leg pleated trousers. “It’s not that very, very slim fit that we'd seen for so many years, but it still needs to be refined,” he says. “I don’t think it would be appropriate to put him in wide-leg or baggy trousers. I just don't think it’s right for Bond.”.

Robert Pattinson, the latest 007, has been the face of Dior’s menswear for over a decade.

Industry observers note that given the intense scrutiny on every relaunch of the Bond franchise, and the tendency of fans to get worked up online over perceived mishandling of a beloved character, Pattinson, Villeneuve, and the film’s yet-to-be-declared costume designers have little room for error. Go too conservative and they’ll be accused of playing it safe; make Bond into a fashion guy, and they’ll incur the wrath of the traditionalists.

Recent findings suggest that “He needs to look current, but also timeless,” Spaiser says. “It’s a hard balance to find.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How to buy and store fresh cranberries.

It has been revealed that look for firm, glossy cranberries and discard any that are soft, shriveled, or bruised. A few pale pink berries are nothing to worry about.

According to recent reports, keep unwashed cranberries in their original bag in the refrigerator for up to four weeks, though they’re best used sooner. To stock up, freeze them in their original packaging or spread clean thoroughly dried berries on a baking sheet until frozen, then transfer to a freezer bag. They’ll keep their quality for up to a year. Many cooked cranberry recipes work with frozen berries straight from the freezer; check the recipe before thawing.

In a recent development, that vivid magenta filling is no food-coloring trick: Cranberries and plenty of lime give the curd its electric hue and tang. Let the pie set overnight, then pile on billowy meringue and break out the kitchen torch.

Sources indicate that A 12-oz. bag of cranberries, sugar, orange zest, and about 10 minutes at the stove are all you need for this tangy Thanksgiving essential. Make it up to five days ahead and save any leftovers for turkey-cranberry sliders.

Layers of tender buttermilk cake, tart cranberry jam, and silky white chocolate frosting make an excellent argument for serving cake on Thanksgiving. The sugared cranberries on top are like little sour candies.

Imagine Key lime pie dressed for the holidays. The punchy cranberry-lime curd meets a crisp press-in crust made with gingersnaps and pecans. A generous dollop of whipped cream rounds out the tartness.

Sources indicate that here’s a reason to keep canned cranberry sauce around after Thanksgiving. Jellied sauce melts into a glossy, sweet-and-sour glaze that coats chicken and green beans. Think orange chicken, with a cranberry twist.

It has been revealed that cranberries turn this classic upside-down apple tart a beautiful rosy pink while cutting through its buttery sweetness. Homemade rough puff pastry supplies the flaky base; vanilla ice cream is very much encouraged.

It has been revealed that canned whole-berry cranberry sauce becomes a punchy dressing for pleasantly bitter endive and frisée. Add crunchy candied pecans and salty Manchego, and suddenly cranberry sauce is doing salad duty.

Two layers of buttery, crumbly walnut crust surround a tart cranberry filling in this striking take on a Linzer torte. Save it for a holiday dessert table—or any occasion that calls for something special.

Industry observers note that dress crisp-bottomed Persian rice with dried cranberries, saffron, and fragrant herbs. The berries plump in ghee alongside rosemary, sage, and thyme, adding little pops of sweetness against the savory rice.

If the wobble is the best part of canned cranberry sauce for you, this homemade version delivers. It’s sliceable, deeply fruity, and subtly fragrant with cardamom and bay leaves. Bring on the ridges.

Roasted brussels sprouts get a lively companion in cranberry mostarda, a sweet-tart condiment with mustard seeds, prunes, and a little brandy. Make extra mostarda: It belongs on more than just sprouts.

Recent findings suggest that A warm cranberry-apple topping brings plenty of tart fruit flavor to this crowd-friendly baked oatmeal. It’s a welcome breakfast when the house is full and everyone seems to wake up hungry at once.

Rum, hard cider, cranberry juice, ginger ale, and lime make a lively batch cocktail. Cranberry-studded ice cubes do double duty, keeping glasses cold and making the punch look party-ready.

Jalapeño and lime give classic cranberry sauce a bright, spicy kick. It’s especially good alongside roasted meats or piled onto a leftover turkey sandwich when you want something with a little heat.

Forget the giant roast bird for a minute. These tender, gravy-coated turkey meatballs come with a cranberry-orange marmalade jam that stands in for traditional lingonberries. A heap of mashed potatoes completes the picture.

Fresh ginger gives this cranberry relish some zip, while golden raisins and allspice round out its tartness. Spoon it onto a cheese board or save the leftovers for French toast the next morning.

Sources indicate that herbs in the dredge give this crunchy fried chicken Thanksgiving energy, but the quick cranberry-mustard dipping sauce is the real holiday flourish. It’s a compelling alternative to roasting an entire turkey.

Industry observers note that homemade cranberry-thyme syrup, Campari, and Champagne make a sparkling cocktail that’s fruity, pleasantly bitter, and dressed for a party. Make the syrup up to two weeks ahead; the drinks come together in minutes.

Boxed stuffing mix gets a serious upgrade with aromatic vegetables, dried cranberries, and the savory drippings from crisp-skinned chicken thighs. It’s Thanksgiving-adjacent comfort food, made in one skillet any night of the week.

Recent findings suggest that roasted sweet potatoes and delicata squash get a glossy, sweet-and-sour cranberry sauce made with red wine vinegar and thyme. Make extra: The agrodolce is just as good spooned over Thanksgiving turkey.

Whole orange and a cinnamon stick give this chunky cranberry sauce its fragrant warmth. Blanching the chopped orange first keeps bitterness in check, while a little butter softens the berries’ sharp edge.

A buttery, lemony custard studded with tart cranberries gives this Southern classic a holiday spin. The berries stay mostly intact, offering juicy little bursts of tartness against the rich filling.

Industry observers note that dried figs bring earthy sweetness to this bold cranberry chutney, while ginger, vinegar, and whole grain mustard keep it lively. It’s the sort of condiment you’ll want beside roast pork as much as turkey.

Dorie Greenspan’s warmly spiced Bundt packs in fresh and dried cranberries, toasted almonds, and a little five-spice powder. Greek yogurt keeps the cake rich; orange icing supplies the finishing flourish.

Baker Amanda Mack tucks a tart cranberry-orange filling into exceptionally flaky buttermilk pastry for individual pies. They’re a thoughtful addition to a dessert spread where everyone wants to try a little of everything.

Industry observers note that no simmering required for this bright, crunchy cranberry relish. Walnuts, shallot, mustard seeds, and Fresno chile give it plenty of texture and bite—a particularly good counterpoint to rich holiday mains.

Homemade cranberry-orange jam gives this tequila cocktail its fruity punch. Lime juice keeps it lively, while a sugar-salt-and-five-spice rim makes each glass taste decidedly more festive than a typical margarita.

It has been revealed that chopped fresh cranberries bring little bursts of tartness to an otherwise classic cheddar grilled cheese. A swipe of Dijon mustard ties the flavors together. Sometimes the best cranberry recipe is also lunch.

Have part of a bag left over? These ideas from the BA archives put even a small quantity to good use.

According to recent reports, corn dip is the creamy, cheesy party dip we just can’t get enough of. A cream cheese base with a hint of heat makes this corn-packed appetizer a crowd-pleaser at any gathering. While some corn dip is served cold, we prefer to serve mine hot.

Recent findings suggest that let's be honest: there's no party dip like classic spinach & artichoke. Don't get us wrong, it's perfectly creamy and cheesy on its own, but it's also ripe for additions and creative takes. Don’t worry, we didn’t forget the pumpkin pie! Here, pumpkin pie spice, vanilla pudding, and fresh pumpkin puree are whipped into a light and fluffy dip that’s not as heavy as the classic fall pie, yet still has all of the festive flavors you love.

Not only is this cranberry brie dip perfect for holiday parties, it's the best way to use up those homemade cranberry sauce leftovers. This is one of our most-loved Thanksgiving appetizer recipes: not only is it completely delicious, but it couldn't be easier to make. You only need a handful of ingredients and under 30 minutes.

Whipped Ricotta With Olives & Roasted Red Peppers.

Whipped ricotta is beyond easy to make, even though it sounds so delicate and fancy. That’s what makes this a perfect appetizer to serve for an intimate dinner party or the holidays. Topping with marinated olives and roasted red peppers gives the dip a briney flavor, and the red and green makes it extra festive.

Roasted Shallot & Garlic Caesar Dip.

According to recent reports, this dip starts off with a base of cream cheese and mayo. The addition of Parmigiano, Dijon mustard, freshly ground black pepper, and a wee bit of anchovy brings the Caesar notes fully forward. I love to serve this dip with toasted crostini or pieces of romaine lettuce to simulate salad vibes, but there’s no shame in however you choose to dip.

We’ll use a dirty martini as inspiration for just about anything at this point. Industry observers note that I start brainstorming and visualizing what I want to wear about a week before a trip, but I pack the night before. Everything stays in my closet until then—I write down my looks in a notebook, so the packing starts on paper.

After everything is in the notebook, I do pack in outfits. I gravitate toward natural tones—black, white, cream, and navy—with good patterns and plaids mixed in. That palette helps everything feel cohesive while still leaving me room to play. Because this was a road trip, I had the luxury of bringing a few extra things; I still planned my looks, but found room for another sweater or jacket.

According to recent reports, for this trip, I gravitated toward Guest in Residence, Agolde, and Jeanerica. Their knits, denim, and easy layers felt right for a few autumn days in the countryside.

For this road trip, I brought my REI Co-op Trailgate Gear Bin. It fits everything! I love being able to bring the extra layers and familiar things I want for a few days away. I also brought my one-of-a-kind Bode equestrian bag—the equestrian references fit the feeling of this trip beautifully.

Jeans, a tee, a great sweater, and good boots. Simple and comfortable, but still put together. For this trip, I brought my Blundstones—perfect with denim, corduroy, and all the cozy layers.

Sources indicate that my Louis Vuitton makeup bag always comes with me, whether I’m flying or driving. It keeps my beauty essentials together and brings a little of my home routine with me wherever I’m staying.

Both, actually. I love a good sweater and a scarf—I’m always happy to have an extra layer. For this trip, I packed my Toteme scarf along with plenty of knitwear.

Lesse face spray—it’s a staple in my travel beauty bag.

I keep accessories pretty minimal. My Tiffany & Co. watch is my go-to for every day, so it comes with me everywhere. I also brought a black leather belt with silver hardware that I know works well with both jeans and corduroy pants.

No—I gravitate toward fabrics that need very little maintenance. I like being able to unpack, get dressed, and enjoy wherever I am without too much fuss.

It has been revealed that my Blundstone boots! They’re the pair I reach for for a few days in the countryside. I love them with corduroy, a plaid shirt, and an oversized sweater.

According to recent reports, my Toteme scarf. I wear it around my head or neck, either draped open or tied in a knot. It’s really beautiful, and changing how I wear it gives the same outfit a different feeling. I love it with a simple tee and sweater or tucked into a jacket when it’s particularly cold.

I like to leave a little room for things I find along the way—plus, a road trip gives me a bit more freedom to bring something home.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, gen-Z has revived every minute piece of 2000s pop culture, which means zip-up hoodies are back and have all but usurped the pullover hoodie as the sweat du jour.
  • Uniqlo’s no-nonsense clean aesthetic and low price point has made it a go-to for any menswear enjoyer looking for good style on a budget.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Surveying the best zip-up hoodies for men takes me back to my younger days as a hopelessly romantic high school kid. My formative years were marred by angst, soundtracked by pop punk, emo, and indie rock. The piece of clothing that got me through it all? A zip-up hoodie. It was core to the indie aesthetic, with every forlorn frontman sporting one over a thrashed band tee, skinny jeans, and shredded Chucks. But nostalgia never seems to stay in the past, especially when fashion is involved.

According to recent reports, gen-Z has revived every minute piece of 2000s pop culture, which means zip-up hoodies are back and have all but usurped the pullover hoodie as the sweat du jour. The zip-up is inherently versatile in both practical wear and sheer styling dexterity. With the flick of the zip, you can put your beloved Death Cab for Cutie tee on full display while letting your pits breathe, or keep it zipped up when it's just a bit too nippy out. To find the best zip-up hoodies on the market, I dusted off Transatlanticism and went on a deep dive. The good news is that the old classics are still good. The better news is that there's a lot of great competition to choose from.

Uniqlo’s no-nonsense clean aesthetic and low price point has made it a go-to for any menswear enjoyer looking for good style on a budget. While the brand excels at cashmere sweaters, T-shirts, and a slew of homerun collabs, the Japanese label’s sweats are criminally underrated. We’d go so far as to say that they should be talked in the same breath as brands like Champion and Sunspel. This zip up hoodie took us by surprise thanks to its comfy midweight, all-cotton fabric and solid construction. But the main selling point is the impeccable fit.

So many other brands cut their hoodies too long in the body and leave you looking like Jack Skellington’s pubescent brother. Uniqlo managed to cut its French terry hoodie to sit right at the hips which makes for a more classic and natural silhouette that’s neither lanky nor sloppy. Because of the fabric, the feel, and the overall fit, this is my favorite zip-up hoodie by a sizable margin. It’s my most-worn hoodie and has yet to show signs of any fraying.

Industry observers note that hoodies were originally meant for sportswear, as warm up gear before a grueling game of football. These days, they’re more often worn for lounging on the couch to watch the kickoff. And if you want to kick it in comfort while saving your pennies for booze and amuse bouche for the massive game with the boys, the best budget zip up hoodie to buy is Hanes’ EcoSmart zip hoodie. The fit is spot on—relaxed, but not sloppy, comfy in the body and the sleeves without swallowing you like a sand pit.

Recent findings suggest that the fit is impressive for the price, and the overall quality means you’re getting a little more than what you pay for. It’s not a hoodie that’ll last you for too long, but it is a good quality piece for just 15 bucks. And when other hoodies offer lesser quality and worse-fitting options for about the same price? The answer is clear.

According to recent reports, it’s hard not to sing the praises of Reigning Champ, a brand that built its fleece empire on sweatpants and hoodies. The Canadian label’s flagship midweight terry fabric has drawn the attention of streetwear royalty and menswear buffs alike and its dedication to quality has elevated the humble hoodie to oxygen-deprived heights. We named Reigning Champ’s crewneck sweatshirt and pullover hoodie as among our favorites in their respective categories, and the same goes for its zip-up hooded sweatshirt. It’s made of the same 100% cotton French terry fabric as its superlative-earning brethren and is cut with high-quality flatlock stitching for a smooth, un-bulky feel.

According to recent reports, I had high expectations for Reigning Champ, given my previous experience, and I’m not surprised at all with how nice this zip-up is. And while I'm partial to the standard fit, it’s also available in a slim fit version, too.

Hoodies live in a universe well beyond the sportswear world from which they originated. And while we still enjoy the OGs and the classics that made the hoodie a bona fide menswear must-have, we also love seeing all the ways the style has been pushed, tweaked, and freaked. Our Legacy's Level Hood has been a successful avenue for the Stockholm-based brand to explore the limits of the hoodie and this particular version strikes a delicate balance between the freaky and the fashion-curious. It's made of an English wool knit into an all-over ribbed texture for a throwback '90s feel. The cropped, boxy silhouette and elongated sleeves harken back to the grunge-y era, while the sultry dual-tone nightshade colorway throws you off in the best way possible.

According to recent reports, menswear influencers will be happy to regale you with their TedTalk on the golden ratio of clothing proportions. Essentially, that means your outfit should be divided into three equal sections where the top takes up one third of the outfit. Basically, your tops should be cropped and sit closer to your natural waist. Follow it up with some high-waisted pants with a wide silhouette and you’ve instantly garnered 300K views on TikTok (RIP). With so many indie brands and influencers scrambling to make their own versions of “the perfect cropped hoodie” you’re probably tired of wading through all the choices. Do yourself a favor and go to Abercrombie.

Sources indicate that the Moose’s version is backed by actual trend forecasters, actual designers, and actual fit models. What does that mean, exactly? It means that its cropped zip hoodie fits really well and uses surprisingly beefy fabric. It was a revelation for me, too—Abercrombie wasn’t a name I associated with hoodies, but after I saw this in person, I had to readjust my menswear word cloud.

Some of the best zip-up hoodies for men are made by a brand you never see in brick and mortar stores. Camber has been crafting the most durable sweats for decades, right here in America and have been the shining example of the difference between good quality and great quality. Sure, you have to order through an old-school web 1.0 website and wait for several weeks to actually get your hoodie. But trust us when we say that the relatively minor inconvenience is completely worth it.

The heavyweight fleece is almost as thick as a leather jacket and can stand in as outerwear if you wanted it to. While other hoodies are washed to hell in giant industrial washing machines to reach a super soft texture by the time it gets to you, Camber’s actually require you to do the work yourself. It sort of feels like you’re being swaddled by an anaconda, which means if you’re a proponent of hard clothes like raw denim, you’ll like Camber’s hoodie a lot.

Cashmere zip hoodies, once the exclusive province of Silicon Valley unicorn founders and PJ-flying nepo babies, have been democratized, none better than Naadam's take. You know the brand for bringing thoughtful, sustainable cashmere pieces at “really, only that much?” prices. Its zip hoodie is as soft as it gets, with extra credit points awarded for coming in a classic fit (too many cashmere hoodies err on the side of slim) and six colors, including this decidedly handsome olive. Wear it on weekends, work-from-home Fridays, and long flights—even if it's just Economy+.

Sources indicate that shoutout to brother in arms Louis Cheslaw, GQ Recs contributor, whose writing for the newsletter Magasin put us on to young brand Cease. From seed to sewing, it's beefy 20-ounce cotton is fully American-made. Assembling the fabric vertically means the hoodie will shorten up to a slightly cropped, oversized fit. Act fast if you want some of the less-boring colors—they move fast.

In a recent development, we can’t deny Russell Athletic’s contributions to the hoodie space. And while its formula has changed over the years, the latest hoodies are still pretty good for the price. The fabric is soft and lightweight, and it’s available in a rainbow of colorways. Plus, if you’re looking for a hoodie with a little more length, this is a great option.

Bold graphics aren’t usually deemed classics, but Gap’s retro-leaning collegiate-style block logo has staying power almost as much as the Levi’s red tab. Add to that a wonderfully fluffy midweight fleece material and a tailored straight fit and you’ve got something you’ll see on moodboards for generations to come.

It has been revealed that champion’s Reverse Weave fabric is iconic for its nearly shrink-proof quality and almost unsettlingly rough exterior. Flip it to the inside and you’ve got a luxuriously brushed interior that’ll have you feeling like you’re melting into a cloud. Heads-up that pricing varies kinda wildly by size on Amazon.

In a recent development, the secondhand market is chock full of navy-blue hoodies that have been sun-faded and beaten down with time. They'll cost you just as much as this Mfpen version, but will also fall apart faster than you can zip 'em up.

Les Tien's dedication to all things sweats results in a catalog of luxurious fleece and terry cloth with a modern approach. Featuring high-end Cobrax hardware, RiRi zippers, raw-edge hems and sleeves, and a heavyweight brushed fleece, no detail is phoned in.

The Real McCoy's is considered by many to be Americana repro wizards. This revival of an early 20th-Century hoodie is just one small piece of the brand's preservation prowess. It's made using beefy sinker-knit fleece, old-school Talon-style zippers, and vertical patch pockets.

Sources indicate that A.Presse's chokehold on the menswear illuminati refuses to let up and it's pieces like this vintage-inspired hoodie that keep the pressure on. Based on very rare “after-hood parkas", this made-in-Japan hoodie features an idiosyncratic attached hood, super dense and lofty fleece, with artfully distressed details throughout.

Sources indicate that think of the zip-up as the pullover hoodie's elder brother, but with way more layering potential. In its most natural state, it can cuddle up to a matching set of sweatpants and a baggy tee with flair. (Top it off with a swanky necklace, crisp sneakers, and some stellar shades and you’re left with a fit on par with Shai Gilgeous-Alexander at his tunnel-trotting best.).

Recent findings suggest that unzipped and left open, it can also take on the role of a picture frame ready to display your sickest graphic tee—much like the cardigan, another treasure of 2000s fashion. Or make like a mid-Aughts garage band ironically donning corporate attire and wear your zip-up over a dress shirt and baggy tailored trousers, a high-minded fashion move with a jolt of kooky Scandinavian cool.

It has been revealed that style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Sources indicate that our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

It has been revealed that to kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Industry observers note that across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.).

Latest Update: A Latest Book Explores the Lessons We Can All Learn From Indigenous Wellness Traditions

💡 Key Takeaways

  • For millennia, Indigenous communities have prioritized connection to nature, practiced reciprocity with community, and upheld sacred cultural traditions.
  • “Everybody in North America should understand Native American home teachings because we’re all living on this land,” says Luger, who is an enrolled member of the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa and a descendant of the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the global wellness industry has reached a fever pitch—and shows no signs of slowing down. Overstimulated, under-rested, and on the brink of burnout, we’re desperately seeking antidotes to the ills of the digital era. But what if the answers to our modern-day woes lie in ancient Native American wisdom, not in a supposed cure-all gadget, supplement, or fitness routine?

For millennia, Indigenous communities have prioritized connection to nature, practiced reciprocity with community, and upheld sacred cultural traditions. We can all embrace these holistic principles in our daily lives, says Lakota/Anishinaabe wellness advocate Chelsey Luger. That’s the premise behind her latest book, Native Home: The Ancestral Art of Creating Healing Spaces. In it, she offers tangible ways to incorporate these concepts into our living spaces to promote mental, physical, spiritual, and emotional balance.

“Everybody in North America should understand Native American home teachings because we’re all living on this land,” says Luger, who is an enrolled member of the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa and a descendant of the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe. “There’s a movement in the home industry right now centered around ensuring our surroundings support our well-being. This might be an emerging conversation in the wellness space, but Indigenous communities have been living this way for centuries.”.

According to recent reports, luger and her husband, Onk Akimel O’odham fitness educator Thosh Collins, co-founded the grassroots initiative Well For Culture back in 2013, with the aim of revitalizing Indigenous wellness practices. Since then, they’ve been traveling to tribal nations across the country to both teach and learn from these communities. Native Home is the culmination of those lessons.

Recent findings suggest that she underscores that these principles are applicable to everyone, no matter their heritage, with this caveat: The difference between appreciation and appropriation is all in the approach. “I’m not encouraging you to do exactly what Indigenous communities do,” she says. “I’m encouraging you to apply these teachings to your own home in a way that reflects your own culture.”.

For example, in a Native worldview, every home should tell a story through its design and decor, Luger explains. Her ancestors painted their tepees with images representing their familial experiences. Similarly, the artwork adorning our walls should feel curated and specific to our identity.

With this in mind, Luger encourages people to stay intimately involved in their home’s design and decorating process, as she’s doing with her family’s in-the-works house on Arizona’s Salt River Reservation (where Collins is from). But you needn’t be building a newly introduced abode to reap the benefits of Indigenous wellness. There are easy, everyday ways to embrace these principles—and they don’t cost a thing.

Sources indicate that starting small is as simple as decluttering one room to reduce sensory overload, letting in more natural sunlight to balance circadian rhythms, opening up your windows for cross-drafting airflow, or carving out an area for movement—even if it’s only a designated stretching space. Next-level applications encompass philosophies like Indigenous minimalism and Native geomancy (auspicious arrangement, akin to feng shui), which are all explained in the book.

It has been revealed that like most Indigenous wisdom, Luger’s advice is pretty intuitive—and yet, it isn’t how we lead our lives today. “We might say that we don’t want to overconsume, but Americans tend to think the bigger the house, the better,” she claims. “Our generation is facing a housing crisis, and we should all embrace smaller living. Not only is it easier to maintain, but it keeps us better connected. That’s what this is ultimately about: interconnection.”.

Here, Luger offers five tips for incorporating Indigenous wellness in your home.

“We’ve always had a respect for the elements—air, fire, water, and earth. Air in particular is considered sacred by most Indigenous communities. Here in the United States, we use air conditioning more than most other countries in the world. It’s a wonderful luxury, but our indoor environments should better reflect the outdoors. Try keeping your windows open for part of the day, no matter the season.”.

It has been revealed that “Doorways are considered portals, which are places of high energy. Growing up, my dad would hang a hand drum or a medicine wheel above our door. It’s a way to bring good energy both for those arriving and for those leaving. Honor the doorway by hanging something that represents the presence of your ancestors and offers both protection and peace.”.

It has been revealed that “It’s a very European idea to have a separate room for everything. In contrast, Indigenous homes historically tended to be more fluid, with communal rooms that foster togetherness. That interconnection is part of our values as Indigenous people. Let at least one space in your home feel more multi-use, where family members can share space.”.

“Many traditional Native structures are round, which represents women, Mother Earth, and our egalitarian values. Indigenous architect Douglas Cardinal (Métis/Blackfoot), who designed the National Museum of the American Indian in Washington, D.C., often expresses this with curvilinear forms. But you don’t have to build a round house or room. Choose a circular dining table, rugs, and pillows rather than square or rectangular ones.”.

According to recent reports, “As Native people, we’ve never lost that closeness to our ancestors, even through colonization and the boarding school era. That spiritual and practical connection to who we are as people is just part of our culture. Whoever you are, wherever you come from—everybody has ancestors they can and should feel connected to. Take time to learn about your culture, and then make your home a reflection of that.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Start by preheating your oven to 325°F.
  • In a recent development, once the brownies are out of the oven, bump up the temperature to 350°F.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Making Thanksgiving dinner is already a Herculean task, but adding dessert to your list of responsibilities can feel like almost too much. This pecan pie makes things easy, giving you the perfect sweet treat to serve after a long, filling dinner without adding too much extra work. This seasonal twist on brownies skips the pie crust and combines two classic desserts in one delicious bite. The syrupy pecan pie topping seeps into the brownies, making them rich, flavorful, and just the right amount of moist.

Start by preheating your oven to 325°F. Grab a 9"x9" baking pan, grease it with cooking spray, and line it with parchment paper. Next, make the brownie batter following the directions on the box. Pour it into the pan and bake until the brownies are just a little underdone—poke the center with a tester, and if you see a few moist crumbs, they’re ready (this should take about 20 minutes). While the brownies are baking, grab a medium bowl and whisk together the corn syrup, brown sugar, butter, molasses, vanilla, and salt until nice and smooth. Add the eggs and whisk until everything’s well combined. Then, stir in the pecans so they’re all coated in the mixture.

In a recent development, once the brownies are out of the oven, bump up the temperature to 350°F. Spoon the pecan mixture over the brownies and spread it out evenly. Pop the pan back in the oven and bake for another 40 to 45 minutes, or until the pecan topping feels springy and has thickened up.

Let the brownies cool down to room temperature first, then pop them in the fridge for about an hour until they’re cold and set.

If you’d like, finish them off with a drizzle of caramel sauce before serving.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

These brownies are the perfect make-ahead dessert for your holiday party. Make them the day before the party, pop them (tightly wrapped or in an airtight container!) into the fridge, and forget about them until ready to serve.
