💡 Key Takeaways
  • Frozen lasagna is a meal for when you just don’t have it in you.
  • For this taste test, we sampled nine varieties of store-bought meat lasagna, cooking each from frozen and concealing the brand names from our tasters.
  • After grumbling our way through several contenders and questioning mankind’s ability to produce a decent supermarket lasagna, Trader Giotto’s Family Style Meat Lasagna restored our faith with a hearty meat sauce and genuinely tasty noodles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Frozen lasagna is a meal for when you just don’t have it in you. For when you need the comfort of pasta, cheese, and sauce, but you’re not prepared to spend hours boiling, sautéing, and layering. And that’s okay. A great frozen lasagna might not hold a candle to BA’s Best Lasagna, but at the very least it should hold together, with distinct layers, plenty of sauce, gooey cheese, and bouncy pasta.

For this taste test, we sampled nine varieties of store-bought meat lasagna, cooking each from frozen and concealing the brand names from our tasters. Three stood out: Trader Joe’s tasted the closest to homemade, Marie Callender’s was a solid backup, and Rao’s was our favorite for a single serving.

After grumbling our way through several contenders and questioning mankind’s ability to produce a decent supermarket lasagna, Trader Giotto’s Family Style Meat Lasagna restored our faith with a hearty meat sauce and genuinely tasty noodles.

Why it won us over: Trader Joe’s frozen lasagna had a homemade vibe. There were distinct layers of pasta, cheese, and meaty sauce. The cheeses—ricotta, mozzarella, Romano, and Parmesan—each pulled their weight. And the noodles had a fresh bounce. “There’s a whole tomato!” exclaimed senior editor Kelsey Jane Youngman upon finding a chunk of diced tomato in her sample. Other tasters complimented the bright aromatics—fennel was prominent, backed up by oregano and basil. The evenly distributed ground beef and pork were the cherry on top.

Trader Giotto’s Family-Style Meat Lasagna, 32-oz.

More great frozen foods at Trader Joe’s →.

It has been revealed that big Lasagna would have you believe you’ll always want to cook a frozen lasagna for a crowd, but sometimes it’s about you and you alone. The 9-oz. Rao’s Made for Home Meat Lasagna is just enough for a single serving—and it doesn’t sacrifice flavor.

In a recent development, why it won us over: Our tasters were excited to report that Rao’s delivered on structure. While other lasagnas were soupy, floppy, or otherwise unbalanced, Rao’s stayed intact, layer on top of layer, as we ate. It had sturdy (but not tough) noodles, a tomato sauce that was full of umami, and herbal accents that didn’t overpower. Some tasters noted a robust beefy flavor; others were more focused on the garlic and onion. Everyone went in for a second bite.

Rao’s Made-for-Home Meat Lasagna, 9-oz.

Maybe you don’t live by a Trader Joe’s—our condolences—and Rao’s proves elusive. You still deserve a serviceable frozen lasagna. Marie Callender’s Lasagna With Meat Sauce offers a sweet and tangy tomato sauce punctuated by well-seasoned meat and noodles that hold their shape.

It has been revealed that why it won us over: This contender avoided many of the pitfalls other brands fell into. It had a solid tomato sauce that was just slightly sweet and tangy, and the meat—both beef and sausage—was flavorful and varied enough in size to give each bite some dynamism. The pasta sheets were springy, not gummy. And while it wasn’t drowning in dairy, there was enough cottage cheese and mozzarella to make itself known.

Marie Callender’s Lasagna With Meat Sauce, 10.5-oz.

We cooked each lasagna from frozen according to its package instructions. While most contenders offered both oven and microwave directions, we stuck with the oven. Tasters sampled each lasagna without knowing which brand they were trying, evaluating each for flavor, texture, and structural integrity. Although Giovanni Rana’s Meat Lasagna is sold refrigerated, we froze it before baking, following the brand’s instructions for cooking from frozen.

Recent findings suggest that the best frozen lasagna should deliver on the fundamentals of structure, flavor, and texture—a tall order for many of our contenders. That meant distinct layers; sheets of pasta that were bouncy, not flimsy; tomato sauce with concentrated flavor and enough body to cling to the pasta; meat that stood out instead of getting lost; and cheese—or many cheeses—that added milky flavor and melty cohesion.

The Secret to Better Gravy Is Already In Your Pantry

💡 Key Takeaways

  • There are few things on the Thanksgiving table that people have stronger opinions about than gravy.
  • Making good turkey gravy isn’t particularly complicated, but getting that deep, rich flavor can be tricky.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

It only takes a splash to give homemade gravy the rich, savory flavor you're after.

There are few things on the Thanksgiving table that people have stronger opinions about than gravy. Everyone seems to have a preferred method, a secret ingredient or a little trick they’ve been using for years. My mom has always sworn by Kitchen Bouquet, a seasoning sauce that gives gravy a little color and kick of flavor. I’m fairly certain she’s had the same bottle since the Reagan administration, and that it only comes out of the cupboard on Thanksgiving.

Making good turkey gravy isn’t particularly complicated, but getting that deep, rich flavor can be tricky. Even with plenty of turkey drippings and a well-made stock, sometimes it needs a little something extra. Over the years, I’ve experimented with all sorts of ways to give my gravy more flavor, but the one I come back to every time is an ingredient I always have in my pantry.

I’ve been adding a splash of soy sauce to my gravy for years, and it’s one of those little tricks that makes a noticeable difference without anyone being able to put their finger on why.

According to recent reports, soy sauce is rich in umami, the deeply savory flavor that makes foods like mushrooms, Parmesan cheese and the golden crust of a steak so satisfying. Adding a little soy sauce to gravy enhances those same savory flavors, giving it a richness that might otherwise require a longer cooking time. It doesn’t make your gravy taste like soy sauce, provided you use a light hand. It just makes it taste more like really good gravy.

Recent findings suggest that worcestershire sauce is another popular addition that works for much the same reason, bringing its own combination of savory flavor, acidity and a hint of sweetness. I’ve tried plenty of different additions over the years, and while they all have their merits, soy sauce remains my favorite. I love the depth it brings without competing with the flavors of the turkey and stock.

The trick with soy sauce is knowing when to add it and, perhaps most importantly, when to stop. You’re not trying to introduce a fresh flavor to your gravy so much as coax a little more out of what’s already there. If someone can identify soy sauce in the finished product, you’ve probably been a bit too generous.

It has been revealed that I always add mine at the end, once the gravy has thickened and I’m happy with the consistency. Start with about a teaspoon for every two cups of gravy, stir it in, and give it a taste. Depending on the stock and drippings you’ve used, that may be all you need. If not, add a little more, tasting as you go.

One thing worth remembering is that soy sauce is salty. Very salty, in fact, so save your final seasoning adjustments until after you’ve added it. This is particularly important if you’re using store-bought stock, which may already contain plenty of sodium. Reduced-sodium soy sauce is an option, too, but I generally use the regular stuff and adjust accordingly.

Recent findings suggest that and don’t save this trick for Thanksgiving! It works beautifully in beef and chicken gravy, too, especially when the pan drippings aren’t quite as flavorful as you’d hoped. A splash of soy sauce won’t make up for a badly made gravy, but it can do an impressive amount of work for an otherwise perfectly respectable one.

Have you used soy sauce in gravy before? Let us know in the comments below!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, chicken Francese is a staple at your favorite Italian restaurants. But sometimes, you don't want to empty your wallet for this classic dinner favorite. That's where I come in! Francese is a preparation (much like Milanese) that can be used with all types of meat and seafood, from shrimp to veal. For chicken, it involves dredging cutlets in flour and beaten egg, creating a pseudo-batter. The cutlets are then pan-fried and made crispy, albeit temporarily. See, chicken Francese is one of those dishes that epitomizes "crispy gone soggy"—a texture sensation that is one of my absolute favorites. In this case, the chicken becomes "soggy" because you finish them by simmering it in a rich, lemony sauce that will knock your socks off.

It might seem strange, but it’s such an iconic flavor/texture combination. Also, it is very easy to make and comes together in under an hour. What could be better?!

In a recent development, place 1 chicken breast on a cutting board. Using a sharp chef’s knife held parallel to the cutting board, slice into the thickest side of the breast, cutting three-quarters of the way through. Fold the top piece back (as if you were opening a book) and continue to cut until the breast is divided into 2 thinner cutlets. Repeat with the remaining chicken breast for a total of 4 cutlets. Working one piece at a time, place each cutlet between 2 sheets of plastic wrap. Using a meat mallet or the bottom of a small heavy skillet, pound the chicken to about 1/4" thick. Season all over with salt and pepper.

It has been revealed that in a shallow dish, beat eggs, garlic powder, and a pinch of salt. Pour 1/2 cup flour into another shallow dish.

It has been revealed that in a large, heavy skillet over medium heat, heat oil. Working in batches, coat cutlets in flour, shaking off excess, then dip into the egg mixture, turning to coat.

Place cutlets in the oil, being careful not to overcrowd the skillet, and cook, turning halfway through, until golden brown, 5 to 7 minutes.

Transfer cutlets to a paper towel-lined plate to drain and season with salt and pepper.

Wipe out the skillet, then heat over medium heat. Add five Tbsp. butter and the remaining one Tbsp. flour, stirring until just beginning to foam and the butter is melted, 3 to 5 minutes. Whisk in wine. Increase heat to medium-high and bring to a boil. Cook, stirring, until slightly reduced, 1 to 2 minutes. Add stock, lemon zest, and lemon juice and return to a boil. Reduce heat to medium and cook, whisking constantly, until the sauce is reduced by about one-third, 3 to 5 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add lemon slices and remaining 1 Tbsp. butter and cook, stirring, until the sauce is glossy, 2 to 3 minutes more.

Return chicken to the sauce and cook, turning halfway through, until heated through, 2 to 3 minutes.

According to recent reports, transfer chicken to a platter and pour the sauce over. Top with lemon slices and parsley.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

In a recent development, if you have any leftovers, store them in the refrigerator in an airtight container for up to 4 days. Luckily, this dish is used to being a tad soggy and lends itself well to being reheated in the microwave.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Half a can of pumpkin leftover pumpkin may not be enough for another pie, but you can definitely put it to use in other fall recipes.

In a recent development, our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Recent findings suggest that fall baking has a way of leaving you with awkward amounts of leftover canned pumpkin. So many recipes call for half a can or some other quantity that leaves you wondering what exactly you’re supposed to do with the rest. You put the open can of Libby’s pumpkin puree in the refrigerator with every intention of using it, yet a few days later, there it is, still waiting for you to come up with a initiative. It’s not as though you can make half a pumpkin pie.

Fortunately, you don’t need much pumpkin to make something wonderful. In fact, one of the best things I’ve made with leftover pumpkin requires less than a cup, a handful of pantry staples and very little effort. It’s the sort of recipe that makes having leftover pumpkin feel less like a nuisance and more like a stroke of good luck.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

These are a little different from the dense, chewy blondies you might be accustomed to. They have golden edges and a wonderfully soft, almost cakey center, thanks in part to the pumpkin puree. Brown sugar gives them their rich, buttery sweetness, while cinnamon and pumpkin pie spice make them taste unmistakably like fall. The recipe lists the chocolate chips as optional, though I’d argue strongly in favor of including them. Chocolate and pumpkin are excellent together, and the little pockets of melted chocolate are delicious against all those warm spices.

The pumpkin blondies also almost suspiciously easy to make. Everything comes together in one bowl, using ingredients you probably already have on hand. There’s no frosting to fuss with, no dough to chill and no pie crust to negotiate. Just spread the batter into a 9-inch pan and bake it for 25 to 30 minutes. You’ll have a dozen soft, spiced bars that are equally at home on a Thanksgiving dessert table as they are next to your morning coffee.

It has been revealed that best of all, the recipe calls for just 1/2 cup of canned pumpkin. That’s a particularly convenient amount when you’ve got the remains of another baking project taking up residence in the refrigerator. And if you have a full cup left, making a double batch seems like a perfectly reasonable course of action.

And there’s no reason to limit pumpkin to sweet recipes. A few spoonfuls can add body and richness to soups, pasta dishes and risotto, especially when paired with sage, garlic and Parmesan. Just be sure you’re using plain pumpkin puree rather than pumpkin pie filling, which already contains sugar and spices and isn’t as versatile.

In a recent development, if you’re not quite ready to commit to another pumpkin project, you can always freeze your leftover pumpkin puree. That way, the next time a recipe calls for an odd amount of pumpkin, you’ll have some on hand.

  • The class, Lobster 101, was led by Bon Appétit manager of audience strategy Carly Westerfield and Krista Tripp, founder of Aphrodite Oysters in South Thomaston, Maine.
  • It has been revealed that tripp explained that her oysters, cultivated in the cold tidal waters of the Lower Weskeag River, take three years to reach maturity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Attendees of Bon Appétit Live experienced a taste of Maine through a hands-on lobster cooking class and a demonstration of wild blueberry cornmeal shortcakes, both hosted by Visit Maine.

The class, Lobster 101, was led by Bon Appétit manager of audience strategy Carly Westerfield and Krista Tripp, founder of Aphrodite Oysters in South Thomaston, Maine. Attendees learned how to break down a whole, steamed two-pound Maine lobster and transform the meat into a rich, creamy lobster dip—ideal for holiday hosting. Guests then enjoyed the fruits of their labor, sampling the freshly made dip with Ritz crackers before tasting oysters.

It has been revealed that tripp explained that her oysters, cultivated in the cold tidal waters of the Lower Weskeag River, take three years to reach maturity. Known for their distinctive fluted shells, they offer a briny, mineral-rich flavor balanced by a mellow sweetness.

It has been revealed that after years as a lobster harvester, Tripp started Aphrodite Oysters to diversify her lobster business and has since shifted her focus to oyster cultivation full-time. She’s come to appreciate the many environmental benefits of farming and consuming them. Her oysters filter up to 50 gallons of water a day, taking in nitrogen and sequestering some for their growing shells. “Eating an oyster is contributing to the environment,” she declared. Indeed, water test scores have improved at her farm, demonstrating that bivalves help create a healthier ecosystem.

According to recent reports, before the end of the class, a few brave attendees volunteered to shuck their first oysters. Krista guided them through the process, demonstrating how to safely do it at home by protecting the hand holding the shellfish with a towel and gently working the knife into the hinge until the shell released. The well-earned reward was another taste of the Penobscot Bay, as fresh and pristine as the waters themselves.

Later in the day, guests in the Demo Kitchen were treated to Cornmeal Shortcakes with Blueberry Compote, prepared by Bon Appétit senior Test Kitchen editor Jesse Szewczyk. The compote featured wild Maine blueberries from Brodis Blueberries, a multigenerational family farm in Hope, Maine, stewarded by Ron Howard and his family. Howard joined Szewczyk for the demo, where he shared that 99% of the wild blueberries grown and harvested in the United States come from Maine. Attendees learned that they have been growing since the end of the Ice Age, when the tenacious plants, fortified by ericoid mycorrhizal fungi, began to grow and colonize the newly exposed land as glaciers retreated. An key food source for Native Americans, wild blueberries were valued by Indigenous communities for their nutritional benefits well before the modern superfood movement.

Sources indicate that speaking passionately, Howard discussed the many challenges facing Maine growers, including tariffs and currency exchange fluctuations, particularly the impact of a stronger Canadian dollar. Like many Maine farmers, the family has had to get creative. Howard invested in newly introduced equipment, including a more efficient type of harvester that allowed the business to scale up and sell to retailers. They created a shelf-stable, freeze-dried product with no added ingredients, allowing them to ship their product beyond the local area. Howard and his son started a distillery, where they use wild blueberries to make an eau de vie and vodka. They have also begun hosting a Wild Blueberry Weekend, opening the doors to the farm and educating the public about the unique benefits of their crop and their growing process.

Carolann Ouellette, director of the Maine Office of Tourism, emphasized that visiting Maine and engaging with local growers and producers such as Howard and Tripp was the best way to experience the state’s diverse bounty. “The relationship between people and nature is inseparable, and stewardship is an important part of the state's identity,” she reflected. Ouellette grew up in New Jersey but relocated to Maine over 40 years ago. Her family used to visit Maine when she was a child, and she recalls those experiences vividly: “As a kid, I remember, when you get to Maine, you can smell the pie or smell the spruce.” It’s those potent memories that drew her to the state permanently, a place she described as “filled with hardworking, welcoming communities that depend on one another.”.

A few years ago, Visit Maine began placing greater emphasis on the state’s culinary identity. Ouellette noted that awareness of Maine as a food destination continues to grow, “Sea to table with local ingredients is what we were doing before it was a thing.” Beyond the lobster, Visit Maine has been intentional about showcasing the breadth of the state’s agricultural, fishing, and heritage industries. Apples, potatoes, kelp, seaweed, and grains are just a few of the local ingredients featured in Visit Maine’s newsletter and Bountiful Plate video series, which highlights food and beverage producers throughout the state. Ouellette noted that Maine’s food culture is more diverse than many people expect, and its abundance of local products has attracted an interesting mix of exceptional chefs, many of whom are deeply embedded in their communities. Ouellette cited Tripp’s practice of personally delivering her oysters to local restaurants as an example of how the hospitality ecosystem is interconnected.

Most important, Ouellette emphasized that sustainability and stewardship are central to the state’s approach to its food systems and relationship with the landscape. “You can’t get much fresher than food in Maine,” she concluded.

Bon Appétit LIVE 2026 was sponsored by East Fork, Visit Maine, and S.Pellegrino® Sparkling Natural Mineral Water with thanks to All-Clad, As Ever, Bachan’s, Better Sour, Field Tech giant, Floura, Gimme Seaweed, GOODLES, Graza, Hedley & Bennett, Kann Coffee, Material Kitchen, Misen, Owala®, Rip Van, SharkNinja, and Staub.

According to recent reports, the holiday season is on the horizon, and Costco is celebrating with plenty of festive foods in every corner of the warehouse. Aside from the obligatory pumpkin pie, you can find party-approved appetizers, cozy bakery treats, and plenty of fall-forward snacks.

In a recent development, I spend all year keeping tabs on the latest and greatest products to hit Costco shelves. And as someone who writes about Costco for a living, I have a hot take: The food at the warehouse right now is the best it’s been all year.

Here’s what’s available this November—there are some treats you don’t want to miss.

The viral sensation has officially hit Costco. The Dot Cakes is a bakery on Long Island, Newly introduced York, that exploded in popularity this summer thanks to its signature dessert: a single-serving cake in a cup covered in a generous layer of nonpareil sprinkles. Now, instead of waiting in long lines or trying to recreate it at home, Costco members can buy a six-pack of the real thing.

It has been revealed that each box includes both chocolate and vanilla cake, and both flavors are perfectly nostalgic. They taste like the best-ever birthday cake from your childhood, and the crunch of the sprinkles makes the experience even more fun.

It has been revealed that it admittedly takes a lot for us to get excited about grapes—but these are worth the hype. Shine Muscat is a premium variety from Japan, famous for its large, sweet, seedless fruit. Many of the ones sold in the U.S. are imported from East Asia, including these Korean grapes now available at Costco.

I’ve had the pleasure of trying the grapes in smoothie form at a Costco food court in Seoul, but the real thing is even better. Our editors couldn’t stop eating them and compared the flavor to a plum or lychee. And at $10.99, they’re a fun upgrade that costs only a bit more than standard table grapes.

Want takeout flavors without takeout prices? Costco is now selling a noodle stir-fry kit that can feed the whole family for around $15. Each tray includes crispy breaded chicken pieces, yakisoba noodles, vegetables, and a sweet-and-savory sauce.

In a recent development, the meal is super easy to put together: Just crisp up the chicken in the oven or air fryer, then heat everything else in a pan. Costco is generous with the chicken and noodles, so the kit can provide at least four substantial servings. But if you need just one reason to add it to your cart, do it for the sauce. It’s just sweet enough with the slightest hint of spice.

Recent findings suggest that cabot Creamery has already combined its cheddar with popcorn, but this fall-forward version balances the sharp, salty flavor with a bit of sweetness. Each bag includes two types of popcorn: one seasoned with Cabot’s famous Seriously Sharp Cheddar and another with a maple syrup-flavored coating. Both are delicious on their own, but together? Magic happens.

It has been revealed that the salty-sweet combo really works here, reminding us of those large popcorn tins with three different compartments, except everything’s mixed together. Your holiday movie marathon needs a bag of this.

According to recent reports, fans of the Kirkland Signature peanut butter pretzels need to grab this sweet treat. Jif’s Snappers combine mini pretzels, the brand’s creamy peanut butter, and a drizzle of milk chocolate. We love that there’s a higher peanut butter-to-pretzel ratio than with Kirkland Signature's version (and the PB is much softer). This snack has everything: It’s salty, sweet, crunchy, creamy, and impossible to put down.

According to recent reports, step aside, Snap, Crackle, and Pop. The brand Cloud 9 has upgraded the cereal-based sweet with flavors inspired by mango sticky rice. Each bar combines puffed rice with dried mango, coconut milk, and shredded coconut. And the Delish team agrees: This is arguably the best snack Costco has sold all year. It’s loaded with mango, lightly sweet, and full of interesting textures. Buy a bag and thank us later.

In just a few years, Swedish candy went from an uncommon novelty to a permanent fixture in the candy aisle. Now, Costco carries a Rolling Pin variety pack that includes sour gummies and foam candy (a Swedish staple with a marshmallow-like texture).

Sources indicate that this 30-ounce bag features a wide variety of chewy textures and fruity flavors. If you’re just now dipping your toes into the world of Swedish candy, this is a great (and affordable) way to start.

Need fall breakfast inspo? Look no further. The newest addition to the Costco bakery is this maple pecan coffee cake, which is loaded with cream cheese, pecans, and maple flavor. The cake is topped with a crumbly pecan butter streusel and drizzled with the same icing Costco uses on its danishes.

It has been revealed that each coffee cake is $15, but it’s arguably worth much more given its sheer size. This thing is a behemoth—it’s tall and absolutely loaded with toppings. There’s also a thick layer of filling in the center that tastes nearly identical to pecan pie filling.

It has been revealed that baked brie is a party showstopper, and Costco now carries a kit with everything you need in one convenient package. Stonemill Kitchens’ kit includes puff pastry, a wheel of brie, chopped pecans, and caramel apple cranberry chutney. You’ll need to assemble it yourself before you throw it in the oven, but the instructions couldn’t be simpler. The puff pastry even comes with a sheet of parchment paper to protect your baking sheet!

And the results are straight-up showstopping. The melty, creamy brie pairs perfectly with the pastry and toppings. The chutney, despite the caramel in the name, isn’t too sweet—it adds just the right amount of festive holiday flavor. It’s so good that News and Features Editor Amanda Mactas even did a happy dance after taking a bite.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Senate Republicans are preparing to make the transition from the majority to the minority — and their top leaders will seek to retain their positions in the 120th Congress, even after the political drubbing they endured Tuesday night.
  • Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., will run for minority leader during next week’s GOP leadership elections, a spokesperson for his office said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that senate Majority Leader John Thune, seen here at the Capitol on Sept. 15, is hoping to bounce back from Tuesday’s losses and “not stand idly by.” (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Senate Republicans are preparing to make the transition from the majority to the minority — and their top leaders will seek to retain their positions in the 120th Congress, even after the political drubbing they endured Tuesday night.

Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., will run for minority leader during next week’s GOP leadership elections, a spokesperson for his office said.

After enjoying a 53-47 majority, he will face a very different chamber next year, with Democrats looking to control between 54 to 56 seats, depending on how the dust settles.

In a post on X just after midnight on election night, as the extent of the losses became clear, Thune wrote, “Over the last two years, Senate Republicans have put up a strong record of accomplishment that’s created safer streets, more money in Americans’ pockets, and fresh opportunities for families and businesses to get ahead.”.

“As we head into 2027, Senate Republicans will not stand idly by as the far-left, socialist wing of the Democrat Party attempts to unwind everything we’ve done,” he remarked. “Thankfully, we still have President Trump in the White House, and we’ll work with him to stop the worst impulses of Democrat extremism.”.

Recent findings suggest that thune, 65, has served as the majority leader for nearly two years since winning a three-way race to succeed Mitch McConnell of Kentucky as the chamber’s top Republican. That was a spot McConnell had held since taking his party’s leadership reins in early 2007, making him the longest-serving Senate party leader in history, counting his time in both the minority and the majority.

Thune at times had a tumultuous relationship with the president as Trump pushed legislation, like the voter-ID related bill known as the SAVE America Act, that never had a chance of passing the chamber.

Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso of Wyoming is expected to seek his current role in the minority as well.

Recent findings suggest that “Republicans had a tough night last night. We lost great Senators in hard races,” he mentioned on X Wednesday afternoon. “There are clear lessons to be learned from the results.”.

“We should listen to what voters unmistakably remarked last night,” Barrasso, 74, said. “In the Senate, we will aggressively oppose terrible ideas that drive our country toward the socialism Democrats embraced. Our commitment is to common sense. And our focus should not waiver from the top priority of driving down prices that have remained stubbornly too high.”.

“I’m here for the fight,” he added.

The leadership elections for Senate Republicans will take place on Tuesday, Nov. 10, at 9 a.m. in the Old Senate Chamber.

So far, no one has publicly come forward to challenge Thune, and his fellow Republican colleagues were already coalescing around him ahead of the midterms.

Recent findings suggest that florida Sen. Rick Scott, who ran against Thune in 2024 and is a friend of the president’s, stated in September then he was not planning on challenging him again.

In a recent development, sen. James Lankford, R-Okla., is expected to seek a repeat as vice chair of the Republican conference, while Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.V., is set to run again for Republican Policy Committee chair, according to people familiar with their prepares.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are only so many dishes you can make in your oven on Thanksgiving, so we’ve made it easy for you with a no-bake stuffing that doesn’t require taking up oven space. Instead, we use a slow cooker that’ll help you whip up your stuffing alongside the stars of the show (roast turkey and pumpkin pie, obviously!). While you buzz around the kitchen, the slow cooker will cook your stuffing for you — resulting in a delicious Thanksgiving side dish waiting for you to serve up.

Industry observers note that arrange a rack in the center of the oven and preheat it to 350°. Spread bread on a baking sheet. Bake the bread, tossing it halfway through, until it is crispy and feels dry. The edges should just be starting to turn golden, which should take about 15 to 20 minutes. Meanwhile, melt butter in a large skillet over medium heat. When melted, add celery, onion, and herbs. Season with salt and pepper and cook until the onions are translucent, about 7 minutes. Remove from heat and let cool.

Grease your Crock-Pot bowl and add the toasted bread. Pour the vegetable mixture, eggs, broth, and parsley over the bread. Toss to combine and cover.

Cook on low for 3 to 4 hours, stirring after 2 hours have passed. Garnish with parsley before serving.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Thanksgiving is hectic, we get it. This is the perfect dish to set aside while you prepare everything else. After the 3 hour cook time, switch the pot to the "keep warm" setting—just give it a stir every 30 minutes or so to make sure the bread around the edges doesn't dry out. If the stuffing is ready hours before dinner time, you can add up to ¼ cup of broth every few hours to keep things hydrated.

Serious bakers will appreciate the hefty, high-quality materials in this 6-piece set. It's also gloriously nonstick.

Recent findings suggest that when I got married a few years ago, I put a cohesive bakeware set on my registry to replace years of mismatched Goodwill finds. While it worked well for a few months, within a year it began to show serious signs of wear and tear. Baked-on grease stains, rust spots and even warping had me in the market for a newly introduced bakeware set much sooner than I expected.

So, when I heard that my favorite cookware brand was releasing a bakeware set promising a sturdy, nonstick experience, I jumped at the chance to test it. Here’s everything you need to know about the latest HexClad bakeware line, including my honest thoughts after two months of testing.

HexClad’s fresh hybrid bakeware set features six core pieces:.

It merges the benefits of stainless steel and nonstick into one easy-to-clean package. HexClad’s “hybrid technology” combines hexagonal steel peaks with nonstick valleys to improve heat circulation and release after baking. In other words, this bakeware browns your food evenly without it sticking to the pan.

Other features include ergonomic handles and a 2.5mm tri-ply construction to prevent warping. It’s also oven-safe up to 900 degrees Fahrenheit and dishwasher-safe. You can even use your favorite metal spatula or tongs without scratching the surface. And, like all HexClad cookware, it comes with a lifetime warranty against manufacturer’s defects.

I’ll admit: I’m already a big fan of HexClad. I reach for the brand’s skillets and knives daily, and I’ve hoped for years that they would release a bakeware line.

So, when the offer to test the latest set landed in my inbox, I couldn’t say no. But would it live up to the hype I’d built up in my head? I put all six pieces through the paces for two months to find out.

Katie Bandurski For Taste Of Home.

It has been revealed that like all HexClad products I’ve tried, the bakeware packaging experience is impeccable. The set arrived securely in one significant box, separated with foam. Each piece was also wrapped in a protective dust bag, which is a nice touch.

Immediately, I was awed by the construction of these pans. Just by touch, I could tell they were high quality. I grabbed my food scale to compare the weight of the HexClad pans to my go-to carbon steel pans. The HexClad options weighed more than twice as much as my existing bakeware. Talk about heft!

In a recent development, now, some folks might not appreciate that extra weight—especially since the pans get even heavier when full of food. But as someone who often replaces her bakeware every few years due to warping or rusting, I’m excited for a sturdier option. I hope this is the last set of bakeware I ever need to order.

As a final step, I washed each piece and got ready to bake!

Katie Bandurski For Taste Of Home.

According to recent reports, one of my favorite things to make with sourdough discard is a big loaf of focaccia bread, so that was a natural first test in the 13×9 HexClad pan. Focaccia dough is sticky, but a generous coating of olive oil helps prevent it from gluing to the pan. Still, after proofing and baking my bread as usual, I was impressed that the final product pulled slightly away from the pan’s edges, making it slide out with complete ease. The bottom and edges got nice and toasty brown, too.

In a recent development, A few nights later, I used the same focaccia dough to make a focaccia pizza. Same sticky dough, made even stickier with tomato sauce, cheese and toppings. Plus, since it’s such a rich dish, I cut back on the amount of olive oil I used. Despite all the add-ons, this focaccia baked and released from the pan just as beautifully as the first loaf.

Katie Bandurski For Taste Of Home.

In a recent development, next, I made a chocolate layer cake with the 9-inch round cake pans. Now, I’m typically a ride-or-die parchment paper user. I find cutting out perfectly sized parchment circles a tedious task, but it’s worthwhile insurance against my cakes sticking. But to truly put the HexClad pans’ nonstick properties to the test, I skipped adding parchment and simply greased my pans with a little butter and flour.

After baking and 10 minutes of cooling came the moment of truth: Would it stick? Luckily, no! Both cakes released with minimal effort. I simply ran a butter knife around the rim of the cake before using the cooling rack to flip ’em out. It’s a good thing, too, because this was my dad’s birthday cake!

Katie Bandurski For Taste Of Home.

My nonstick tests continued with the 8×8 square pan when I whipped up a batch of candy bar blondies. These blondies used an assortment of leftover Halloween candy, so I thought for sure the caramel ooze from a Baby Ruth bar would cause some issues. But nope! Even without parchment paper, treats slipped right out of the pan.

Sources indicate that but how does HexClad bakeware perform with healthier treats? For one final test, I baked a completely made-up “brownie” recipe with pumpkin seed butter, applesauce, molasses and cocoa. It was a gooey, chocolaty mess by the time I put it in the pan, yet it baked and released beautifully.

Finally, I put the baking sheet to the test.

Now, I already own the HexClad pizza steel, which I use almost daily. It’s my go-to for everything from frozen pizza to galettes to roasted broccoli, and I find that it works even better than an air fryer to yield crisp, golden brown bakes. I’ve said on many occasions that it’s my all-time favorite piece of bakeware, especially for savory foods.

Both the pizza steel and baking sheet utilize HexClad’s tri-ply construction with an aluminum core and TerraBond nonstick coating. The former is a jet black colorway, while the baking sheet is gray.

Industry observers note that across the board, I found the baking sheet could handle every task I threw its way—including roasting a spaghetti squash. Oftentimes, I find myself scrubbing for what feels like days after roasting squash and scouring off that sticky, burnt-on residue. The HexClad pan cleaned with a simple swipe from a damp paper towel.

It has been revealed that during testing, I found the bottoms and handles of the HexClad bakeware smudged a bit. After all, it is made of stainless steel. This didn’t bother me, and it was easy to clean by handwashing and drying it immediately. Over time, I may need to use a more abrasive regimen to clean stainless steel.

Sources indicate that while the HexClad pans are very sturdy, you should still let them fully cool before washing. Don’t throw a hot pan directly in the sink. The pans are also dishwasher-safe, though handwashing is recommended. (And honestly, so easy thanks to the nonstick coating.).

In a recent development, across the board, I’m impressed with the new HexClad bakeware line. I hope we see even more pieces in the future, like a muffin tin and loaf pan. Only time will tell exactly how it holds up, but from what I’ve experienced so far, this set really is designed to last a lifetime. (And I’ll be continuing to long-term test the set, and patch this review accordingly.).

In a recent development, ready to take your bakes to the next level? This all-in-one set is great for beginners and pros alike.

Industry observers note that you can shop the full 6-piece bakeware set on the HexClad website for $399. Select styles, like 2-pack sets of small and medium baking sheets, are also available.

In a recent development, inspired by the iconic egg and sausage sandwich on a pancake bun, this breakfast casserole is cheesy and just a smidge sweet from the brushing of maple butter at the very end. Destined for holiday brunch tables everywhere and best enjoyed while you’re still in pajamas, this cozy bake will feed a full house. (Don’t be surprised if you find yourself making it again long after the last guest leaves though!).

More high-protein breakfast recipes here.

According to recent reports, place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Lightly coat a 13x9" baking dish with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Whisk 2½ cups (313 g) all-purpose flour, ¼ cup (50 g) sugar, 2 Tbsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Set aside.

Recent findings suggest that cook 2 lb. breakfast sausage, casings removed if needed, in a large skillet set over medium-high heat, stirring and breaking into small pieces with a wooden spoon, until browned and cooked through, 10–12 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer sausage to a small plate, leaving fat behind. Pour fat into a heatproof measuring glass. You want ½ cup fat; spoon out any excess or pour in vegetable oil as needed if you don’t have enough. Stir 2 large eggs and 2 cups whole milk into fat. Let sausage cool slightly, then crumble into small, even pieces with your hands.

Sources indicate that pour fat mixture into reserved dry ingredients and stir until just combined and no large dry pockets of flour remain (batter may be thin and lumpy; it’ll be fine). Set aside ½ cup sausage and ½ cup cheese from 8 oz. sharp yellow cheddar, coarsely grated (about 2 cups), for topping, then add remaining sausage and cheddar to batter and stirring until evenly distributed.

Scrape batter into prepared baking dish and evenly scatter reserved sausage and cheese over. Bake casserole until top springs back when gently pressed with your finger and a tester inserted into the center comes out with just a few moist crumbs attached, 20–30 minutes.

Sources indicate that just before casserole is done, heat 2 Tbsp. pure maple syrup and 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a small skillet over medium, stirring occasionally, until butter is melted, about 2 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that brush maple butter over casserole and let cool 10 minutes. Cut into squares. Serve with more maple syrup and butter alongside.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries addresses an election night watch party in Washington on Tuesday after Democrats were projected to win the House. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Democrats were savoring their midterm election rout Wednesday after decisively flipping both the House and Senate.

Sources indicate that “Last night was beyond even our largest expectations of what could happen,” Arizona Rep. Greg Stanton mentioned on a press call.

Hakeem Jeffries, the top House Democrat in line to become the first Black speaker, predicted Democrats would hold at least 255 seats next year, which would be the largest majority for either party since Democrats won 257 seats in 2008.

In the Senate, the Democratic Caucus was poised to hold at least 54 seats after seismic red-state gains, with two key races too close to call.

Recent findings suggest that “What we have now seen is a generational remake of the Senate map that is going to change America not only now but on into the future,” Charles E. Schumer, the chamber’s top Democrat, mentioned Wednesday.

Here are six takeaways from the midterm elections:.

Industry observers note that democratic gains were so sweeping that both ideological wings of the party had plenty to celebrate. The moderate Blue Dogs more than doubled their current membership, with at least 22 Blue Dog PAC-endorsed candidates winning Tuesday. Meanwhile, the Congressional Progressive Caucus anticipated at least 25 new members.

For House progressives, swing-seat wins in Michigan and California were signs that their candidates’ message resonated in battleground races and that Democrats should move to implement those progressive ideas next year.

“Substantial majorities can get big things done,” Congressional Progressive Caucus Chair Greg Casar said on a Wednesday press call.

In a recent development, illinois Rep. Brad Schneider, the chair of the center-left Fresh Democrat Coalition, told reporters he had a strong relationship with Casar and envisioned different factions of the party working together.

According to recent reports, “It doesn’t matter what you call your idea. If your idea is going to help us move the ball forward, join us at the table,” Schneider mentioned.

Army veteran Cait Conley, who was leading GOP Rep. Mike Lawler in a race that remained uncalled Wednesday afternoon, said she’d been open about having differences with incoming New York Democrats aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America. But she said Democrats across the political spectrum needed to prioritize “real solutions for the American people.”.

“If we don’t make that our priority, if we don’t show that that is more key than anything else … then I think the voters are going to show us in 2028 that they’re not going to accept that,” she said on the Newly introduced Dems press call.

While the president cast a shadow over the entire midterm map, three of his marquee candidates were among the night’s biggest busts.

It has been revealed that trump was behind appointed South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham every step of the way, helping her win a contested primary to replace her late brother, Lindsey Graham, on the ballot. But Graham lost to Democrat Annie Andrews in a stunning upset. In North Carolina, Trump had publicly urged Michael Whatley to run for the state’s open seat. But the former Republican National Committee chairman lost to Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper by 20 points. And most significantly, in Texas, Trump elevated scandal-plagued state Attorney General Ken Paxton over Republican incumbent Sen. John Cornyn. But the president’s support wasn’t enough to stave off a general election drubbing at the hands of Democrat James Talarico.

Sources indicate that even Rep. Julia Letlow, Trump’s pick for Senate in deep-red Louisiana, won her election by less than 2 points.

Industry observers note that republicans in seven states successfully embarked on a mid-decade redistricting spree aimed at boosting GOP candidates. But the push couldn’t overcome the political headwinds that battered the Republican brand. In California, where Democrats introduced a redistricting push in response to the Texas redraw, the new map proved more beneficial: Democrats are poised to flip at least four seats they redrew in their favor.

Republican Alex Mealer was the heavy favorite to win a redrawn Houston-area seat that Trump would have carried by 20 points. She raised $2.8 million to first-time Democratic candidate Leticia Gutierrez’ $215,000. Yet Gutierrez won the contest by double digits. In an interview on MS NOW, Gutierrez stated her campaign proved that “you don’t need money to buy a congressional race.” She wasn’t the only under-the-radar House contender to pull off an unexpected victory Tuesday. In North Carolina, several low-profile and under-funded Democrats appear poised to pull off unlikely upsets, though the races remain too close to call.

Democrats have chased the dream of a blue Texas for more than 30 years — and always came up short. Until Tuesday. The party notched a series of stunning wins in the nation’s most consequential red state — from Talarico’s decisive victory in the Senate contest to winning several key House races to capturing the governor’s mansion. Democrats seized every elected statewide position on the ballot and flipped the state House, according to The Associated Press. “They noted it could not be done,’’ Democratic Rep. Christian Menefee told supporters Tuesday night. “We did it.”.

Democrats made deep gains in red states and districts across the country, flipping Senate seats in Texas, South Carolina and Kansas, while races in Alaska and Mississippi remained too close to call. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis called it “probably the political worst case scenario for a midterm election.”.

But Democrats didn’t appear convinced that their brand had completely rebounded from deep losses two years ago, saying they had work to do over the next two years.

“Many of the folks who voted for us yesterday, of course, are still skeptical,” Schumer said.

Similarly, Casar and Rep. Pramila Jayapal both warned Democrats not to assume that Tuesday’s wins had resolved the party’s branding challenges.

“We still are not particularly popular as a Democratic Party across the country,” Jayapal told reporters. “I think we’ve got a shot to show that we can deliver on the kind of bold populist change that people ran on and won on.”.

Nina Heller contributed to this report.

#7367. Latest Update: Is Pink Turkey Safe to Eat?

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (828 w)
📖 Baca

Latest Update: Is Pink Turkey Safe to Eat?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (828 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tasteofhome

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pink turkey doesn't necessarily mean your Thanksgiving feast is ruined.
  • Sources indicate that I’ll never forget the Thanksgiving when I was convinced I’d ruined the holiday for everyone.
  • Industry observers note that imagine my surprise and horror when I carved that gorgeously browned roast turkey and discovered it was pink inside.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Pink turkey doesn't necessarily mean your Thanksgiving feast is ruined. Here's how to know if your bird is safe to eat so you can stay calm and turkey on.

Sources indicate that I’ll never forget the Thanksgiving when I was convinced I’d ruined the holiday for everyone. I wasn’t an experienced cook at the time, and it was one of my first attempts at making a Thanksgiving turkey. I used a helpful guide for how long to cook a turkey and even invested in a meat thermometer to be sure it reached at least 165°F. It looked great, and I was so proud!

Industry observers note that imagine my surprise and horror when I carved that gorgeously browned roast turkey and discovered it was pink inside. I was so nervous my guests would assume the turkey was undercooked. I didn’t know then that pink turkey can be perfectly safe to eat—as long as it’s cooked to that vital internal temperature.

Cooked turkey can look pink for a few reasons that have nothing to do with doneness, including the age of the bird, how it’s prepared and natural pigmentation.

Industry observers note that “Poultry naturally can have a pink hue,” says Heidi Diestel of turkey farm Diestel Family Ranch in Sonora, California. “The legs and thighs have more of the natural pigments that give meat its darker color. Those pigments, along with changes that happen during cooking, can leave some pink even when the turkey is fully cooked.”.

The pigments Heidi refers to are proteins called myoglobin and cytochrome c. The more of these proteins the meat has, the darker it will be. Older animals tend to have more proteins, and therefore darker pigmentation, as do any regularly exercised muscles. That explains why leg meat is darker than breast meat, as turkeys spend the bulk of their days walking and running.

Cooking can also cause a chemical reaction with these proteins that contributes to a pink color. Smoked turkey often stays pink from the reaction of the meat to the smoke inside the grill or smoker, but even oven-roasted turkey can have a pinkish hue. Myoglobin usually turns white during the cooking process, but cytochrome c is more resistant to heat and can maintain a pink blush.

Grace Natoli Sheldon for Taste of Home.

Using a meat thermometer is the best way to know if your turkey is safe to eat.

According to recent reports, poultry is considered safe to eat when it meets a cooking temperature of at least 165°. However, the Taste of Home Test Kitchen recommends cooking the leg and thigh meat to 170° for the best texture. For stuffed turkeys, don’t forget to take the temperature of the stuffing as well, which should reach at least 165° when the thermometer is inserted in the center of the stuffing.

If your turkey comes embedded with a round plastic doneness indicator that pops when the turkey is ready, don’t use that as an absolute; they are notoriously inaccurate.

To check if the turkey is done, insert the thermometer in a thick, meaty area, making sure the tip doesn’t touch any bones (bone will show a higher temperature).

Sources indicate that if you’re using a probe thermometer that you insert before cooking, double-check its position once the turkey has been cooking for a while. Meat contracts as it cooks, so it may no longer be in the best spot.

In a recent development, if any part of your turkey is below 165°, you should continue cooking the turkey until all parts reach a safe temperature. It’s common for the thermometer to register different temperatures in different areas, since white meat cooks at a faster rate than dark meat. Don’t be tempted to cut off the parts that aren’t ready and return only them to the oven. It’ll increase the risk that undercooked juices will run onto your cutting board and contaminate the properly cooked turkey.

According to recent reports, if the legs and thighs aren’t done but the breast is, I like to baste the white meat and loosely tent it with foil to try and lock in as much moisture as possible. If the dark meat is ready but the breast needs more time, there’s no need to sweat it. Dark meat has enough natural fat and moisture that it won’t become dry with a little extra time in the oven.

You should never knowingly eat undercooked turkey. According to the CDC, undercooked turkey can contain harmful bacteria, like Salmonella, Clostridium perfringens or Campylobacter, that can cause foodborne illnesses.

There’s also a risk of bacteria if the turkey isn’t thawed or prepared correctly. Give yourself plenty of time to thaw a frozen turkey, either in the refrigerator or in a cold water bath. Also, make sure to keep the counter or cutting board where you’re prepping the turkey clean and sanitized before and after handling the raw bird.

Latest Update: Which Thanksgiving Foods Belong in the Same Bite?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (794 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tasteofhome

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that some Thanksgiving food combinations are obvious.
  • For years, my kids refused to let any two foods touch on their plates.
  • Recent findings suggest that of course, plenty of adults also have strong opinions about which Thanksgiving foods should mingle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Recent findings suggest that some Thanksgiving food combinations are obvious. Others might earn you some questioning looks at the dinner table.

For years, my kids refused to let any two foods touch on their plates. I found this particularly maddening at Thanksgiving. There’s an entire table of food to fit onto a single plate and only so much room to negotiate separate territories for the mashed potatoes and green bean casserole! Thankfully, they’re a little more accommodating these days and, like me, have come to appreciate the occasional overlap between dishes.

Recent findings suggest that of course, plenty of adults also have strong opinions about which Thanksgiving foods should mingle. There are those who insist on keeping every dish separate, those who permit a little gravy to stray onto the stuffing but draw the line at cranberry sauce, and those who deliberately assemble the perfect combination on every forkful. Then there’s always the unhinged relative who stirs the entire contents of their plate into a single, gravy-saturated mass and eats it with the serene confidence of someone who has never once questioned their choices.

According to recent reports, personally, I’m firmly in favor of combining foods, although I do believe a little discretion is in order. Thanksgiving dinner offers a wonderful assortment of rich, savory and tart flavors, and knowing which ones to bring together is part of what makes the meal so satisfying. There’s a culinary reason that cranberry sauce belongs alongside turkey, and that stuffing and mashed potatoes are particularly good together. And once you understand why those combinations work, you can start building some excellent bites of your own.

Absolutely. In fact, some of the most familiar food pairings are built around the idea that one ingredient can supply something another lacks. Think of a rich cut of meat served with a sharp, acidic sauce, or a creamy dish finished with something crisp. Neither component is necessarily lacking on its own, but the contrast makes the combination much more interesting.

The same principle applies to Thanksgiving foods. Acidity helps balance richness, sweetness can temper salty or intensely savory flavors, and a change in texture can make a forkful more interesting. It’s not particularly complicated, but there’s a difference between understanding why two foods complement each other and simply hoping for the best.

Some combinations are simply better than others, though saying so at Thanksgiving dinner may invite more opinions than you bargained for.

Sources indicate that turkey and cranberry sauce: There’s a reason this pairing has endured for generations. Turkey, particularly the breast meat, is relatively mild, and the tartness of cranberry sauce gives it a welcome lift. It’s also an excellent remedy for turkey that’s spent a little too long in the oven, a situation that has befallen even the most conscientious Thanksgiving cooks.

Mashed potatoes, stuffing and gravy: I consider this one of Thanksgiving’s greatest achievements. The smooth, buttery potatoes and herbaceous stuffing are excellent together, and a generous spoonful of gravy makes the whole arrangement even better. There’s nothing particularly subtle about it, but Thanksgiving dinner isn’t generally celebrated for its subtlety.

Recent findings suggest that sweet potatoes and turkey: The natural sweetness of roasted sweet potatoes makes a lovely contrast to savory turkey, particularly the richer dark meat. A traditional sweet potato casserole can work, too, although I draw the line somewhere around the marshmallow topping. I have nothing against marshmallows, but I prefer to encounter them after dinner.

Green bean casserole and mashed potatoes: These are two of my Thanksgiving essentials, and I see no reason they shouldn’t share a fork. The creamy green beans and buttery potatoes are lovely together, but it’s the crispy fried onions that really make the combination work. That salty crunch is a welcome addition to the softer textures.

Sources indicate that turkey, stuffing and cranberry sauce: This is probably my favorite combo of the bunch. The savory turkey and seasoned stuffing are practically made for one another, while a little cranberry sauce cuts through the richness. It’s essentially a Thanksgiving leftover sandwich without the bread, although I wouldn’t object to adding a dinner roll to the equation.

Industry observers note that macaroni and cheese and cranberry sauce: I realize this combination may call my culinary credentials into question, but hear me out. Rich, creamy mac and cheese practically begs for something sharp and acidic to cut through it, and cranberry sauce does exactly that. It’s not so different from serving a sharp cheddar with fruit preserves on a charcuterie board, although I concede that putting cranberry sauce on macaroni and cheese is a considerably harder sell. But that’s half the fun of Thanksgiving dinner: discovering which combinations you’re willing to defend.

#7361. The Tucson Restaurant Turning Cactus Into Fine Dining

The Tucson Restaurant Turning Cactus Into Fine Dining

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (920 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that traipsing through Tucson Mountain Park, a Midwestern blow-in might not identify much to eat.
  • Gray, tangled brittlebush, which the average Tucsonan walks or drives by almost daily, can be pressure-cooked, caramelized until black, and baked into cake.
  • Don’t even get Lopez started on the dozens of cacti varieties that thrive here, which the restaurant sources from local grower Toadlet Farm and which Lopez harvests throughout the year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that traipsing through Tucson Mountain Park, a Midwestern blow-in might not identify much to eat. Plants armed with burs, barbs, and spines all but scream “do not touch.” For chef Aaron Lopez and June Chee, however, this prickly, dusty landscape stocks a pantry of possibility. The married co-owners of Ursa see the Arizona desert as a rich ground for foraging.

Gray, tangled brittlebush, which the average Tucsonan walks or drives by almost daily, can be pressure-cooked, caramelized until black, and baked into cake. Dusty, sage-colored salt bush, when hung to dry, takes on an intensely umami, aquatic saltiness like seaweed. The sweet buds of the Seussian-green palo verde tree become briny, like olives, when suffused with lye.

Don’t even get Lopez started on the dozens of cacti varieties that thrive here, which the restaurant sources from local grower Toadlet Farm and which Lopez harvests throughout the year. The restaurant processes the young and mature paddles, fruit and their seeds, buds, and flowers, which are then grilled, poached, cold-smoked, juiced, dehydrated, nixtamalized, or preserved into jam, wine, and vinegar.

There are hundreds of edible plants in the Sonoran Desert. Ursa strives to showcase their potential, one 10-course meal at a time.

“We treat Ursa as an art showroom, demonstrating to people what these plants can do, what sustainable means, and what was here before it got easy,” states Lopez. The idea was inspired in part by his Sonoran grandfather, Hector Lopez, who died in the spring. “He was the first person I ever heard say they’re proud to be from the desert,” the chef mentioned.

Ursa began as a pop-up in El Centro, California, in 2023. Lopez and Chee moved to a historic brick building in downtown Tucson, re-opening their doors in October 2025. It’s a homecoming of sorts for the couple, who are both from the Sonoran Desert borderlands. They met in Hawaii, where Chee was working in clean energy and transportation. Lopez, meanwhile, spent roughly 18 years cooking in fine dining and modern progressive restaurants like Redbird and Orsa & Winston in LA, and Pai Honolulu. But he was longing for the desert.

In a recent development, after helping a friend open a restaurant and hosting a few popups in Austin, Lopez and Chee bought a desert foraging guide, packed up their two dogs and began driving around the Southwest. It made sense to settle in Tucson, which was recognized by UNESCO in 2015 as a Creative City of Gastronomy for its continuous 4,000-year agricultural history and deeply rooted Sonoran Desert food traditions.

“That’s a unique thing about being here, the connection from seed to plant to restaurant that we hadn’t been able to grasp before,” Chee notes.

Consider a recent course that Ursa built around tepary beans, in which the ancient, nutty bean is refried and topped with h:al squash that’s been lactofermented. The squash’s leaves are fermented to make Japanese-style kosho and its flowers are pickled, dried, crushed with dried saltbush, then tossed with barrel cactus seeds for a desert furikake. It’s served with grilled coins of chorizo made from Lopez’s great-grandmother’s recipe and housemade flour tortillas, to all be washed down with an amazake drink made from fermented wheat and goat fat. Don’t get too attached, however. Riffs owing to finicky ingredient availability occur here almost daily.

Running a restaurant using only ingredients foraged and farmed from within about eight to 10 miles means abiding by pretty intense guardrails. The only wheat used is pima club, an ancient soft white variety cultivated for centuries by the Akimel O’odham (Pima) people. Ursa does not use cucumbers, radishes or citrus.

“We’re not trying to substitute anything, like, ‘How do we achieve cucumber? Let’s grab a cactus,’” Lopez indicates. “We have to throw everything out, really strip it down. Sometimes we have to let the ingredients be bitter or spicy. We have to put our egos aside and let the ingredient be the star.”.

For staff who didn’t grow up or learn to cook here, the learning curve at Ursa can feel a little like alighting on a latest planet, even if certain flora happen to resemble prickly weeds in their own backyards.

According to recent reports, “We have these really cool moments in the restaurant where people are like, Oh! I have lamb’s quarter just growing in my yard!” Chee indicates of the spinach-like desert green that appears all over Ursa’s menu.

A young Aaron Lopez with his grandfather Hector Lopez.

Industry observers note that ursa’s approach isn’t always easy for customers to understand, so the couple came up with a more down-to-earth option. This fall, the restaurant debuted a four-course, family-style Lineage menu for $75, alongside the existing 10-course Harvest menu ($150). There’s now a pozole course inspired by the family’s annual springtime tradition of roasting goat in agave leaves, barbacoa-style, and shredding it for soup, and a red masa tamal with glazed quail and yucca blossoms in mole made with burnt mesquite bread, a technique Lopez remembers from childhood.

The idea took shape during Ursa’s extended summer break, as Lopez recovered from foot surgery and reflected on the loss of his late grandfather, the tenacious keeper of family traditions.

“I feel so much closer to my ancestors and the land; we want Ursa to be less esoteric and more soulful,” he claims. “The story of Ursa is partly of the desert, partly my family. Now we’ve advanced to the point where they’re symbiotic, and I can't tell them apart.”.

She reminisces about a fruity street snack sold by a chaat vendor near the Hyderabadi train station. Sweet pineapple, tangy lime juice, sour-salty chaat masala, chile powder, cilantro, and pomegranate seeds created what she describes as “a decadent mosaic of colors and plucky flavors.” Chauhan suggests swapping in ripe mango or watermelon when in season, or drizzling the finished dish with lightly salted yogurt for added richness and depth. Serve as a snack, or as a side dish for barbecued meats or seafood.

Even in an election cycle marked by surprises and upsets, Capitol Hill observers will spot some familiar faces (identical twins notwithstanding) among this year’s midterm winners.

At least seven former members won comeback bids Tuesday.

Sources indicate that the winners included alumni who dusted themselves off after election losses just two years ago. But other winners haven’t been in office in nearly two decades, their service predating the addition of a women’s restroom in the House (more recent than you may guess).

Here’s how these former members did on election night:.

According to recent reports, carl lost a primary to fellow Republican Rep. Barry Moore in 2024 after a newly introduced map placed them in the same district. But with Moore running for the Senate in 2026, Carl had an easier path back to his old seat, which was redrawn again this year. He defeated his Democratic opponent Tuesday by 18 points.

It has been nearly two decades since Solis last served in Congress. She left in 2009 to serve as President Barack Obama’s first Labor secretary. Solis was in her sixth term as a Los Angeles county supervisor when she confirmed a bid for Congress after California voters approved a map that created five Democratic pickup opportunities.

According to recent reports, solis faced limited resistance on her path to victory in the 38th District, especially after Democratic Rep. Linda T. Sánchez opted to run for the redrawn 41st District.

Bean is making her way back to the House after losing her suburban Chicagoland seat in the conservative tea party wave of 2010.

It has been revealed that A decade-and-a-half later, she won an eight-way primary for the 8th District seat Democrat Raja Krishnamoorthi vacated for an unsuccessful Senate bid. Winning the nomination all but guaranteed Bean a November victory in the deep-blue seat.

One of the cycle’s biggest comeback stories was in the Buckeye State, where Sherrod Brown was mounting a bid two years after Republican Bernie Moreno had unseated him. Positioning himself as an opponent of data centers, Brown defeated appointed GOP Sen. Jon Husted in a special election for the remainder of now Vice President JD Vance’s term. He could take office as early as December but would have to run again in 2028 if he wants another full term.

It has been revealed that first elected in 2018, Allred left Congress two years ago after an unsuccessful Senate campaign against Republican incumbent Ted Cruz. After briefly launching a second Senate bid, Allred switched to a redrawn open House seat and won his primary over Rep. Julie Elizabeth Johnson, his successor in the chamber. Allred had no trouble winning his general election Tuesday for a fourth House term.

#7353. How to Make Whipped Cream Perfectly, Every Time

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bonappetit ↗ Open Full Page

How to Make Whipped Cream Perfectly, Every Time

📅 27 Jul 2017 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1405 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you love a low-effort, high-reward kitchen assignment, learning how to make whipped cream is a walk in the clouds.
  • Industry observers note that in whipped cream, and in life, the key challenge is knowing when to stop.
  • Industry observers note that to make whipped cream at home, all you need is cold heavy cream, a large bowl, and a whisk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you love a low-effort, high-reward kitchen assignment, learning how to make whipped cream is a walk in the clouds. The only ingredients are time and heavy cream. You can use an electric mixer, a whisk, or a mason jar and strong-armed devotion.

Industry observers note that in whipped cream, and in life, the key challenge is knowing when to stop. Desserts like Strawberry Eton Mess or Triple Chocolate Mousse Cake fare best with silky, unsweetened, soft-peaked whip. Others, like this show-stopping Berries and Cream Mille-Feuille, gain structure from sturdier peaks.

Industry observers note that to make whipped cream at home, all you need is cold heavy cream, a large bowl, and a whisk. You can also use a handheld mixer or a mason jar and some elbow grease (more on that later).

Recent findings suggest that if you’re opting for a bowl-and-whisk combo, choose your tools wisely. Cream roughly doubles in volume as you whip it, so use a bowl with three to four times the capacity of your liquid. A large balloon whisk, rather than a narrow sauce whisk, helps incorporate plenty of air into the cream.

Be strategic in the dairy aisle too. Heavy cream and heavy whipping cream contain at least 36% milk fat and can be used interchangeably. Skip anything labeled simply “whipping cream”—or, heaven forbid, “light cream”—which contains less fat and won’t hold its loft as well.

For a basic batch, start with 1 cup cold heavy cream, which makes about 2 cups whipped cream. For lightly sweetened whipped cream, add 1 Tbsp. powdered sugar; for vanilla whipped cream, add ½ tsp. vanilla extract or paste.

With your equipment and ingredients in hand, there are only five steps and infinite possibilities.

Because whipped cream is usually eaten with or as dessert, you might not need to sweeten it at all. To keep flavors balanced, we tend to serve whipped cream au naturel with Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie or Diner-Style Rice Pudding.

According to recent reports, but there are no hard-and-fast rules. Maybe you love sweetened whipped cream, or you’re serving it with something less sugary—like, say, a bowl of tart blackberries and torn mint leaves.

For lightly sweetened whipped cream, start with about 1 Tbsp. sugar per cup of cream. Powdered sugar dissolves easily and contains a little stabilizer (usually cornstarch), which can lend the whipped cream some extra holding power. Some cooks prefer the cleaner flavor of granulated sugar, which takes a little longer to dissolve. Either way, add the sugar before you start whipping.

If you’re gazing at a bowl of fluffy, ethereal whip and thinking, “Could I make this even more enchanting?” the answer is yes. There are two primary ways to make flavored whipped cream: infuse or stir.

Sources indicate that kitchen professionals and advance planners tend to cold-infuse. Combine your cream with flavorings like rice (for a creamy Horchata) or bourbon (to take a classic pumpkin pie over the top), then store it in the fridge anywhere from three hours to overnight. Strain out any solids before whipping.

It has been revealed that you can also add simple flavorings, like vanilla extract, a small splash of liqueur, cocoa, ground spices, citrus zest, or coffee syrup, before you start whipping. For heavier or chunky additions, such as toasted nuts or chopped chocolate, use a rubber spatula to gently fold them in once the cream is whipped.

Peaks are the shape your whipped cream takes when you pull the whisk out of the bowl and hold it upright like the Statue of Liberty’s torch.

Soft peaks are cloudlike and slump over when you lift the whisk. Stiff peaks stand upright and hold their shape. Somewhere in between are medium peaks, which have enough structure to hold a shape while remaining soft and supple.

Most Bon Appétit recipes, such as these Mix-and-Match Fools, involve whipping cream to soft peaks. That velvety texture is our go-to when we’re dolloping whipped cream atop pecan pie.

But we aren’t always such softies. Medium peaks help this Ginger-Raspberry Icebox Cake keep its shape. And old-fashioned chocolate mousse involves whipping batches of cream into stiff and soft peaks: The former is folded into the chocolate mixture for structure, while the softer stuff tops the dessert.

There’s more than one way to whip.

By hand: Our preferred method, whipping cream by hand requires the most time and effort, but it also gives you optimal control over its final texture. Even if you use a mixer to get your whipped cream started, switching to a whisk for the final few moments makes it easier to stop exactly where you want.

Industry observers note that in a Mason jar: No whisk? No mixer? No problem. To make whipped cream with your bare hands, put a container with a tight-fitting lid, large mason jar, or leak-proof cocktail shaker into the freezer for five minutes. Get the heavy cream very cold and make sure you have ample headspace in your vessel of choice. About one cup of liquid in a four-cup container is a good amount.

In a recent development, secure the lid and shake it like you mean it. For the creamiest results, a consistently assertive pace is better than intermittent spurts of brute force. When the liquid stops sloshing and starts feeling and sounding heavier, open the lid and take a peek. If it looks underwhipped, close it back up and keep shaking.

It has been revealed that good news for meal preppers: You can make whipped cream hours in advance. Err on the side of underwhipping it during your prep. Store the lightly whipped cream, covered, in the fridge for up to four hours before serving, then give it a few energetic whisks to bring back its bounce right before you dollop it onto dessert.

According to recent reports, you can also freeze whipped cream (no, seriously). It takes a bit of effort, though. Line a baking sheet with parchment, then pipe or scoop spoonfuls of whipped cream onto it. Freeze until the whipped cream nuggets are solid, then peel them off the parchment and store them in an airtight bag in the freezer for one to two months. When you’re ready to serve, let them thaw at room temperature for about 15 minutes.

Instant vanilla pudding is the key to luscious, long-lasting whipped cream.

It has been revealed that need it to hold up longer? Instant vanilla pudding mix is one of BA’s favorite shortcuts for stabilized whipped cream. For every cup of heavy cream, add 1 Tbsp. instant vanilla pudding mix (call it pastry cream powder if anyone gives you sass) and 2 tsp. powdered sugar, then whip as usual. The modified starch in the pudding mix absorbs excess moisture and helps prevent the cream from separating, keeping it fluffy for up to 24 hours.

For something tangier, sour cream adds both flavor and body. Our Pecan Cream Pie whisks ¼ cup sour cream into 1 cup heavy cream; the sour cream cuts the richness while helping the topping hold its shape.

In any case, your dinner party guests don’t have to sit quietly as you furiously whisk their dessert topping to order. Prep work never tasted so sweet.

If your whip isn’t coming together quite right, don’t fret. Simple solutions abound.

Industry observers note that this is probably a temperature matter. Cold cream whips more readily and holds onto the air you’re incorporating more effectively, so it comes together faster—and stays fluffy longer. Pop the bowl, whisk, and cream back into the freezer for five minutes, or into the fridge for up to 30. Once everything is cold, resume whisking.

Another possible culprit is the fat content of your cream. Opt for heavy whipping cream or heavy cream over half-and-half or other heavy cream substitutes.

In a recent development, if the cream is just a little too stiff or starting to look grainy, add a splash of chilled heavy cream and slowly whisk it in. Add more, a little at a time, until the texture smooths out.

Keep a close eye on it: If you whisk for too long, you’ll end up with a bowl of butter.

In a recent development, you can find goat meat at your local halal butcher or substitute lamb. If opting for goat, Gurjar recommends requesting a bone-in “curry cut,” which means the butcher will cut the meat into 2- to 3-inch pieces that are ideal for braising.

Sources indicate that while you can use store-bought garam masala, Gurjar always DIYs her own spice blend inspired by the one her mother used to make back in India. “It’s the secret ingredient that often leaves my guests wondering why my Indian food tastes so exceptional,” she writes. “This version perfectly balances the warming notes of cloves and nutmeg, and it’s the one I return to time and time again.” You can also customize your blend: Add more cinnamon and fennel for a sweeter garam masala, or up the black pepper and cloves for a spicier kick.
