Sources indicate that democrat Annie Andrews, here addressing supporters at her election night party in Charleston, S.C., on Tuesday, is the first woman elected to the Senate from South Carolina. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

The incoming freshman class of the 120th Congress includes several people who scored historic wins in their states and the nation at large.

Industry observers note that among them were women breaking glass ceilings in the Senate and trailblazers for Native American representation. Beyond Washington, a handful of nominees pulled off milestone victories in gubernatorial elections, including four Black candidates. Congress is also poised to witness history next year with New York Democrat Hakeem Jeffries expected to become the first Black speaker.

Here are some of the candidates who made history on election night, both in Congress and in the governor's mansions:.

Alfonso, the son-in-law of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, is the first Gen Z Republican elected to Congress with his victory in Wisconsin’s open 7th District, a seat his father-in-law once held.

Andrews, a pediatrician, becomes the first woman elected to the Senate from South Carolina after defeating appointed Republican incumbent Darline Graham, the first female senator from the Palmetto State.

Sources indicate that with her victory in New York’s 13th District, Avila Chevalier becomes the first Muslim person elected to Congress from the Empire State. She succeeds Democratic Rep. Adriano Espaillat, whom she defeated in the primary.

Benitez-Thompson, a former majority leader of the Nevada State Assembly, is the first Democrat elected to represent the state’s 2nd District since its creation after the 1980 census.

Sources indicate that with his victory over Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, Colom, a district attorney, will be Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction. He will also be the Magnolia State’s first Black senator elected directly by voters.

Conely, a Navy veteran, unseats Republican Rep. Mike Lawler to become the first openly gay woman elected to Congress from Newly introduced York.

Dandiya, the daughter of Indian immigrants, becomes the first South Asian American elected to Congress from Florida with her victory in the redrawn 22nd District. She is also one of the first adherents of Jainism to be elected to Congress, along with Arizona's Amish Shah (see below).

With his victory over Republican Mike Rogers, El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, becomes the first Muslim person elected to the Senate.

Industry observers note that A member of the White Earth Band of Ojibwe, Flanagan becomes the first Native American woman elected to the Senate with her victory over Republican Michele Tafoya. The outgoing Minnesota lieutenant governor is also the first Native American to represent the state in Congress.

Ford, a state senator, unseated Republican Rep. Victoria Spartz to become the first openly gay person elected to Congress from Indiana.

It has been revealed that hamawy, a former Army surgeon who emigrated from Egypt to the U.S. as an infant, is the first Muslim person elected to Congress from New Jersey, with his victory in the state’s 12th District.

Killin, an Army veteran and onetime chief of staff to former second gentleman Doug Emhoff, is the first Democrat elected to represent Colorado’s 5th District since its creation after the 1970 census.

In a recent development, kiros, who upset Rep. Diana DeGette in the Democratic primary for Colorado’s 1st District, easily won the general election to become the first Black woman elected to Congress from the Centennial State. Kiros, who was born in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, and emigrated to the U.S. as an infant, is also the first Gen Z woman elected to Congress.

It has been revealed that koh, the son of a Korean American father and a Lebanese American mother, is the first Asian American elected to Congress from Massachusetts. The former Biden administration alumnus will succeed Democrat Seth Moulton in the state’s 6th District.

According to recent reports, letlow, the first Republican woman elected to the House from Louisiana, earns the same distinction in the Senate with her victory over Democrat Jamie Davis in the open-seat race to succeed GOP Sen. Bill Cassidy.

Limtiaco will be the first Chamorro woman to represent Guam in Congress after she unseated Republican Del. James C. Moylan. She previously was the first woman to serve as U.S. attorney for the Districts of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands.

McCann, a state senator, defeated Republican Rep. Bill Huizenga to become the first Native American elected to Congress from Michigan. McCann is a member of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation.

Moss, the president pro tempore of the Michigan Senate, keeps Rep. Haley Stevens’ 11th District in Democratic hands, becoming the first openly gay person elected to Congress from Michigan.

The grandson of a Mexican immigrant, Ojeda, who defeated National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Richard Hudson, is the first Latino elected to Congress from North Carolina.

By defeating former Sen. John E. Sununu, Pappas, a fourth-term congressman, becomes the first openly gay man elected to the Senate.

It has been revealed that the daughter of immigrants from Chile and Cuba, Powell is the first Latino person elected to Congress from Nebraska after flipping the state’s 2nd District. She is also the first Democratic woman elected to Congress from Nebraska.

Unofficial returns show Sarauw winning the open-seat race to succeed outgoing Del. Stacey Plaskett, making her the first openly gay person elected to Congress from the U.S. Virgin Islands.

The son of Indian immigrants, Shah is the first South Asian American elected to Congress from Arizona. The former state legislator is also one of the first adherents of Jainism to be elected to Congress, along with Florida’s Pia Dandiya.

A citizen of the Ysleta del Sur Pueblo Nation, Valdez is the first Native American elected to Congress from Upcoming York. The New York State assemblywoman will succeed retiring Democratic Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez.

Wiener, a state senator who succeeds former Speaker Nancy Pelosi in California’s 11th District, is the first openly gay person elected to represent San Francisco in Congress.

Industry observers note that with her victory over Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, Acton becomes the first woman elected governor of Ohio. Republican Nancy Hollister briefly served as the state’s top executive in the late 1990s but was never elected governor.

The son of Mexican immigrants, Becerra, a former congressman and Health and Human Services secretary, is the first Latino to be elected governor of California. He is the state’s second Latino governor after Romualdo Pacheco, who was never elected to the role but briefly succeeded an incumbent in 1875.

Blackburn, Tennessee’s first female senator, will soon become the Volunteer State’s first female governor after her victory over Democrat Jerri Green.

Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, will be the first Black person elected governor of Wisconsin after he defeated Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany.

Republican Rep. Byron Donalds will become Florida's first Black governor after he defeated Democrat David Jolly, a former GOP congressman.

Ford, the current Nevada attorney general, will become his state’s first Black governor after defeating Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo.

Haaland, a member of the Pueblo of Laguna, will become the first Native American woman to be elected governor in the U.S. after defeating Republican Gregg Hull. The former Interior secretary was also one of the first Native American women elected to Congress, along with Kansas Rep. Sharice Davids, in 2018.

Hinojosa, a state representative, will become the first Hispanic person elected Texas governor since statehood after she unseated three-term Republican incumbent Greg Abbott.

Klobuchar, the first woman to be elected senator from Minnesota, makes history again with her election as her state’s first female governor.

Sources indicate that with her victory over Republican businessman Rick Jackson, Lance Bottoms becomes the first woman to be elected governor of Georgia. The former Atlanta mayor is also the state’s first Black governor and the first Black woman to be elected governor anywhere in the country, along with Del. Stacey Plaskett in the U.S. Virgin Islands.

According to recent reports, unofficial returns show Plaskett, the nonvoting delegate from the U.S. Virgin Islands, becoming the first woman to be elected governor of the island territory. She is also one of the first Black women to be elected governor in the country, along with Lance Bottoms in Georgia.

Breaking: Keeping the Diwali Flame Burning in Latest York City

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1266 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Saveur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the akhand diya, the continuously burning flame, has one purpose: to stay lit.
  • As a teenager, I remember feeling that I had crossed an invisible threshold into womanhood.
  • In a recent development, in many ways, this transition is happening outside of me.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the akhand diya, the continuously burning flame, has one purpose: to stay lit. It is a small but enduring presence, tended to around the clock, its care passed from one person to the next so that the light never goes out. I’ve often thought about how much of life is like this, how we are constantly passing the torch from one version of ourselves to another.

As a teenager, I remember feeling that I had crossed an invisible threshold into womanhood. I was becoming someone different from the girl I had been, carrying parts of her with me but beginning to understand the world through a upcoming lens. Now, years later, I find myself at another such transition: I am becoming a different version of a woman, one I am still getting to know.

In a recent development, in many ways, this transition is happening outside of me. Thirteen years ago, I moved away from my family in Mumbai and the home where Diwali had always been celebrated. For all those years, the rituals continued, even as I participated in them from thousands of miles away, mostly over video calls. Back in Mumbai, Diwali meant a house full of family and friends, kitchens bustling with cooking and frying, and the warm glow of diyas illuminating the mandir. I was no longer physically there, but I remained part of it. This year, for the first time, I hosted my parents for Diwali in the home I’ve built for myself in New York City.

In a recent development, it felt cataclysmic, or at least I was making it feel that way in my head. As I welcomed a different version of myself, I was also taking on a new role within my family. I was no longer simply the daughter returning to their house for Diwali; I was the one opening my home, preparing the food, tending to the rituals, and making space for the people who first taught me what this celebration means. There is perhaps no greater joy than watching the people I love receive and experience care. And yet, this was a responsibility I had chosen to take on, and one that felt particularly daunting as the eldest daughter. I wanted to get it right.

According to recent reports, for me, that care has always found its way to the table. Food is how my family celebrates, how we mark occasions, and, perhaps most importantly, how we look after one another. So naturally, much of my energy went into planning the meal. Despite my best efforts, my dad promptly assigned himself the task of making the goat kari—apparently, even after 13 years away, some things hadn’t changed. We headed to our local butcher in Brooklyn to buy fresh goat meat, and almost immediately, his attention turned to the spice tolerance of my guests.

Sources indicate that “How much spice can your friends tolerate?” he kept asking me. “Should I keep it at a level six? But our level six might be their level ten. What do I do?” he lamented. “Relax, they’ll be able to handle it! Just make it our level five,” I told him.

According to recent reports, I gave in and handed over part of the kitchen to my mother, too. She took charge of the paneer, cooking generous chunks in a luscious onion-tomato gravy and making the chapatis. Selfishly, I didn’t mind relinquishing that responsibility: This would be my one chance for the year to eat chapatis fresh off the tava, puffed up and piping hot, and made by my mother.

As the days drew closer, I found myself loosening my grip on the plans I’d made. My parents had their own ideas about what needed to be cooked, and while I was initially resistant to them taking over (any immigrant will tell you how hard it is to get our parents to just relax!), I was learning that hosting didn’t necessarily mean doing everything myself. It also meant making room for everyone to contribute and allowing upcoming rituals to form.

In a recent development, the evening began with freshly fried moong vadas. My mother, of course, insisted on frying them for everyone, right before serving. Made from soaked and ground mung lentils, these little fritters are crisp and golden on the outside, with a soft, almost creamy interior. They have a naturally earthy, nutty flavor from the lentils, sharpened with green chiles, ginger, and spices.

Moong vadas are best eaten immediately, still hot out of the oil, with a tangy green chutney. The scene reminded me of Diwalis back in Mumbai, when the vadas rarely even made it to the serving platter: Everyone would gather around the kitchen, waiting for the next batch to come out of the kadai, reaching for them before they had a chance to cool. I saw the same thing happening in my kitchen in Newly introduced York.

In a recent development, in the meantime, my friends Leanne and Christina took charge of the tamarind margaritas, my ode to the soft, sweet-tart tamarind candies I grew up savoring as a kid. The tangy cocktails were a welcome counterpoint to the savory fritters, the perfect way to wake up our taste buds (and made exercising some restraint with those moong vadas before dinner particularly difficult). My brother helped set the table and move furniture around, just as we used to do for our parents back in Mumbai. There was something deeply comforting about watching us fall into these old rhythms.

According to recent reports, the table eventually came together with a mix of dishes that felt both familiar and celebratory. There was chana masala from my cookbook, East to East, alongside my dad’s goat kari, slow-cooked with spices until the meat was tender. My mother’s saucy tomato-onion paneer was accompanied by a pile of chapatis that disappeared almost as quickly as they came off the stove. We served everything family-style, laying out the dishes on kansa thalis, traditional Indian plates made from bronze or bell metal, an alloy of copper and tin. They reminded me of the way my grandparents served meals, and I wanted to bring a little of that into our Diwali celebration.

At the center of the spread was a vegetable pulao, fragrant basmati rice cooked with carrots, cabbage, cauliflower, and whole spices. Alongside it, I placed bowls of pickled onions and mango achaar, whose sharp, tangy bite cuts through the richness of the karis. There was also cucumber raita, cool and creamy, offering a welcome respite from the heat of the spices. These accompaniments might seem like small additions, but they are essential to the balance of an Indian meal. Every bite can be a little different, depending on what you bring together on your plate.

For dessert, I made homemade gulab jamun, my brother’s favorite. The soft dumplings are made from milk solids and fried until golden, then soaked in a warm saffron-and-cardamom-scented sugar syrup.

It has been revealed that as I sat cuddled among both my families, I realized that while it wasn’t the perfectly orchestrated dinner I’d imagined when I first started planning, it was something better. The family I was born into celebrating Diwali alongside the family I’d chosen and built in New York, all gathered around the same table and enjoying every minute of it. Perhaps keeping the flame alive was never about re-creating the past exactly as it was but about allowing it to illuminate whatever comes next.

While we love a showstopping main, appetizers are almost always the course that excites us the most. Especially if you’re hosting, it’s a nonnegotiable that appetizers impress. Perfect apps have to be easy, fast, and above all, delicious. Puff pastry dough makes hitting those benchmarks a cinch. Though making it from scratch is a lengthy process that includes folding tons of butter into dough (kind of like making croissants), store-bought frozen puff pastry is just as good (maybe better, considering the convenience!). Check out our 26 best puff pastry appetizers to see how versatile the dough can be, and we bet you’ll stock up, too.

The best thing about puff pastry appetizers is how truly impressive they look without a ton of effort on your part. Looking for something super simple? Puff pastry and cheese are a match made in heaven. If you want something handheld, try our sausage or Reuben pinwheels, our spinach dip rolls, or our pumpkin spice hot honey brie bites. Caramelized Onion & Goat Cheese Bites.

Pumpkin Spice Hot Honey Brie Bites.

Sweet and savory with a kick of heat, these pumpkin, Brie, and hot honey bites are the perfect fall appetizer to serve during the holidays, or really at any dinner party. The honey provides the perfect balance for the sweetness of the pumpkin and the savory, melty Brie.

Pepper Jelly & Cream Cheese Bites.

Instead of serving with crackers, we put the cream cheese and pepper jelly inside puff pastry for the perfect bite-sized appetizer.

Upside-Down Cream Of Mushroom Tartlets.

Recent findings suggest that this beginner-friendly TikTok-inspired pastry hack transforms store-bought puff pastry and the sweet or savory filling of your choice into a beautiful bite-sized snack. Our version leans heavily into savory territory with a cream of mushroom soup-inspired filling.

Turn your favorite party dip into a personal serving with these cheesy, flaky, savory spinach dip rolls. Bell pepper + cream cheese + cheddar cheese make for a pimento-inspired bite.

Inspired by spanakopita, we stuff our pinwheels with an unbeatable combination of cheeses, chopped spinach, dill, and lemon zest. Then we added chopped artichoke hearts and roasted peppers to give the filling a tangy, slightly briny zing that'll brighten up your holiday plates.

If you love the TikTok-famous baked feta pasta and the delightful sophistication of our cranberry brie bites, then brace yourself: These little appetizers are the culinary revelation that combines the best of both worlds.

We took the croque monsieur, a classic French sandwich made with toasty bread, melty cheese, salty ham, and a silky béchamel, and turned it into an appetizer that hits all the high notes: buttery, crispy, creamy, cheesy, salty, and a little nutty.

If you love meaty, savory, tangy Reuben sandwiches, then you'll love these crispy Reuben pinwheels. Made with store-bought buttery puff pastry and layered with corned beef, gooey Swiss cheese, creamy thousand island dressing, and crunchy sauerkraut, these bites have everything you love about the classic sandwich in a party-ready shape.

With sweet tomatoes, fresh mozzarella, bright basil, and zingy balsamic glaze, this refreshing salad has inspired countless mains, sides, and apps here at Delish. We decided to use one of our favorite store-bought ingredients—puff pastry—to transform these classic flavors into a new, poppable app: baked Caprese bites.

Green bean casserole is one of the most iconic Thanksgiving sides, and one that brings together the best flavors of the season. Baked in crescent roll cups with crispy fried onions, a rich, creamy mushroom sauce, and tender-yet-snappy green beans, these handheld wonders hit every note.

According to recent reports, here, the classic British sausage roll gets a Christmas–appropriate makeover. First, sweet Italian sausage gets a flavor boost from sautéed onions, plenty of chopped herbs, and some Worcestershire sauce. Next, the sausage gets rolled up in store-bought puff pastry with a little Dijon mustard.

Cheesy Green Bean & Mushroom Tart.

This is a classic combo we never get tired of, and that goes double for this shareable tart. Fresh blanched green beans are layered onto a creamy blend of ricotta and goat cheese, topped with garlicky mushrooms and cheddar cheese, then baked on a puff pastry crust until perfectly melty.

Industry observers note that we filled our baked brie with raspberry jam, but feel free to use your favorite spread or jelly. Drizzle it with some honey, and you'll have a warm, cheesy app that feels extra-fancy in no time at all.

Industry News: Astronomers Discover a Chilling Preview of Our Solar System’s Future

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (916 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that astronomers have discovered an extraordinary ring system surrounding a dead star, offering a possible preview of what awaits our Solar System billions of years from now.
  • “We have known for some time that planets may survive beyond the transformation of their central star, but this is the first example of a complex system with a double debris disc and potentially two surviving planetesimals,” says Nicola Gentille Fusillo, an astronomer at the Università degli Studi di Trieste in Italy and lead author of the study published in Nature Astronomy.
  • Industry observers note that at the center of this remarkable system is J1328−1450, a white dwarf.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that astronomers have discovered an extraordinary ring system surrounding a dead star, offering a possible preview of what awaits our Solar System billions of years from now. Using the European Southern Observatory’s Very Large Telescope (ESO’s VLT), researchers identified two separate rings of planetary debris with a distinct gap between them. The unusual structure may be maintained by two planetary bodies that survived the death of their star, including one potentially as large as Pluto or even the Moon.

“We have known for some time that planets may survive beyond the transformation of their central star, but this is the first example of a complex system with a double debris disc and potentially two surviving planetesimals,” says Nicola Gentille Fusillo, an astronomer at the Università degli Studi di Trieste in Italy and lead author of the study published in Nature Astronomy.

Industry observers note that at the center of this remarkable system is J1328−1450, a white dwarf. These incredibly dense stellar remnants are what remain when stars similar to our Sun exhaust their nuclear fuel and reach the end of their lives.

According to recent reports, when a Sun-like star approaches the end of its life, it swells dramatically before shedding its outer layers. During this transformation, nearby planets can be swallowed and destroyed. Other rocky objects may survive the initial upheaval, only to break apart later and create rotating discs of debris around the star’s remaining core.

Astronomers have observed such debris discs around white dwarfs before, but J1328−1450 stands out. Instead of a single ring of vaporized planetary material, it has two concentric rings of gas separated by a well-defined gap.

“The structure we see in this system is particularly intriguing because the two gaseous rings are remarkably stable and remain separated by a gap,” notes co-author Felipe Lagos-Vilches, an astronomer at the University of Warwick in the UK and at the Universidad Técnica Federico Santa María in Chile.

“The system is a rare glimpse of the violent, chaotic process by which a planetary system meets its end, and it hints that dead stars can have disc structures far more complex than previously realized,” adds Gentile Fusillo, who is also affiliated with the INAF-Astronomical Observatory of Trieste.

In a recent development, what keeps the two rings separated? The researchers suspect that two surviving planet-like bodies, traveling along different orbits, are helping maintain the unusual arrangement.

Sources indicate that the smaller object, associated with the inner ring, could be comparable to a typical asteroid, measuring just a few kilometers across. The larger body, associated with the outer ring, may be roughly the size of Pluto or even Earth’s Moon. Although their presence has not been directly confirmed, these objects could explain why the debris remains divided into two stable rings.

Until now, astronomers had identified debris discs around white dwarfs through a characteristic observational signature associated with a single, flat, rotating disc. However, observations of J1328−1450 revealed something entirely different.

Using the X-Shooter instrument installed on ESO’s VLT in Chile’s Atacama Desert, the researchers detected the distinctive signature of a double disc, showing that planetary debris around dead stars can form more complicated structures than previously recognized.

The rings also contain key clues about the worlds that once orbited the star. Astronomers detected calcium, oxygen, magnesium, and iron, elements commonly found in rocky planetary material throughout our Solar System.

In a recent development, even more intriguing, the two rings have noticeably different chemical compositions. The inner ring contains abundant magnesium gas, while the outer ring has very little. This difference suggests that the debris feeding the rings may have come from two separate planets with distinct compositions.

Another possibility is that the material originated from different layers of the same planetary body. For example, one ring could contain debris from a planet’s crust, while the other holds material from its core.

The discovery may also reveal something unsettling about our own cosmic future. Billions of years from now, the Sun will undergo a similar transformation, expanding as it nears the end of its life before eventually becoming a white dwarf. Earth could be destroyed during this process, while other planetary bodies may survive and leave behind rings of debris.

The unusual system around J1328−1450 suggests that the aftermath of a star’s death can be far more complex than a simple cloud of shattered planetary remains. Even after a planetary system experiences catastrophic destruction, some of its original bodies may endure and continue shaping the wreckage.

“The system therefore offers a remarkable glimpse of what the future of planetary systems, including systems like our own, might look like,” concludes Lagos-Vilches.

In a recent development, reference: “A double debris disc around a white dwarf sculpted by two planetary bodies” by Nicola Pietro Gentile Fusillo, Felipe Lagos-Vilches, Boris T. Gänsicke, Christopher J. Manser and Detlev Koester, 26 October 2026, Nature Astronomy. DOI: 10.1038/s41550-026-03004-3.

Recent findings suggest that the team is composed of Nicola Pietro Gentile Fusillo (Dipartimento di Fisica, Universita‘ di Trieste and INAF-Osservatorio Astronomico di Trieste, Italy), Felipe Lagos-Vilches (Department of Physics, University of Warwick, UK and Departamento de Física, Universidad Técnica Federico Santa María, Chile), Boris T. Gänsicke (Department of Physics and Centre for Exoplanets and Habitability, University of Warwick, UK), Christopher J. Manser (Department of Physics, Astrophysics Group, Imperial College London, UK), Detlev Koester (Institut für Theoretische Physik und Astrophysik, University of Kiel, Germany).

#7344. A Chef’s Guide to Eating and Drinking in Santo Domingo

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Saveur ↗ Open Full Page

A Chef’s Guide to Eating and Drinking in Santo Domingo

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1887 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Saveur

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On a Friday night in July, Nidia Evangelista walked with her arms crossed over the Puente Flotante toward East Santo Domingo.
  • On the other side, we turned a corner and found hundreds gathered around a dance floor in the undercroft of a bigger bridge.
  • According to recent reports, bur normally walks (or bikes) everywhere.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On a Friday night in July, Nidia Evangelista walked with her arms crossed over the Puente Flotante toward East Santo Domingo. Six lanes of traffic jockeyed inches from her left shoulder, while the black waters of the Río Ozama coursed below. “Oh my God, Oli, what are we doing?” she said. “Nobody does this.” Evangelista is the communications manager for Santo Domingo’s most intriguing restaurant, Casarré. Her boss, Swiss Dominican chef Olivier Bur, was leading Evangelista, photographer Clay Williams, and me beyond the fortified walls of the Zona Colonial, where few travel on foot.

On the other side, we turned a corner and found hundreds gathered around a dance floor in the undercroft of a bigger bridge. Live bachata drowned out the traffic overhead. Bur procured a substantial bottle of Presidente and plastic cups from a vendor, poured, and raised a “Salud!”.

According to recent reports, bur normally walks (or bikes) everywhere. Moving slowly, he’s learned the textures of the city. Still, for the next six days, he took Williams and me to his most beloved restaurants by car. We visited a string of chimi stands where hawkers compete for clientele through the night; a chicharrón spot where couples dance shoeless on the cool tile floor; and a cafeteria where boys shuffle stewed eggplant, beets, and goat to bus drivers en route. Places like these are the “infrastructure for life,” Bur stated. “Thirty years ago, there was nothing else.”.

Over the last couple of decades, however, another dining scene has sprouted. Dominican chefs have returned from kitchens in Mexico, Japan, or Switzerland to explore the forgotten and sometimes shunned ingredients of their (or their parents’) homes. They served us conch, cassava, breadfruit, and djon-djon mushrooms in sashimis, foams, tostones, and surprising dessert creams. The dishes were fresh and exciting, but local and global traditions have always mingled—as such, the cuisine is not “Latest Dominican,” it’s simply “Dominican,” fully expressed.

Calle Andrés Julio Aybar 13+1 829 545 7503.

According to recent reports, the Piantini neighborhood was once verdant and sleepy, according to Bur. Now it’s a bustling business district. Most of the remaining vegetation decorates the façades of restaurants, like Ajualä’s. Brushed palm thatch and a bushy barba de Fidel (Fidel’s beard) tree greet you at the tall aged-steel door.

In a recent development, venezuelan chef Saverio Stassi is a leader among the culinary new guard. His treatment of local ingredients is virtuosic. He confits guinea hen in cocoa butter and tops breadfruit tostones with local yellowfin and Cambita avocado; and over two days, his team bathes the succulent goat from the northwest—where they famously graze on wild oregano, self-infusing their meat—in Seville orange juice before roasting it in a barbacoa pit.

Calle Max Henríquez Ureña 14+1 809 547 3592.

In a recent development, chef Erik Malmsten has cooked at his parents’ cabaret in Gothenburg, Sweden, at Aquavit in New York, and at Bocuse d’Or competitions around the world. But to take his career to the next level, he returned to his mother’s homeland to open a Nordic-Japanese restaurant.

According to recent reports, “You’ll see, it’s really good,” Bur told us. The meal starts with “lobster chicharrón,” with a reduced crustacean bisque, fried into airy orange sheets of bubbly crackling and served with tōgarashi Kewpie. Then, a parade of sashimi, like king fish, served with brown butter soy emulsion, ikura, and lemon zest. It ends with Dominican chocolates, molded, painted, and plated to look like koi fish on a synchronized swim.

Calle Caonabo 35+1 809 584 9481.

If, like me, you come from a pizza region, you might not be inclined to use one of your Santo Domingo meal slots on a pie. But I urge you: Make time for Casa Gazcue. Spanish Dominican chef Francis Pena’s 48-hour-fermented crust comes blistered and sometimes covered in honeyed sesame seeds. Iterations are variously laden with spicy Dominican oxtail, chimi sandwich sauce, pistachio, and jamón ibérico, but you don’t have to choose: For groups, he serves a rosca (a round with an open middle) of six sections arranged like floral pizza petals.

Calle Pablo Casals+1 809 562 6060.

It has been revealed that in 1954, the Bonarelli family opened the legendary Italian restaurant Vesuvio. For decades, it was the place—the only place—to go out for a formal sit-down meal around here. Vesuvio closed over 20 years ago, but the founder’s grandson, Giancarlo Bonarelli, now runs Bottega Fratelli in a sleek modern building in Naco (Piantini’s equally upscale neighbor).

Recent findings suggest that you’ll notice a great variety of beet dishes in the Dominican Republic. Farmers harvest them year-round in the cool, pine-forested Costanza Valley. Try them here, roasted and served with blue cheese, chèvre, candied nuts, and honey. Also try a carpaccio of king mackerel, caught off the eastern coast, or any of the risottos, an emblem of the family’s enduring Italian culinary influence.

Calle del Seminario #57+1 809 565 1621.

According to recent reports, hideyoshi Tateyama’s parents opened Samurai in 1990. The restaurant joined Vesuvio, along with one or two others in that era’s small restaurant scene. It still stands out today among the many dozens.

It has been revealed that be sure to order the guatapaná con coco. A tried-and-true combo of shrimp and coconut imbued with native guatapaná leaf, tobiko, sesame seed, and scallion—it’s been on the menu for two decades. Also, don’t miss the chance to sample a sashimi of the meter-long “calamar diamante” from the Samaná region. It’s simply brightened with lemon zest. Meals are capped with a green tea amaro. Once a month, Tateyama personally runs a chef’s-choice omakase service.

Avenida Independencia 312+1 809 682 1433.

On the day we visited Villar Hermanos, lines formed around the block for each of two buffets. Women balanced towers of takeout containers tightly wrapped in plastic. It was the World Cup Final, and people were rushing to get some of the city’s best comfort food to their coffee tables. “This is the place to come for all the Dominican classics,” Bur told us.

In a recent development, we found a large table under the sprawling canopy of a banyan tree and ordered mofongo. It was moist, punctuated with crisp chicharrón crackling. The sancocho, the classic Domincan stew thick with potato and yuca starch, assumed extra body when alternating spoonfuls of broth and rice. While I didn’t have my coveted mangú and tres golpes (salami, queso frito, and eggs), I would trade my house and car to live next door and eat breakfast there every morning under the filtered sun.

Avenida San Vicente de Paúl, Santo Domingo Este 11504+1 809 244 8906.

In a recent development, on Avenida San Vicente de Paúl in East Santo Domingo, scooters zip down the busy street all through the night, many popping over a curb into the Plaza Del Chimi. The “plaza” is a stretch of  10 to 15 “chimi” sandwich stalls outfitted with griddles and prep stations heaped with roasted pork shoulders. Dealers swiftly slice the meat, lay it on the griddle, flip it onto a squishy pan de agua roll, and top it with cabbage, tomato, and tangy pink sauce before sliding it into your mitts. The stalls are open till 6 a.m. When they run out of beer, a man runs bottles from a cooler at his house and serves them in paper bags.

Avenida Independencia KM 8+1 809 532 2580.

It has been revealed that across from a shopping mall on Avenida Indepencia, about a dozen cars cram into five parking spaces for the lunch or late-night staple pica pollo. Behind a crowded serving station, a woman slides eight pounds of chicken into a hotel pan, and the picking begins. Six sets of tongs compete for room, like bird beaks, snapping the chicken into styrofoam containers before barely holding them shut with strained rubber bands. Another eight pounds comes out less than two minutes later.

Pica pollo is one of the lasting influences of Chinese immigrants in Santo Domingo. Usually cooks marinate it in bitter orange, garlic, and oregano before coating it in flour and spice (in this case we detected Chinese five-spice) and deep-frying it to golden brown.

Avenida Cayetano Germosén+1 809 286 2141.

At Parque Mirador Sur, teens and whole families perch along concrete walls and hilltops eating fried yuca and succulent mojo-dipped chicharrón with long toothpicks. It comes from the crowded, steel-barred serving window across the street: Chicharrones Light de la Cayetano.

Recent findings suggest that among all the chicharrón we ate in the city (there was a lot), theirs stood out. There’s a small covered seating area where you can order beer to share. Bachata plays loud over a hanging speaker. Women take turns kicking off their heels to do the four-step shimmy with their jevos (boyfriends).

Calle Ciriaco Ramirez 70+1 809 689 5544.

In a recent development, the Colmado, Bur states, “is essential to Dominican life. Everything happens there.” For 70 years, Colmado La Venganza has anchored a prominent corner in the Don Bosco neighborhood. It’s hosted thousands of late-night domino games and sports viewing parties. We were there during the World Cup.

At the entrance, a man with a crisp-edged haircut, big sunglasses, and a pressed floral shirt parked his shoe on a milk crate while a boy polished it with a rag. Inside, groups spanning all ages gathered at high-tops and around the bar. Folks shared triple-stacked ham, pickle, and cheese sandwiches, pressed, cubed, and spiked with toothpicks: the “sándwich especial.” Leaving the bar, chef Raniel Cruz (part of our party) texted his mom in Montreal. She responded: “Wait, you’re at Venganza? I used to drink there.”.

Calle Luperón 52+1 849 460 5600.

One couldn’t understand the Dominican Republic’s vast culinary splendor in a lifetime, but if you had just one night to try, you’d want to dine at Casarré. Every Tuesday, the team takes excursions. We accompanied them to meet the countryside cooks, who wrap guáyiga root masa in leaves from the almond trees on Najayo beach and bake it in coal-covered pots. We visited a produce market, where vendors passed fruit samples, like little red “frutas milagrosas” that, when chewed beforehand, make bitter limes taste like sweet limeade.

At night, in a candlelit, contemplative room in the Zona Colonial, Bur and his team showcase their findings in a series of sublime, thoughtful dishes. On our visit, they presented djon-djon mushrooms from the Haitian borderlands in a sweet, guáyiga-thickened foam and in the broth of a citrusy okra and fish soup. Chef Isabella Sánchez explained: “The broth is murky, like the current state of the Río Ozama. It represents the negative aspects of our water—contamination and conflict—and the beautiful: the fish, the beaches, and our grandmother’s tea.”.

Avenida Lope de Vega 44+1 809 816 7200.

In a recent development, smoke from an open Uruguayan-style parrilla floats in the soft light over two stories. Our waiter said, “We want this to feel like a Sunday asado.” Indeed, the smoke, the char, and the Malbec are there. This asado, though, also has Negronis smoked tableside and poured from a glass goose. As we awaited a perfect aged rib eye, we enjoyed paper-thin beef carpaccio with foie, and a paella-esque rice with soft leeks, cilantro, and pork trotters.

Recommendations on where to dine, shop, and stay, wherever you’re headed next.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Divinity candy is a classic Southern dessert.
  • In the large bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment, combine the egg whites and salt.
  • In a medium pot, combine the sugar, corn syrup, and water.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Divinity candy is a classic Southern dessert. If you haven't heard of it yet, I promise you'll be coming back to this recipe over and over again after making it just once! It’s a simple confection made of sugar, eggs, and corn syrup that looks like clouds, with the crunch of meringue and the chew of a perfect marshmallow. It does require a candy thermometer and a bit of patience, but once you know what to look for, it’s extremely simple to make.

In the large bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment, combine the egg whites and salt.

In a medium pot, combine the sugar, corn syrup, and water. Attach a candy thermometer to the pot before you go any further. Heat the mixture over medium-high heat, undisturbed, until the thermometer registers 250°, which should take about 10 minutes. When the thermometer registers 235°, start whipping egg whites on high speed until stiff peaks form, which should take another 2 to 3 minutes.

Sources indicate that with the mixer running on medium speed, carefully add sugar syrup to egg whites in a thin stream. Make sure to go slowly! The whole process should take about 1 to 2 minutes. Then beat in the vanilla extract.

Proceed to increase mixer speed to high and continue to whip until the mixture comes together and loses some of its gloss, which should take approximately 5 to 10 minutes. Let it all cool until the mixture is slightly thickened and holds its form when spooned onto parchment, another 1 to 2 minutes.

In a recent development, grease 2 spoons with cooking spray, and working rapidly, spoon candy onto a parchment-lined baking sheet. Swirl it as desired to make the shapes you want! Immediately top the dessert with sprinkles. (The sprinkles won’t stick if you wait too long!).

According to recent reports, let the candy sit until it’s completely dry, just about 2 hours more. Store in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 1 week and enjoy!

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Recent findings suggest that the candy can be made 1 week ahead. Store in an airtight container at room temperature.

11 Leftover Turkey Sandwiches to Look Forward To

💡 Key Takeaways

  • These Thanksgiving sandwiches make the most of what you’ve got, whether that’s a few slices of turkey or enough stuffing and cranberry sauce for an encore.
  • This turkey sandwich takes inspiration from one of the all-time greats: the tuna melt.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It is a universal truth that the food the day after Thanksgiving is just as exciting (if not more so) as what’s served on the holiday itself. With a fridge full of Thanksgiving leftovers, the possibilities are endless. But leftovers reach their most perfect form in a sandwich, where all the components play off one other for a few transcendent bites.

These Thanksgiving sandwiches make the most of what you’ve got, whether that’s a few slices of turkey or enough stuffing and cranberry sauce for an encore. Go all in with a gooey melt, load a pita with spiced turkey and crunchy vegetables, or give turkey the chicken salad treatment. There’s no need for post-holiday blues when a leftover turkey sandwich is on the horizon.

This turkey sandwich takes inspiration from one of the all-time greats: the tuna melt. You might be surprised by how well turkey takes to the format. For the full diner experience, serve it with potato chips and a dill pickle.

These leftover turkey sliders have a lot going on, in the best way. Picture: melty cheese, cranberry mayo, garlic butter, turkey, mashed potatoes, and more where that came from.

Give your Thanksgiving leftovers the club treatment by layering turkey and cranberry sauce with crisp bacon and lettuce. And don’t forget that middle slide of bread. We’re not animals, after all.

In a recent development, need a break from heavy Thanksgiving fare but still have turkey to use up? Shred it, toss it with butter-bloomed spices, and tuck it into a pita with a bright, tangy slaw.

According to recent reports, in this play on a turkey club, the middle slice of bread gets swapped out for leftover stuffing fried in bacon fat. (We repeat: stuffing fried in bacon fat.).

Turkey and cranberry sauce already have a salty-sweet thing going on. Why not play that up by swapping plain bread for custardy French toast?

Sometimes it’s best to keep a leftover turkey sandwich simple. Turkey, cranberry sauce, cheese, and fresh sage, pressed until golden, give you all the flavors of Thanksgiving in four ingredients (plus bread).

Industry observers note that though the recipe calls for cooked chicken, you guessed it—you can swap in leftover turkey seamlessly. The apple and fennel both provide lots of crunch and freshness.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The European Space Agency’s (ESA) Hera spacecraft has captured its first close-up image of the Didymos asteroid system, revealing a surprisingly different side of the larger asteroid that scientists have never seen in such detail.
  • The discovery comes as Hera prepares to investigate the aftermath of NASA’s historic DART mission, which deliberately crashed a spacecraft into the smaller asteroid, Dimorphos, on September 26, 2022.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft has captured its first close-up image of the Didymos asteroid system, revealing a surprisingly different side of the asteroid near NASA’s historic 2022 collision site.

The European Space Agency’s (ESA) Hera spacecraft has captured its first close-up image of the Didymos asteroid system, revealing a surprisingly different side of the larger asteroid that scientists have never seen in such detail.

The discovery comes as Hera prepares to investigate the aftermath of NASA’s historic DART mission, which deliberately crashed a spacecraft into the smaller asteroid, Dimorphos, on September 26, 2022. The collision successfully altered Dimorphos’ orbit, demonstrating that humans can change the course of an asteroid.

Recent findings suggest that hera’s upcoming image was taken from a distance of just 60 km using its monochromatic Asteroid Framing Camera. Although shadows obscure most of Dimorphos, which measures 151 meters across, the much larger Didymos, measuring 780 meters in diameter, is clearly visible. Dimorphos orbits Didymos as its smaller companion.

“The first thing we remarked was wow!” observes Hera Principal Investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at CNRS / Observatoire de la Côte d’Azur. “This is the other side of Didymos from the one that DART’s camera showed us shortly before impact, so this feels like looking at a whole new world.

“This side of Didymos has the same central ridge along its equator that we saw before, but otherwise appears very different, with multiple boulders and craters and what look like patterns of grooves or ridges.”.

Recent findings suggest that the unfamiliar terrain raises intriguing questions about whether NASA’s impact may have changed the surface of Didymos as well as the orbit of its smaller companion. Scientists believe material blasted off Dimorphos during the collision could have traveled across the approximately 1 km separating the two asteroids and landed on Didymos.

It has been revealed that ESA’s Hera mission scientist Michael Kueppers adds: “Since we expect a lot of impact-ejected material to have made it across the approximately 1 km of space from Dimorphos to Didymos, it may be that some of these characteristics originate from this transport of material, and we have exciting work ahead of us to sort it out. We look forward to seeing much more of both bodies and systemically mapping all the changes we identify.”.

Although Dimorphos is largely hidden in the latest image, it holds a unique place in space exploration history. It became the first object in the Solar System to have its orbit measurably changed by human intervention.

NASA achieved that milestone by sending its 580 kg DART spacecraft hurtling into Dimorphos at approximately 6.1 km/s. The impact shortened the asteroid’s orbital period around Didymos by 33 minutes, with a margin of error of about one minute. That change was substantially greater than scientists had predicted.

After a two-year journey, Hera has reached the binary asteroid system, located approximately 196.8 million km from Earth. The spacecraft is now preparing for a detailed ‘crash site investigation’ to determine how the collision affected both asteroids.

Hera’s findings could have major implications for planetary defense. While DART demonstrated that deliberately striking an asteroid can change its trajectory, scientists still need to understand precisely how the process works and what determines the size of the resulting orbital change.

Recent findings suggest that by closely examining Dimorphos and Didymos, Hera will help researchers refine the kinetic impact technique, which uses the momentum of a spacecraft collision to alter an asteroid’s motion. The goal is to transform NASA’s successful experiment into a predictable, repeatable method that could one day protect Earth from a threatening asteroid.

“Seeing this image is a hugely exciting moment for the whole Hera family,” comments Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli. “It has taken years of hard work and dedication to reach this point – but we’re motivated to know that the adventure is only beginning!”.

More detailed images of both asteroids are scheduled to be unveiled on November 25, offering scientists an even closer look at the aftermath of humanity’s first successful asteroid deflection experiment.

Scientists Discover a Hidden Magnetic Effect That Produces Signals 100 Times Stronger

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (729 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Antiferromagnets could pave the way for faster, more energy-efficient electronics, but accurately measuring their properties remains a major challenge.
  • Recent findings suggest that A nearly invisible layer of magnetic material can overwhelm scientific measurements, producing signals more than 100 times stronger than those of the material researchers are trying to study.
  • It has been revealed that the research focuses on antiferromagnets, materials in which neighboring atomic magnetic moments cancel one another out, leaving little or no overall magnetization.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Antiferromagnets could pave the way for faster, more energy-efficient electronics, but accurately measuring their properties remains a major challenge.

Recent findings suggest that A nearly invisible layer of magnetic material can overwhelm scientific measurements, producing signals more than 100 times stronger than those of the material researchers are trying to study. Scientists at Martin Luther University Halle-Wittenberg (MLU) and the Max Planck Institute for Microstructure Physics discovered this problem while investigating a promising material for ultrafast electronics. Their findings, published in Advanced Materials, also show how to prevent the interference.

It has been revealed that the research focuses on antiferromagnets, materials in which neighboring atomic magnetic moments cancel one another out, leaving little or no overall magnetization. Unlike conventional ferromagnets, they are resistant to electromagnetic interference and can switch magnetic states up to 1,000 times faster. These properties could help engineers develop faster electronic components that consume less energy.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers investigated Mn₃Sn, a compound made of manganese and tin that belongs to a special group called chiral antiferromagnets. Its magnetic moments are arranged at 120-degree angles rather than pointing in opposite directions. This arrangement has a property called chirality, meaning it cannot be superimposed on its mirror image simply by rotating or moving it.

In a recent development, “Chiral antiferromagnets combine the advantages of both classes of magnets while minimizing their drawbacks. However, they are often difficult to control,” explains Professor Georg Woltersdorf from the Institute of Physics at MLU and spokesperson for the Cluster of Excellence “Center for Chiral Electronics”.

Researchers in the cluster are exploring ways to use chirality in spintronics, an approach to electronics that exploits the spin of electrons as well as their electrical charge. Spin is an intrinsic form of angular momentum that gives electrons magnetic properties. Controlling it could enable electronic devices that operate at extremely high speeds while using less energy.

According to recent reports, to examine Mn₃Sn, the team fabricated layers just a few nanometers thick and combined them with either platinum or a nickel-iron alloy. They then exposed the samples to ultrashort laser pulses and measured the resulting electrical voltages on picosecond timescales, equivalent to trillionths of a second. These measurements allowed the researchers to investigate rapid changes in magnetic order.

Recent findings suggest that however, the samples containing platinum produced unexpected results. The researchers traced the problem to a heating step used during fabrication to repair defects in the crystal structure. During this process, atoms at the interface between the materials reacted to form an unintended ferromagnetic compound.

Recent findings suggest that this thin interfacial layer generated magnetic signals more than 100 times stronger than those produced by Mn₃Sn itself. As a result, the measurements were dominated by the newly formed compound rather than the antiferromagnet the scientists intended to investigate.

“It was only when we modified the process and allowed the Mn₃Sn layer to be cure fully before depositing the platinum that the material remained unchanged. Before that, we had essentially only been measuring a layer that was an unintended result of the sample preparation process,” explains the study’s first author Paul Marschall from the Institute of Physics at MLU.

By completing the heating treatment before adding platinum, the researchers avoided forming the unwanted magnetic compound. Properly prepared samples then allowed them to investigate the actual properties of Mn₃Sn, including how efficiently it converts spin currents into measurable electrical voltages.

When the scientists directed a spin current from the nickel-iron layer into Mn₃Sn, they found that the conversion efficiency was approximately 10% of that typically achieved with platinum. This provided a more reliable assessment of the material’s behavior without the interfering magnetic layer.

Industry observers note that “Interfaces are not just a peripheral aspect of spintronics, they are often the actual component. If we want to harness chiral antiferromagnets for technological applications, we must first understand and be able to control what happens within these few atomic layers,” concludes Woltersdorf.

It has been revealed that reference: “Spin Transport Across Interfaces With the Non-Collinear Antiferromagnet Mn3Sn” by Paul A. Marschall, Wolfgang Hoppe, Prajwal Rigvedi, Börge Göbel, Franziska Ziolkowski, Samir Lounis, Banabir Pal, Stuart S. P. Parkin and Georg Woltersdorf, 20 September 2026, Advanced Materials. DOI: 10.1002/adma.75024.

The study was funded by the German Research Foundation (DFG).

Alexis Nikole Nelson, aka the Black Forager, Makes Nature Her Buffet

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1987 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Saveur

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is Amused Bouche, SAVEUR’s food questionnaire that explores the culinary curiosities of some of our favorite people.
  • Alexis Nicole Nelson’s life mantra is simple: “Don’t put things in your face hole unless you know what they are!” This mostly applies to foraging wild foods, something she has been doing since she was a kid with her mom and has since turned into a flourishing career and community.
  • According to recent reports, nelson’s journey to becoming the Black Forager started with an interest in vegetarianism as a 5-year-old, which, at the time, was discouraged by her family.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is Amused Bouche, SAVEUR’s food questionnaire that explores the culinary curiosities of some of our favorite people. This interview series will dive deep into their food routines, including dinner party strategies, cherished cookbooks, and the memorable bites they’d hop on a flight for.

Alexis Nicole Nelson’s life mantra is simple: “Don’t put things in your face hole unless you know what they are!” This mostly applies to foraging wild foods, something she has been doing since she was a kid with her mom and has since turned into a flourishing career and community. She has showcased her adventures and recipes as @blackforager since 2018 (with millions of curious followers across Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube) and now in her debut cookbook, Happy Snacking, Don’t Die! This comprehensive guide to finding and cooking with ingredients from your backyard or nearby forests and fields is organized by season and anchored by Nelson’s vibrant personality and boundless energy, encouraging readers to get out of their comfort zones and educate themselves on edible plants hiding in plain sight.

According to recent reports, nelson’s journey to becoming the Black Forager started with an interest in vegetarianism as a 5-year-old, which, at the time, was discouraged by her family. “You have to finish growing first!” Nelson recalls her mom saying. Nelson ate meat products to keep from wasting food her parents prepared until she was 12, when she decided to start packing her own lunches. “It was a lot of undressed Boca burgers and French fries. It was a bleak time,” she admits with a laugh. She went fully vegan at 24 and hasn’t looked back.

I am not a very outdoorsy person, but I was captivated by the whimsical way Nelson goes about foraging and sharing online, and even more so after chatting with her on a recent Zoom call. When I asked for easy gateway foraging ideas, she immediately suggested field garlic or onion grass: “I am a biased party, because that is the first forageable that my mom taught me. Once you notice it, you see it everywhere, and it has a foolproof test, which is the smell test. If you break it and it doesn’t very fragrantly smell of onions and garlic, you have the wrong plant. Easy, easy!” She recommended looking for little purple flowers or round pink spiky balls, and on my next walk with my dogs, I spotted some. I haven’t picked and cooked with any yet, but now I’m on the lookout (and smell-out) for this abundant allium and strategy on pairing it with the maitake bacon recipe from her book. Nelson suggested making a “BLT-adjacent sandwich with whatever mild greens are in season, a slice of tomato, and maitake bacon on toasty sourdough.”.

Whether you’re a foraging beginner or an expert, Nelson’s edition of Amused Bouche will be equally eye-opening and mouthwatering. Read on for her adventures and misadventures in the fields and in her home kitchen.

If you could only eat one thing 24/7/365, what would it be?

Industry observers note that I love a tofu scramble and mixing in whatever is in season, and I bring home mushrooms, greens, and aromatics. In the springtime, it’ll be ramp leaves and oyster mushrooms. In the summer, it’s chanterelle and bicolor bolete with some nodding onion flowers from my front yard. As we move into winter, I’m thankful that we get enoki mushrooms pretty consistently all throughout the season in the woods. I do a combo of firm silken and super-firm tofu because I want the best of both worlds. Eggs don’t just have one texture; the whites and yolks are different, and I always want to try to get as close to eggs as I can with my tofu textures. I’m perpetually on a search for a forageable legume that I can make my own tofu with. One of my friends, Jesse Akozbek (@feralforaging), makes tofu with black walnuts.

What’s the first thing you learned how to cook?

The first thing that I remember cooking is baking cakes with my dad—usually just a basic frosted vanilla cake. My mom used to be a cool head-honcho character at Procter & Gamble, and she would be gone for two or three weeks at a time for work. We’d bake the cake the night before [she got back], frost it, and then just before she came home, we’d leave the cake out and hide.

How about your latest kitchen adventure?

In a recent development, I broke out my food mill because I went a little overboard harvesting cornelian cherries with my fiancé this year. They’re fun to harvest, and we brought a step stool to reach more and ended up going home with a couple gallons of fruit. It’s all fun and games until you see them all on the counter and realize they’re gonna go bad so I gotta figure out what I’m doing with all of this. I thought of doing a glacé cornelian cherry like I’ve done with chestnuts before, but the water content of the cherries is so high that when I simmered them in a sugar syrup, they just disintegrated and disappeared. I tried to stir it carefully, but it all just turned into goo. I fished them out with my little spider, put them in my food mill, and ground it. They have big ol’ pits on the inside, and I am not trying to eat any of those. It was an applesauce consistency in the end, but like what if applesauce had dreams? What if applesauce was the star of a Studio Ghibli movie? I made cornelian cherry shortcakes with it, and my fiancé was like, “So I’ve had three…” and we realized that when you eat a lot of fruit and fiber at once, you remember it later. I also saved the flavored syrup that was created after straining out all of the goopy fruits, and I am saving it specifically for making Shirley Temples!

What’s your treat-yourself splurge?

My favorite way to treat myself is getting dinner with my fiancé at Agni, an amazing Bengali American fusion restaurant here in Columbus, led by my friend, chef Avishar Barua! They have these french fries that take three days to make, and I—no joke—dream about them sometimes.

What’s your most cherished cookbook?

It has been revealed that marie Viljoen’s Forage, Harvest, Feast is the cookbook that showed me as a recent college graduate that foraging, the weird thing I’ve been doing since childhood, could become such elevated cuisine. It’s absolutely stunning, and she is a recipe and photography genius—she does it all! I remember checking that book out from the library for the first time and my jaw dropping at how she used foraged foods in ways I had never even let myself consider. She gets shouted out in my cookbook because I used a few of her recipes as a jumping-off point then over time I started changing things to make them my own. A decade later, it becomes something different but still has the heart of that original recipe, like my milkweed nectar is definitely the child of her milkweed cordial! Her book was eye-opening for me even before I knew this was what I was going to end up making my career, back when it was something I just did because I loved it and I was a poor recent grad. A really great way to spruce up a 59-cent pack of ramen is wild greens and mushrooms!

Is there a cooking disaster that made you swear off a dish forever?

I keep doing this thing where I start fermenting drinks and then travel, which is dumb. Don’t do that! My most explosive ferment was actually not mine, it was a gift from fellow foraging friend Gabrielle Cerberville (@chaoticforager). She very kindly brought me a bottle of her wild plum wine, and I did not put it straight into the fridge because I was not using my noggin. Three days later, I went to open it to pair with dinner, and it was like my world was in slow motion and it was just a geyser everywhere! Wine on the ceiling, wine on the walls, a lot of wine on the floor, a lot of wine on me. I cleaned it up sadly, shooing my pets away. No drunk pets! I also had a milkweed cordial explode, which meant I had to scrub sticky pink off every single thing in the refrigerator. Do not recommend it.

Which nostalgic foods from childhood bring you the most comfort?

I grew up in the Cincinnati area, so there will be a soft spot in my heart for Cincinnati chili forever. It’s just ingrained within me. Thankfully Skyline has vegan rice and beans using the same spices that you can also put onto pasta like a wild Ohioan. That will always taste like a Friday evening with my dad, because my mom is from New England and famously hates Cincinnati chili. I think calling it a chili was maybe its biggest downfall—when you learn about the history behind it and how it’s actually the child of a Greek meat sauce, suddenly the spice palette makes so much more sense. I think people would be so much cooler with that, but everyone’s expecting Tex-Mex chili, and that is not what you are signing up for!

When you’re playing dinner party DJ, what’s spinning?

There was a podcast I was obsessed with called The Dinner Party Download a decade ago, and I named my playlist after that. It has been evolving throughout the past 10 years and has Mitski, which I know feels sad for a dinner party but it’s mellow, some alt-J, Bill Withers, The Contours. A lot of Motown-era music, like The Supremes, Stevie Wonder, The Four Tops, Staple Singers. And then Janelle Monáe, Kate Nash, “Rhapsody in Blue” by George Gershwin is thrown in there. I go all over the place, but I think it creates a general buzzy atmosphere. I don’t want it to necessarily be as dancey as a dance party, but I also don’t want people to fall asleep, either.

What is your biggest entertaining flex to impress guests?

According to recent reports, I really love plating things and cutting things into fun shapes and making them look pretty. I took a cooking class in Japan with Elizabeth Andoh, a very prolific cookbook writer, a couple of years ago, and after my fiancé and I walked out of it, we were just like, “Dang, our food’s real ugly!” A huge part of her class was how much presentation matters and how the first way that you are consuming the food is with your sight, with your eyes, so why not make it look cute?

Tell me about a meal so good you would hop on a flight to relive it.

While my fiancé and I were in Florence for a friend’s wedding, we knew that Italy, historically, was not the easiest place to be vegan. You can find things but maybe not that many things, and maybe not the things that look as good as the things everybody else is eating. So I was big sad the entire time until we stumbled into a tiny hole-in-the-wall vegan restaurant called Il Vegano. We found it on Google by searching “vegan restaurants near me,” and it had the best pasta with tomato sauce and tiramisù that either of us have ever had. Mind you, my fiancé is not vegan and very much could still eat real tiramisù and did on that trip. And the night ended with us essentially begging in broken Italian for the head chef to write a cookbook. We waddled back to our hotel saying it was the best meal we’ve ever had.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists conducting atmospheric research in rural Oklahoma unexpectedly detected a toxic class of industrial chemicals never before measured in the air of the Western Hemisphere.
  • Toxic industrial chemicals used in everything from metalworking fluids to plastics have turned up in an unexpected place: the air above rural Oklahoma farmland.
  • Researchers detected medium-chain chlorinated paraffins (MCCPs) in the region while investigating an entirely different atmospheric process, marking the first reported detection of these pollutants in North American air.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists conducting atmospheric research in rural Oklahoma unexpectedly detected a toxic class of industrial chemicals never before measured in the air of the Western Hemisphere.

Toxic industrial chemicals used in everything from metalworking fluids to plastics have turned up in an unexpected place: the air above rural Oklahoma farmland.

Researchers detected medium-chain chlorinated paraffins (MCCPs) in the region while investigating an entirely different atmospheric process, marking the first reported detection of these pollutants in North American air.

The University of Colorado Boulder researchers identified the pollutants during a 2023 field campaign near Lamont, Oklahoma. Their findings, published in ACS Environmental Au, also reveal how atmospheric MCCP concentrations fluctuate with temperature.

In a recent development, using a nitrate chemical ionization mass spectrometer, the team continuously monitored air at an agricultural site for nearly a month. While examining the chemical signatures in the measurements, CU Boulder chemistry PhD student Daniel Katz noticed unusual isotopic patterns that he eventually identified as MCCPs.

“It’s very exciting as a scientist to find something unexpected like this that we weren’t looking for,” stated Katz, the study’s lead author. “We’re starting to learn more about this toxic, organic pollutant that we know is out there, and which we need to understand better.”.

The instrument detected 18 groups of gaseous MCCPs. Their estimated average concentration was approximately 3.1 nanograms per cubic meter, although the researchers consider this a lower-bound estimate. Concentrations were substantially higher than those reported in remote polar regions, suggesting nearby sources may be contributing to the pollution.

Industry observers note that the researchers also observed a consistent daily cycle: gaseous MCCP concentrations increased during warmer daylight hours and declined at night. Their analysis suggests that temperature controls how these chemicals move between the gas phase and airborne particles, potentially affecting how long they remain in the atmosphere and how far they travel.

In a recent development, MCCPs are widely used in metalworking fluids, PVC manufacturing, and textiles. They can enter wastewater and accumulate in sewage sludge, which is sometimes processed into biosolid fertilizer and spread on agricultural fields. Researchers suspect this practice could explain some of the pollution detected in Oklahoma, although they have not confirmed its source.

It has been revealed that “When sewage sludges are spread across the fields, those toxic compounds could be released into the air,” Katz mentioned. “We can’t show directly that that’s happening, but we think it’s a reasonable way that they could be winding up in the air. Sewage sludge fertilizers have been shown to release similar compounds.”.

MCCPs are chemically related to short-chain chlorinated paraffins (SCCPs), which have faced restrictions because of their toxicity, environmental persistence, and potential to accumulate in living organisms. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency began regulating SCCPs in 2009, and the Stockholm Convention added them to its list of persistent organic pollutants in 2017.

Researchers suspect restrictions on SCCPs may have encouraged greater use of MCCPs as substitutes, potentially increasing their environmental presence.

Industry observers note that “We always have these unintended consequences of regulation, where you regulate something, and then there’s still a need for the products that those were in,” noted Ellie Browne, CU Boulder chemistry professor, CIRES Fellow, and study co-author. “So they get replaced by something.”.

According to recent reports, although the team identified MCCPs in Oklahoma’s air, their exact source remains unknown. Wind measurements suggest several possible sources in the surrounding region, while the observed temperature fluctuations indicate that interactions with airborne particles influence their concentrations. The researchers also detected compounds consistent with products formed when MCCPs undergo atmospheric oxidation.

Further measurements across different seasons and locations could establish how widespread these chemicals are and clarify their atmospheric transport, chemical reactions, and environmental persistence.

According to recent reports, “We identified them, but we still don’t know exactly what they do when they are in the atmosphere, and they need to be investigated further,” Katz said. “I think it’s key that we continue to have governmental agencies that are capable of evaluating the science and regulating these chemicals as necessary for public health and safety.”.

Reference: “Real-Time Measurements of Gas-Phase Medium-Chain Chlorinated Paraffins Reveal Daily Changes in Gas-Particle Partitioning Controlled by Ambient Temperature” by Daniel John Katz, Bri Dobson, Mitchell Alton, Harald Stark, Douglas R. Worsnop, Manjula R. Canagaratna and Eleanor C. Browne, 16 July 2025, ACS Environmental Au. DOI: 10.1021/acsenvironau.5c00038.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson, right, here at a hearing in June, lost his reelection bid in North Carolina's 9th District. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

North Carolina Rep. Richard Hudson, the chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee, has lost his race for reelection, a stinging defeat for the man charged with preserving the House majority for the GOP.

Hudson fell to Democrat Richard Ojeda, a former West Virginia state senator who was leading  51 percent to 49 percent Thursday afternoon  when The Associated Press called the race in North Carolina’s 9th District.

Hudson had already conceded the race Wednesday, when it became clear that his path to victory was closing off.

“[The] voters of North Carolina’s 9th District made their choice and I respect it,” he stated in a statement. “Since 2013 I’ve worked for North Carolina families. That includes the soldiers and families at Fort Bragg, who sacrifice more for this country than most people will ever know.”.

Hudson is now the second party campaign chief to lose his seat during a midterm election this decade. In 2022, New York Rep. Sean Patrick Maloney lost reelection while serving as chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

Republicans across North Carolina experienced devastating losses on election night. As of Thursday afternoon, Democrats had also flipped the seats of Reps. Addison McDowell, Brad Knott and Tim Moore, as well as the open seat of retiring Rep. Chuck Edwards. The races for five other GOP-held seats remain uncalled, while Democratic Rep. Don Davis was reelected despite being targeted for defeat under a latest GOP-drawn congressional map. Republicans also lost control of the North Carolina House and lost seats in the state Senate.

North Carolina’s 9th District, which includes the Eastern Piedmont region and the Fayetteville area, was far from the House battlefield for much of the midterm cycle. President Donald Trump carried the seat by 16 points in 2024, according to calculations by Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales, and Hudson won a seventh term the same year by nearly 19 points. Hudson also held a financial advantage over Ojeda, raising $4.2 million to Ojeda’s $2.9 million through mid-October.

But in the waning weeks of the campaign, signs of Republican concern grew and Hudson’s campaign began spending on ads.

Sources indicate that ojeda was first elected to the West Virginia Senate in 2016. He ran for the U.S. House two years later as a Trump-voting Democrat but lost that race to Republican Carol Miller. He then briefly ran for the 2020 Democratic presidential nomination and also challenged GOP Sen. Shelley Moore Capito later that cycle but lost in the Democratic primary.

Ojeda moved to North Carolina in 2020, he told CityView, a local magazine, and he announced his challenge to Hudson last year.

Recent findings suggest that throughout the campaign, he attacked the incumbent over his support for Trump’s agenda, particularly the war in Iran. Ojeda is a retired Army major and the district is home to Fort Bragg, the nation’s largest Army base by population, where the Democrat was previously stationed for more than a decade.

“We did the impossible,’’ Ojeda told supporters Tuesday night. “We took on the chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee, a man with political connections, the billionaire donors, and the entire Washington establishment standing beside him.”.

According to recent reports, hudson, 55, is finishing his seventh term in the House and his second term as NRCC chair. He had no primary opponent this year and had grown used to winning reelection by comfortable margins.

As a legislator, Hudson focused much of his policy agenda on health concerns such as federal pandemic preparedness programs. He serves on the House Energy and Commerce Committee and chairs the panel's Communications and Technology Subcommittee.

Scientists Discover 15,000-Year-Old Clay Figures That Rewrite the History of Human Art
