Tech Report: Longtime West Virginia Sen. Rockefeller dies

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1840 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rockefeller IV, D-W.Va., questions witnesses during a Senate Finance hearing on health care on June 23, 2011.
  • Jay Rockefeller, a five-term West Virginia Democrat and champion for the rural poor, has died at the age of 89.
  • Rockefeller, who retired after the 2014 elections, played key roles on the tax-writing Senate Finance Committee, where he helped write landmark children’s health insurance legislation, as well as the Commerce, Science and Transportation and Intelligence panels which he chaired.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, sen. John D. Rockefeller IV, D-W.Va., questions witnesses during a Senate Finance hearing on health care on June 23, 2011. (Scott J. Ferrell/CQ Roll Call).

Former Sen. Jay Rockefeller, a five-term West Virginia Democrat and champion for the rural poor, has died at the age of 89.

Rockefeller, who retired after the 2014 elections, played key roles on the tax-writing Senate Finance Committee, where he helped write landmark children’s health insurance legislation, as well as the Commerce, Science and Transportation and Intelligence panels which he chaired.

In a recent development, A staunchly progressive lawmaker, he represented a deeply conservative state that turned further to the right in his later years. Rockefeller, scion of a famous Newly introduced York family renowned for its wealth, never wavered in his convictions and retired rather than face a potential backlash from voters upset by the then-Obama administration’s attempts to rein in the coal industry.

It has been revealed that sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., who challenged Rockefeller for his seat before he decided not to seek reelection, released a statement Friday praising her predecessor’s legacy.

Sources indicate that “Jay dedicated his life to serving West Virginia and our nation, leaving a lasting legacy. He was always a true gentleman who treated me with respect, kindness, and encouragement,” Capito noted. “Over the years, we developed a wonderful friendship that transcended politics, and I will always be grateful for that.”.

West Virginia’s Republican Gov. Patrick Morrisey — himself a transplanted Northerner, with roots in Brooklyn and New Jersey — lauded Rockefeller’s record on health care and aid for coal miners and veterans in their adopted state.

“His work helped shape our state and left a lasting mark on the lives of generations of West Virginians,” Morrisey remarked.

Industry observers note that rockefeller was born in Upcoming York City on June 18, 1937, the great-grandson of Standard Oil Co. founder John D. Rockefeller, who was once considered the world’s richest man. Rockefeller attended Harvard University, graduating with an A.B. in 1961. His passion was for the Far East and he spent three years studying at the International Christian University in Tokyo.

He returned to the states and was appointed by President John F. Kennedy to the National Advisory Council of the Peace Corps in 1961, spearheaded the Peace Corps initial program in the Philippines. He worked for a brief time in what was then known as U.S. Department of Far Eastern Affairs before deciding to embark on a public service role of a more personal nature. He enrolling as a VISTA volunteer, in the program which would later be known as AmeriCorps, and moved to the small mining community of Emmons, W.Va., in 1964 at age 27.

Sources indicate that in West Virginia, Rockefeller found his life’s work. He described the experience as being “reborn,” and spoke often the poverty and hardship he encountered living in the small town. “I could not leave,” he said of West Virginia. “I [had] become so devoted to those people and the unfairness.".

According to recent reports, he had planned to remain only one year, but decided to stay and became active in local politics. He broke from his family's long tradition of Republican loyalty and ran successfully for the House of Delegates as a Democrat in 1966. Two years later, he was elected secretary of state.

Sources indicate that rockefeller lost a bid for governor in 1972, but he became the president of West Virginia Wesleyan College and continued to place roots in the state. He married Sharon Percy Rockefeller in 1967 and they started their family. When he ran for governor again in 1976, he won, and served two terms before winning election to the U.S. Senate in 1984, ultimately serving five terms before retiring in 2014.

Rockefeller was determined to increase economic opportunities for West Virginia, for whom he felt was forgotten and abandoned by the rest of the country. He called the people of his state “the hardest-working people I know,” and believed that bringing more business opportunities would help lift the state out of severe rural poverty and the dependence on the coal industry.

Industry observers note that rockefeller traveled to Japan and worked tirelessly to bring a Toyota manufacturing plant to Buffalo, W.Va, one of over twenty Japanese companies he’d brought to West Virginia. He fought for fair trade policies and targeted tax relief to protect West Virginia industries such as steel and chemicals.

Coal mining had long been the economic backbone of West Virginia, but Rockefeller felt more must be done to protect miners, many of whom worked in unsafe conditions or fell ill with pneumoconiosis, or black lung disease, after years of inhaling coal dust.

Sources indicate that but defying the coal industry came with a political cost. When Rockefeller originally ran for governor in 1972, he had opposed mountaintop mining, also called strip mining, or the practice of removing large amounts of earth and rock in order to access underground seams of coal. When he ran again in 1976, he reversed his position and won.

But even as he ascended to the Senate, Rockefeller remained both friend and foe to the coal industry.

Despite growing up on the Upper East Side of Manhattan, figuratively and literally hundreds of miles away from coal mines, Rockefeller understood its deep roots in West Virginia’s economy and culture. He believed it was the miners — rather than industry — for whom he was defending.

He hung a century-old photo of a coal miner in his Senate office in the Hart building, and would point to the photo and remark to visitors that “this is why I’m here and who I work for.”.

Rockefeller fought to secure pensions for miners, especially as coal companies would file for bankruptcy and immediately restructure to do away with pension intends.

In a recent development, in 1990, Rockefeller was one of only 11 senators to vote against the bipartisan Clean Air Act, which he felt disadvantaged workers in West Virginia. But those close to him remarked the decision weighed heavily on him, and Rockefeller privately worried that the lack of such regulations would pollute the air and destroy waterways, the brunt of which would be born by the same disadvantaged people whom he vowed to protect.

In a recent development, he believed strongly in the deliberative aspects of the legislative process, consuming great amounts of reading material to familiarize himself with the issues. During a time of increasing partisan rancor, Rockefeller still reached across the aisle to find a willing partner, even when there was not one to be found.

In 2010, as the Environmental Protection Agency’s greenhouse gas regulations were coming to fruition, Rockefeller came up with a compromise to delay implementation for two years.

In a recent development, he viewed himself as a broker between industry interests and the hard working people from coal-states like West Virginia. He had hoped that his years of standing up for coal miners and West Virginia interests would foster enough goodwill among industries primed to oppose any compromise that was less than an all-out rejection of the existing EPA statutes.

According to recent reports, but industry walked away from Rockefeller, preferring a hard-line opposition to EPA regulations, and lobbied other senators to vote against Rockefeller’s measure. Furious, Rockefeller took to the floor of the Senate to denounce the coal industry and its leaders, an unprecedented action for a popular coal-state senator.

“The reality is that many who run the coal industry today would rather attack false enemies and deny real problems then find solutions,” he said on the Senate floor in June 2012. “Scare tactics are a cynical waste of time, money and, worst of all, coal miners’ hopes. But sadly, these coal operators have closed themselves off from any other opposing voices and few dared to speak out for change — even though it’s been staring them in the face for years.”.

His fury against the coal industry was heard loudly, many speculating that he would retire rather than face reelection.

Sources indicate that he had won reelection to the Senate handily during his five campaigns. In 2008, his final election, he was reelected with nearly 64 percent of the vote. But six months following his fated coal speech, in January 2013, Rockefeller revealed he would retire at the end of his fifth term.

Rockefeller’s legacy may best be known for his fight to expand health care for vulnerable populations, including children, the economically disadvantaged and the elderly. Rockefeller served as one of the chief congressional champions for President Bill Clinton’s proposed health care overhaul, and later he played a critical role and was a loud progressive voice in writing and passing the Affordable Care Act in the Senate.

Industry observers note that rockefeller believed strongly in a public health insurance option, offering it as an amendment in the Senate Finance Committee during the ACA markup. A public-run insurance strategy, he stated, would put patients before profits, and help those people, especially West Virginians, with high health care costs and poor coverage who were left “out in the cold.”.

Sources indicate that "These are people," Rockefeller stated, visibly emotional during his closing arguments to the Senate Finance Committee. "Eleven-year-old kids. These are families, and we have to respect them. And you respect them by giving them a choice.".

According to recent reports, the amendment was rejected. Rockefeller pivoted to strengthening Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program provisions, believing that poor and disadvantaged families could seek refuge within those programs. CHIP had been one of Rockefeller’s signature legislative victories, helping to write that program initially in 1997 and later working on a major expansion that became law in 2009.

Despite his initial concerns and later disappointments — at one time saying publicly he could not support the measure as it stood — he later added his support to the ACA, citing it as a win for all Americans and actively lobbied his colleagues to support it.

Industry observers note that rockefeller was also known for his role on the Senate Intelligence Committee. A former chairman, he was critical of the nation's mismanagement of the Iraq war and clashed frequently with Republicans over the treatment of detainees. After he retired from Congress, Rockefeller served as a distinguished fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations.

Respect for Rockefeller ran deep on Capitol Hill. He was beloved by staff and known as a thoughtful, deliberative lawmaker. He had a fondness for classical music and served as a board member of the Bach Consort, an organization in Washington devoted to the study and performance of the music of Bach and his contemporaries. He admired art and Asian culture, and served as a board member of the Asia Society.

Sources indicate that rockefeller is survived by his wife, Sharon Percy Rockefeller; four children: John D. Rockefeller V, Valerie Rockefeller, Charles Rockefeller and Justin Rockefeller; and nine grandchildren.

Disclosure: the author served as a staffer in Rockefeller’s Senate office from 2009-11.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The best meals in London, from Michelin fine dining to beloved street food, according to a longtime restaurant editor.

The story of the London food scene is one that includes dim sum, Sunday roasts, curries, pizza, sinasir, rarebits, banh mi, udon, pepper pot, sweetbread suya, and natural wine. Across cuisines, neighborhoods, and price points, all these dishes and drinks place London among the very best and most diverse places to eat in the world.

This guide, which I’ve been compiling and iterating on for the better part of the last decade, aims to reflect the best food and most important restaurants in the capital. I want this map to help you navigate a city in which it is all too easy to eat poorly, but in which it is increasingly inexcusable to do so. It will showcase a mix of over three dozen restaurants, which have all done outstanding things in extraordinary times: emerging, surviving, thriving, and continuing to enrich the city and its food culture through more than half a decade of unprecedented change and tumult.

We upgrade this list regularly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing London dining scene. Our write-ups include insider tips, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in pounds), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30.

In a recent development, latest to the map in November 2026: A return to the 38 for Kiln, one of London’s most consistent and innovative modern Thai restaurants, which this year turns 10; Bouchon Racine, a French bistro above a Farringdon pub whose faithful homage to the traditions of simple French cooking have it booked up months in advance; and perhaps the most interesting restaurant to open in London this year: Tramps, a semi-secret, not-often-open restaurant and bar within a gallery space off City Road. Three restaurants added to the map, which collectively exhibit just a portion of the curious plurality of the London dining experience.

It has been revealed that adam Coghlan is a writer and editor based in London. In 2017, he launched Eater London and ran the site until it ceased daily publication in 2023.

Adam Coghlan is a writer and editor based in London. In 2017, he launched Eater London and ran the site until it ceased daily publication in 2023.

Open for: Lunch through late night.

It has been revealed that as Jonathan Nunn wrote in his guide to north London’s best-value restaurants, “Durak, a tantuni salonu run by Dogan Yesil on West Green Road, is the superior late night snack template.” Only the tantuni, a speciality which originates in the city of Mersin on the southern coast of Turkey, is served here. Beef is boiled, seasoned with the likes of tomato, pul biber, sumac, and cumin and subsequently fried in cotton oil before being loaded, meat juices aplenty, inside a thin lavash with chopped parsley, tomato, and onion. It is then given a pleasing bend before being eaten; a selection of high-acid accompaniments — pickled chiles, lemon — provide the necessary cut-through.

Best for: A snack on the way home after a long day.

Recent findings suggest that mukaddes Yadikar’s restaurant near Walthamstow Central station opened in London in summer 2017. It was London’s first strictly Uyghur restaurant, and has become perhaps E17’s finest neighborhood restaurant. To start, go for the Chaomian, a stir-fry of short noodle snippets wokked with chunks of beef, spring onion, and tomato. Third, and most importantly, get the signature da pan ji (“big plate chicken”): a remarkably deep, savoury, and spicy chicken and potato stew, teeming with Sichuan peppercorns, served with flat hand-pulled noodles. This is a warm, homely, and treasured space to eat in east London.

Best for: Casual dinner with a group.

Open for: Lunch and dinner on weekends, dinner only during the week.

Industry observers note that eater London’s Restaurant of the Year 2022 comprises three discrete yet intertwined endeavors. Downstairs in the basement kitchen, George Jephson butchers whole animals, repurposing them as immaculate charcuterie, while upstairs, chef Mike Murphy uses excellent ingredients to prepare simple plates that lean French and southern European — think trout poached in butter with roe and sorrel; or a roast game bird with quince and bitter leaves. Sommeliers Tom Beattie and Fran Roberts, the duo behind the wine importer bearing both names, run the bar and the floor with a small team. Cadet is a wine bar, a restaurant, a charcutier, and a shopfront; it feels French and it feels London; and, from the moment it opened, it has always felt just right.

This diminutive Vietnamese shop on Hackney’s Graham Road serves one of the city’s best sandwiches — inside one of the city’s best baguettes. Although the spot has just one table and three or four seats, it’s difficult to think of warmer hospitality than at Bánh Mì Hội-An. The duo behind the counter prepare fresh sandwiches to go, and while the pork classic is excellent, don’t sleep on the turmeric-heavy fried catfish on Mondays, Tuesdays, and Wednesdays; fragrant with coriander, mayo, fermented chile paste, sriracha, and pickled vegetables, it is an object lesson in flavor, texture, and balance.

According to recent reports, ex-Noma sommelier Yukiyasu Kaneko’s wine bar, set in a cozy space beneath a railway arch close to London Fields, may yet become the newly introduced template for natural wine bars, a category that has grown a little tired and derivative. Few other businesses can rival Yuki’s assured sense of self and pleasing ambience. An extensive (and fairly priced) list includes highlights from the Jura, Savoie, and Loire regions, as well as bottles from elsewhere in the Old World. Food is secondary but not an afterthought, with snacky dishes such as eggs with tahini, house-made potato crisps dressed with sansho pepper, cured beet tops, silken tofu with mushrooms, and made-to-order beef tartare.

Must-try dish: Ask Yuki for his best wines from the Jura or the Savoie.

These days, London has no shortage of excellent new-age wine bars. It’s been a signature category in the city since the days of P. Franco and the likes of Terroirs before. But in more recent times, spots like Cadet, Hector’s, and Yuki Bar have raised the standard of wine bars sharply. At Goodbye Horses, which opened in the second part of 2024 (and where I enjoyed one of my favorite nights out last year), sommelier Nathalie Nelles oversees one of the most interesting wine lists in the city. Nelles has a penchant for excellent French wines from the Jura, Loire, and Burgundy. Go in the evening to enjoy a selection of small plates, which might include an avant-garde beef tartare, some carefully arranged crostini-like toasts, and a cheese plate. But you’re here to drink, really, and to take in the quite extraordinary interior, hand-painted curtains and long, organically shaped wooden bar — which lend the room a World of Interiors vibe in the best way.

Must-try: Complex savagnins from the Jura, elegant chenin blancs from the Loire Valley, grower Champagnes, and a mix of modern and classic wines from regal Burgundian producers.

East Ham is home to London’s largest Kerala community and its greatest concentration of South Indian restaurants. The pick of them is Thattukada, run by chef-owners Biju and Preeti Gopinath. Curries and roasts have a depth of flavor and spicing that belie their simple descriptions, and they should be mopped up with crisp parottas or snow-white appams. But it’s the legendary fries that are unmissable: half a chicken cut into segments, then aggressively and skillfully fried with chiles and crispy onions; little netholi (anchovies) cooked and eaten whole; or battered mussels that pop thrillingly in the mouth.

Must-try dish: Get the mussel fry.

This elegantly designed wine club beneath a Haggerston railway arch now firmly belongs in the top bracket of (French) restaurants in London. Chef Seb Myers and his modern-ish, playful take on French country cooking fits perfectly with the fascinating and broad wine list owned by patron Jonathan Alphandery. With dishes such as a red mullet tartine; grilled leeks vinaigrette with Tunworth cheese; a duck offal choux farcis; and mackerel with coco beans and greens; as well as a caramel tart with blue cheese, Planque has nearly everything that makes a great modern European restaurant great.

Best for: Pairing some of London’s cleverest cooking with some of the best wine in the city.

Open for: Lunch and dinner, with brunch on weekends.

Recent findings suggest that since Cafe Cecilia opened in 2021, it has maintained a steady flow of plaudits from all the coolest places, in part because of chef-owner Max Rocha’s connection to the world of fashion (father John and sister Simone are designers). However, there’s a surfeit of substance as well as style in this stark, minimalist cafe-bistro. And playfulness, too, seen in the likes of recreations of chicken Kievs or deep-fried bread-and-butter pudding in a pool of cold custard. Rocha and his staff are direct descendaents of the ingredients-obsessed tradition of St. John, the River Cafe, and Quo Vadis. Like peer Anna Tobias’s cooking at Cafe Deco, Rocha’s can be colored a bit beige, but it deserves the attention it has received.

Must-try dish: Do not miss the steak and chips with peppercorn sauce, nor fruit tart at dessert.

Sources indicate that this quaint place close to King’s Cross hasn’t been open long, but has been a conversation starter the likes of which the London restaurant scene hasn’t seen for years. Chef and Belfastman Hugh Corcoran’s sub-20-seater venue is open only at lunchtime (midday and 2 p.m. sittings are offered), reservations must be made via the restaurant’s landline (or postcard, honestly), it is cash-only, and the wine menu is all kept inside the faintly grumpy, periodically affable proprietor’s head. You can skip the starters (save, perhaps, the homemade soda bread and butter); just head straight to the mains, where you might find a slice of game bird pie with mash, a portion of braised guinea fowl with cabbage, or a fantastic rendition of a Dublin classic — coddle: boiled, peppery white sausages in a salty broth with root vegetables and lots of allium. This place eschews everything that the London restaurant industry has become, while bringing forth some (if not all) of the good things it once offered. And you can say, “I was there then.”.

In a recent development, the area around Euston station is replete with no-frills, delicious places to eat. This little Malaysian basement setup from chef Sugen Gopal on Doric Way may be the best. Two pieces of freshly made, high-moisture roti canai — to eat in or take away — are best served with curry dal. Roti King has a few other locations throughout London as well.

Know before you go: The newly introduced online queueing system makes for a seamless experience.

Chef Ed Wilson’s hearty French Italian menu is a showcase for his own personal love of food. To eat here is to share that passion, especially now with an increased emphasis on fresh pasta and spectacular comfort food. Wines are predominantly natural and biodynamic. Illustrated wine posters, art, and curios on whitewashed brick walls also make the two relaxed dining rooms on Columbia Road among London’s most handsome and cool.

Vibe check: This place has the city’s smallest and most beautiful bathrooms — among the very first to use Aesop, too.

At the late chef Kate Armah’s outstanding neighborhood Ghanaian restaurant in east London, the sharing platter — which includes tsofi, chicken wings, kebabs, plantains, and more — might be the definition of generosity in hospitality. Other highlights here include akonfem (guinea fowl), red red (fried plantain with black eye bean stew and gari foto), and any of the soups, which come served with choice of starchy sides such as fufu, kenkey, kokonte, or rice.

Vibe check: As the venue of choice for many visiting musicians and performers, Kate’s might be London’s least-appreciated celebrity restaurant.

There is no shortage of decent pizza in this town, but reliably excellent New York-style slices are harder to come by. Tom Vincent’s Vincenzo’s, which has been a bona fide IYKYK destination in Bushey, Watford for the last half decade, made its arrival in central London at the end of 2025 and since then has been treating the city to an excellent roster of classics and innovative pies. There are cheese, tomato, and pepperoni pizzas, all featuring low-moisture mozzarella, good tomato sauce, and a delightfully crisp base. U.S. colleagues might even admire the resistance to tip dip. Beyond the classics, look out for a spanakopita slice featuring feta, creamed spinach, and a Scotch bonnet honey; and the lesser-seen, thicker-based grandma pie for the heads, sometimes topped with vodka sauce, other times with pepperoni and hot honey.

Best for: Probably the best pizza slice in town.

Sources indicate that after a refurbishment of both kitchen and premises, this haven on Farringdon Road is back to the form that has made it one of the most essential of the city’s essential kitchens in recent years. Chef Nick Bramham’s cooking now leans more towards the Aegean, with the likes of giouvarlakia bringing herbed meatballs bobbing in avgolemono. The menu will change weekly and will travel across southern Europe, but look out for Bramham’s clever riffs on BLTs, lobster rolls, and perfectly seasoned pasta dishes, after peerless gildas, before flawless sour cherry cannoli.

Must-try dish: When Nick does pasta or Nick does a sandwich, you must order it.

In a recent development, clerkenwell’s Sushi Tetsu might be the hardest reservation in London. It also pound-for-pound serves the best (value) sushi in the city. To observe Toru Takahashi’s knife skills and to eat his omakase menu while receiving Harumi Takahashi’s gently flawless hospitality (the two are married) is to experience one of London’s most complete and completely brilliant restaurants.

Know before you go: There are only seven seats in the restaurant, all at the sushi counter.

Recent findings suggest that while the original St. John is rightly regarded as the most key British restaurant in a generation, Bread and Wine, the sibling site in Spitalfields, is a better and more interesting restaurant today. If food were a religion, then this would be its church. Welsh rarebit, bone marrow and parsley salad, foie gras on toast, mussels with cider, deviled kidneys, half a dozen madeleines, and a whole pie, which might be filled with pheasant, bacon, and trotter. Praise be.

Best for: Lunch is one of the purest, most heavenly restaurant experiences in London.

Joké Bakare’s small, two-story central London venue is no secret to anyone interested in restaurants: The chef’s modern recreations of classic dishes from Nigeria and the broader West African region have earned recognition from across the globe, including from the Michelin guide, which awarded Chishuru a star. As well as the chef’s immense presence, inventiveness, and ability to convey her love of food, the brilliance of Chishuru’s menu is rooted in age-old practices of fermentation, which lend many of the dishes a deep and lasting umami. It’s there in dishes like beef sirloin and dawadawa short rib with Tokyo turnip and a bitter leaf sauce, as well as grilled guinea fowl breast with celeriac cake, jalapeño, and egusi sauce.

Must-try dishes: Be sure to try Bakare’s jollof rice, and leave room for dessert.

Given the pace at which restaurants are modernizing and as the internationality of food becomes ever more commonplace, the Ledbury’s tablecloths and Franco-modern European style might be classified as old-school-ish. But that would be to ignore the level of craft and conscientious sourcing, and its application of Japanese ingredients and techniques in dishes like Cornish bluefin otoro with miyagawa and black sesame; or veal sweetbread with parsnip, liquorice, pear, and sansho pepper. And, finally, to consider the Ledbury a relic would be to overlook the profound influence chef-owner Brett Graham has had on the professional development of many of London’s best modern chefs — from BRAT to the Clove Club and beyond.

Best for: Birthdays, anniversaries, and one of the most special fine-dining experiences in the city.

Chef Meedu Saad’s hotly-anticipated Soho restaurant feels all at once brand fresh, a fixture of Soho and primed to remain in situ for years to come. Super 8, the group behind it and celebrated venues like Kiln, Brat, and Mountain, has a knack for creating the restaurants that Londoners (and tourists) really want, before they know they want it. Impala embodies the qualities that give the group its edge — a buzzy, handsome dining room, thoughtfully curated playlists, attentive and cool service, plus clever dishes prepared with fine, carefully-sourced produce. The group also promotes its best talent to give them a platform; in Saad, backed by development chef Songsoo Kim, they have a star. This north Londoner, British Egyptian chef is cooking his own food: North African leaning with French and modern British accents, most of it over hot coals or from a wood-fired oven. Try the aish balady with Tunisian harissa, ftira with egg, a grilled squid and green leaf salad, sheftalia, molokhia with lamb, Cantonese-ish-style roast duck with fig sauce, or an elegant pilaf. And save room for the one dessert: a pistachio and date custard tart.

It has been revealed that must-try dish: Cantonese-style roast duck with molasses and fig sauce. (Get it with the pilaf.).

Open for: Breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

Sources indicate that shuko Oda’s little bar in Soho is among London’s most acclaimed Japanese restaurants. Over a long, blond wooden counter, chefs calmly and politely pass hot bowls of steaming broth containing noodles made on-site, topped with proteins like tempura prawn or smoked mackerel, or seasonal green vegetables from Sussex farm Namayasai. The traditional Japanese breakfast is the most steadying in London.

Know before you go: The specials board of small plates changes every day and exhibits some of the city’s best modern British cooking.

In a recent development, bar Italia remains one of London’s most precious institutions, a relic of the mid-20th century sitting indomitably on Soho’s Frith Street. More than almost anywhere else in the capital, Soho is a victim of change, fads, and nonsensical restaurants. (True story: A half decade ago this same street played host to a venue called Flavour Bastard.) But Bar Italia never changes. And for that, we must be grateful. Its consistency and sense of self is what makes it so steadying and reassuring in a world of flux and uncertainty. At Bar Italia you always know your espresso will be bitter, your Peroni will be cold, and your bacon ciabatta will be better than almost anything else you can get in this storied but spoiled patch of the city.

Best for: An iconic, reliable breakfast and espresso.

In a recent development, for my money, Ikoyi may be the choicest special occasion venue in the city. Chef Jeremy Chan and restaurateur Iré Hasan-Odukale’s venue has evolved since its inception in St. James’s in 2017. It now occupies a sleek location in the bowels of 180 The Strand and has matured accordingly, elevating the food yet further to match its fancy newly introduced surroundings. While it is still philosophically rooted in the culinary traditions and flavor profiles of Nigeria and the West African region, Ikoyi is now an archetype of the Ultra-Modern European genre. Recent meals have featured the seductive savory deliciousness of Chan’s signature smoked jollof rice, and the precise application of spice and chile heat to immaculately cooked protein will blow you away, whether it’s sweetbread suya, dry-aged turbot, or charcoal-grilled lobster. A special restaurant, deserving of its two Michelin-starred status.

Best for: A true blowout dinner.

Gerrard Street’s Cantonese institution needs little introduction. Wong Kei is a decades-old London restaurant famous for its multistory dining room, roast meats (duck, char siu), wontons, red-ringed plates, and the now-cult (if much overstated) brusque service. Its enduring appeal — in spite of newer, trendier, regionally diverse restaurants in central London’s Chinatown — is its faithfulness to the traditions of dependable and delicious Cantonese cooking in the U.K., the stuff of a bygone era. In other words, it’s a giant, 500-seat living monument to a time before bubble waffles and Instagram-first openings.

Best for: A nostalgic UK-Cantonese meal with a group.

Chef Normah Abd Hamid and her family team offer a Malaysian comfort menu that makes the restaurant one of the best in the city from a nook of a unit in Queensway Market. Sour, hot assam pedas; roti to rival London’s King in Euston; and beef rendang or nasi lemak to go alongside. Normah’s is quaint and Normah is brilliant; this remains one of central London’s best restaurants to visit with a small group of friends and one to take out-of-towners visiting the city.

Know before you go: The food is halal, and no alcohol is allowed on site.

According to recent reports, mayfair’s two-Michelin-starred Indian restaurant Gymkhana is one of a few places in London that manages to straddle the line between celebrity hype and quality cooking. Tandoori masala lamb chops, chicken butter masala, and the trademark wild muntjac biryani remain standouts 13 years after it arrived on Albemarle Street. The prices match the level of cooking and the illustrious surroundings, making this one for special occasions.

Best for: Special occasions, atmosphere, and some of the finest curries in the city.

Recent findings suggest that together with Saikei, this is one of the great places in London to eat dim sum — particularly, with a major group on a Sunday lunchtime for the whole experience, driving out to the Docklands, walking up the wooden staircase to above a mixed martial arts gym, and putting your name down among the dozens of others to wait for a table. Once inside and seated, it’s a procession of tea and food. Be sure to order extra of the prawn and chive dumplings, and the special fried cheung fun with XO sauce (one of the best rice noodle dishes in the city). You might plump for sui mai, tripe, or some ribs. Barely anything you choose will disappoint. And from there, it might be a selection of sticky-sweet roast meats, or a Cantonese-style steamed seabass with ginger and spring onions and rice to share for the table. There is no way you’ll leave unsatisfied; lunch at Yi-Ban is pure nourishment.

Best for: Sunday lunch with a group (and plane spotting at City Airport).

Open for: Breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

There’s something lazily obvious about including the Ritz on a list of essential restaurants in London, but credit where credit’s due. The chef in charge comes fully garlanded: John Williams MBE is the master of niche, old-school French fine dining, delivering dishes of exceptional precision, yet never at the expense of deliciousness. Despite much frippery and eye-watering expense, when you get down to the brass tacks of a meal at the Ritz, it’s really quite simple: immaculately seasoned ingredients, assembled into balanced dishes, cooked adroitly. That’s true across the menu, but nowhere more so than in the Dorset crab with creme fraiche and Imperial caviar; filet of veal with white asparagus and lovage; the classic beef Wellington; and the theatrical crepe suzette.

Know before you go: The restaurant will make sure you comply with the formal dress code.

Sources indicate that A treasure. Unmoved by the comings and goings of trends, Bermondsey’s 40 Maltby St is a 40-cover answer to the question, pejorative as it may often be: What is British food? Steve Williams is a chef’s chef, cited by James Lowe, Brett Graham, and Florence Knight in their top five in the city. Raef Hodgson of distributor Gergovie Wines — which features low-intervention styles — runs the front-of-house without hubris. Recent dishes included winners such as pork schnitzel with raw celeriac, mustard, and braised potatoes, onion, and thyme, or a chestnut and brown sugar meringue.

Know before you go: Check Instagram for the menu, which always features an in-joke or two.

Recent findings suggest that this vast restaurant dining room sits quite inexplicably on the ground floor of a Holiday Inn Express budget hotel just off the A102 on the south exit of the Blackwall Tunnel. But this is a destination dining room of tremendous pedigree. A mid-length, high-quality dim sum menu features a must-try fried prawn and Chinese chive number that stakes a fair claim to being the best single-bite hot item in the city — a crispy, fatty, sweet, salty umami nugget. Among the noodle plates to share, king prawns are excellent, with the noodles taking on the requisite smoke from the wok, seasoned judiciously. Saikei is a close-to-perfect family and group dining experience.

Best for: Sunday lunch, preferably with a large group.

Open for: Dinner to late night during the week, lunch to late night on weekends.

According to recent reports, in his guide to the city’s best East African restaurants, Riaz Phillips indicates Adulis’s “palatial setting has to make it one of the finest east African and Eritrean restaurants in the capital.” The dark wooden fixtures give every meal here a sense of occasion. The restaurant is well-suited to solo or group dining, with a menu offering selections for one, two, four, and eight persons. Look out for kwanta fitfit, smoked, dried beef with green chile and injera; zilzl assa, grilled red snapper seasoned with Eritrean herbs; and the entire range of vegetarian and vegan stews, comprising spinach, beans, chickpeas, and lentils, all eaten with more of the excellent, subtly tangy, and moreish injera.

Best for: A special occasion with vegetarians and vegans.

Open for: Dinner on weeknights, brunch through dinner on weekends.

The second branch for this south London institution, Nandine — “kitchen” in Kurdish — is run by Pary Baban, husband Pola, and sons Rang and Raman. During the day it serves a menu of brunch dishes, meze, and intricate pastries. Technicolored and abundant meze platters served in the evening include kubba (minced beef and rice patties), onion dolma, and qawarma. Pastries like borek, made with a Kurdish pastry called galgali, and baklava are not to be missed.

Best for: Go for brunch and get the meze, for yourself.

It has been revealed that bruce Poole’s Wandsworth Common institution is best summed up thus: technique, decadence, and salt. There’s skill and execution here that no longer feels commonplace in restaurants in London (explained, perhaps in part, by how out-of-London it feels). It’s classical in almost every sense; the dining room has the breezy, impressionist art-covered air of a destination neighborhood bistro in which Michelin’s inspectors would feel welcome. But what it lacks in new-wave imagination over the course of a meal, it makes up for in professionalism and elan. My favorite dish during a recent visit was a “homemade” (you’ve gotta shout about these things in buzzy Wandsworth) cavatelli with duck and morteau sausage ragu, showered with Parmesan: rich, moreish, sumptuous — a flawless small plate of pasta.

Best for: Special occasions, especially including a glass or two of vintage Champagne.

Possibly London’s best Jamaican jerk shop. On the edge of Crystal Palace’s Selhurst Park, with a smoky aroma detectable from many hundred meters, this stark room is dedicated to one thing: immaculately, judiciously seasoned protein grilled without remorse. The age of these oil drums and the time-honored expertise of chef Murphy Lawrence and his team result in jerked pork belly, chicken, goat, and even lobster, all penetrated with smoke and lifted by allspice, Scotch bonnet, and salt. Tasty Jerk is a heady, intoxicating, and remarkably good-value eating experience.

Know before you go: Buy a bottle of the home-made pepper sauce to take away, but use with caution and keep it in the fridge.

Sources indicate that fascinated by British meats and Thai cooking preparations, restaurateur Ben Chapman opened this homage to northern Thailand on Brewer Street in Soho 10 years ago this year. It has always been a dynamic showcase for rare-breed British meat in spicy, piquant laabs, Cornish dayboat fish in bright seafood curries, and complex, herbaceous salads (a mix of British leaves and Thai herbs), the like of which are seldom found anywhere in the capital. Almost all of the cooking here is done not with electricity or gas, but over charcoal.

Sources indicate that must-try dish: Claypot glass noodles. Don’t skip the wine list.

Industry observers note that despite the proximity of France to Britain, the restaurant traditions and contemporary scenes have little in common. There is just something – the je ne sais quoi – about bistros in France which isn’t often found in venues on this side of the channel. But there are those who manage to recreate the mythos and romanticism of the bistro-proper. Chef Henry Harris’s longstanding practice in the field of French cooking lends him a rare level of expertise. His Bouchon Racine sits above a pub close to Farringdon station, and it feels like a bistro – tables are close, there’s little in the way of frippery, the menu is written out in chalk on a blackboard, which is moved around the dining room. It’s difficult to choose, but a good place to start is with a plate of paté or terrine, followed by one of the finest versions of rabbit in mustard sauce; confit de canard; or a côte de boeuf to share. It would be rude not to finish with a crème caramel and a pate of cheese.

Best for: Lapin à la moutarde, French bistro classics.

Open for: Lunch and dinner during the week (but check opening hours; reservations by email only.).

Best for: The most delicious, hyper-seasonal cooking in the city right now.

Fermi’s 14-Year All-Sky Map Bridges Astronomy’s Elusive "MeV Gap"

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1030 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gamma rays, the most high-energy type of electromagnetic radiation in the universe, have always had a blind spot.
  • The âgapâ comes from a technological blind spot.
  • In a recent development, but why are low energy gamma rays so hard to catch?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gamma rays, the most high-energy type of electromagnetic radiation in the universe, have always had a blind spot. Weâve always had trouble measuring them in the âmega-electron voltâ (MeV) energy range, which astronomers have taken to calling the âMeV gapâ. But a upcoming paper from an international group of scientists working with the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) Collaboration recently published a paper in The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series that takes a stab at closing that gap by identifying 450 cosmic sources in the 20-200 MeV range, providing the clearest view of low-energy gamma rays ever.

The âgapâ comes from a technological blind spot. Scientists have plenty of tools in the lower energy spectra, such as the Chandra X-ray observatory, that can capture radiation at the x-ray end of the electromagnetic spectrum. They also have a great number of tools at the high end of gamma ray spectroscopy, including the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, which is capable of finding higher end ones.

In a recent development, but why are low energy gamma rays so hard to catch? Gamma rays notoriously pass right through mirrors and every other attempt to reflect them. Telescopes like Fermi-LAT can be thought of more as particle detectors in orbit rather than traditional telescopes. They track what happens when a gamma-ray photon hits layers of tungsten and silicon inside their chassis.

Fraser explains what a Quasar is.

At high energies - around 1 giga-electron volt (GeV), the damage done to those layers is catastrophic enough to be able to trace a line back to a source. However, at the lower 20-200 MeV range, the photons scatter much more randomly, making it difficult to track where precisely they came from. Fermi-LAT is only capable of tracking a single 20 MeV photon to a patch of the sky about 20 degrees wide - more than forty times the size of the full moon. Combine that with a massive amount of background radiation caused by everything from the Sun to distant galaxies, and it can be a real pain to pick out the direction of any one particular source.

Recent findings suggest that however, Fermi-LAT has been operating now for almost two decades, and with that much data thereâs some math that can help. The researchers combined 14 years worth of collected data with some advanced statistical modeling techniques to pinpoint 450 distinct gamma-ray sources, what they are calling the Second Catalog of Low-Energy Fermi-LAT Sources, or 2FLE. Cross-checking them with other radio, optical, and X-ray data showed known counterparts for 377 of those objects.

The vast majority of those objects - 325 of them - are far outside the Milky Way. Almost half of the entire group of objects consist of flat-spectrum radio quasars (FSRQs), a very extreme type of active galactic nuclei. FSRQs represent a type of âblazarâ - a supermassive black hole that is pointing one of its twin jets of plasma directly at Earth. The 2FLE catalog confirms that FSRQ blazars pump out the majority of their energy at this 20-200 MeV spectral window.

Fraser and Pamela discuss the differnet "colors" of gamma rays.

Closer to home, the catalogue includes 52 sources from inside the Milky Way. Most of them are pulsars - the spinning leftovers left behind when a supermassive star explodes into a supernova. But one intriguing outlier was gamma rays that appear to be coming from M2, a globular cluster, which would mark the first time itâs ever been observed at gamma-ray energies.

According to recent reports, perhaps the most intriguing part of the paper, though, are the 73 sources that donât have a clear counterpart at other energies. 60 of those appear to be brand latest gamma-ray discoveries. And while some of those signals might turn out to be overlapping signals from neighboring objects, it's likely there are at least some truly new exotic cosmic accelerators in the dataset awaiting follow-up observations. One particular mystery source seems to align with an object called 2FLE J0340.8+5258, which seems to also have been detected by an observatory in China, and appears to be capable of generating light across nine orders of magnitude in energy.

It has been revealed that fermi-LAT itself seems to have reached its limit with this new data set. The researchers have likely squeezed everything they could out of the decades of data of this satellite, which was originally debuted in 2008. However, there are other gamma-ray missions coming online, including NASAâs Compton Spectrometer and Imager (COSI), which is designed specifically to look for gamma rays in the 0.2-5 MeV range using a special type of germanium detector that has only become available in the last few years. Combining that new data with the decades worth of Fermi might finally shed some light on one of the longest-standing blind spots in the extreme physics of the universe.

DESY - A new view of the gamma-ray gap.

In a recent development, A. Adelfio - The Second Catalog of Low-energy Fermi-LAT Sources.

UT - A Giant Burst of Energy In Need Of An Explanation.

UT - Unexplained Gamma-Rays from the Galactic Center Could be from Self-Annihilating Dark Matter.

It has been revealed that andy has been interested in space exploration ever since reading Pale Blue Dot in middle school. An engineer by training, he likes to focus on the practical challenges of space exploration, whether that's getting rid of perchlorates on Mars or making ultra-smooth mirrors to capture ever clearer data. When not writing or engineering things he can be found entertaining his four children, four cats, and two dogs, or running in circles and throwing plastic discs at people to stay in shape.

#7277. Extremely Accurate Measurements of a Pair of Flaring Red Dwarfs

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Universetoday ↗ Open Full Page

Extremely Accurate Measurements of a Pair of Flaring Red Dwarfs

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1553 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • About 59 light years away, a binary pair of red dwarfs are orbiting a common center of gravity.
  • One fundamental fact about low and intermediate mass stars, including M dwarfs, is that they rotate more rapidly when they're younger.
  • The fast rotation generates powerful magnetic dynamos, and young M dwarfs exhibit very large sunspots and more frequent, powerful stellar flares.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

About 59 light years away, a binary pair of red dwarfs are orbiting a common center of gravity. Unlike stars like our Sun, which are relatively radio-quiet, red dwarfs (M dwarfs) can produce strong radio emissions. A team of astronomers used that to their advantage to take precision measurements of a binary pair of M dwarfs about 59 million light years from Earth. They determined the stars' orbits and masses with uncommon accuracy.

One fundamental fact about low and intermediate mass stars, including M dwarfs, is that they rotate more rapidly when they're younger. Stars inherit angular momentum from their formation in gas clouds, and since M dwarfs are so small, that momentum is concentrated, making them spin rapidly. They eventually slow down, but this initial rapid rotation makes them very active.

The fast rotation generates powerful magnetic dynamos, and young M dwarfs exhibit very large sunspots and more frequent, powerful stellar flares.

According to recent reports, one subset of young M dwarfs is even more extreme. They're called Complex Periodic Variable (CPV) stars, and they're very young, between about 10 and 100 million years old. They're M dwarfs that display complex, periodical optical light curves with sharp drops rather than smooth drops found in most stellar light curves. Their drops aren't simple; there can be multiple dips and peaks during a single rotation. Astrophysicists call their light curves multi-harmonic, and the patterns repeat across multiple rotations.

In a recent development, this image demonstrates CPV light curves for three typical CPV stars found by TESS. Notice the sharp drops in the curves rather than typical smooth drops found in other stellar light curves. Image Credit: Bouma et al. 2023. AnJ.

The binary system in this research is named DG CVn, and one of them is a CPV star. Though CPV stars have complex light curves generated by their youthful, rapid rotation, their youthfulness also means they're radio loud. In fact, since both of these stars are young M dwarfs, they're both radio loud. That helped the researchers measure them with such accuracy.

It has been revealed that the measurments of DG CVn are in newly introduced research in Astronomy and Astrophysics titled "Accurate dynamical mass and orbit determination of the M dwarf binary DG CVn using astrometric very long baseline interferometry." The lead author is Paul VLBI , a network system engineer at the Joint Institute for Very Long Baseline Interferometry ERIC (JIVE), and a Leiden Observatory PhD student. It's noteworthy that this is the first mass measurement of a system with a CPV star.

"We present the first dynamical mass measurement of a binary containing a CPV star." - Boven et al. 2026.

Sources indicate that the astronomers' results are based on observations that spanned 18 years. Observations with the National Science Foundationâs Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) between 2023 and 2025 were especially important in their precise results. The VLBA is a system of 10 radiotelescopes across the USA, each one measuring 25 meters. The 10 dishes work as an interferometer, and the VLBA has the longest baseline in the world, up to 8,611 km long.

In a recent development, "Astrometry through very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) allows the monitoring of radio-loud stars and the detection of any reflex motion due to stellar or substellar companions," the authors write. Reflex motion is the characteristic gravitational wobble induced in a star when a companion tugs on it.

That wobble is often used to detect unseeable exoplanets orbiting stars. Even a small planet can make its star wobble, and that's at the heart of the radial velocity method of detecting exoplanet. The DG CVn system was actually found when astronomers were searching for exoplanets with the radial velocity method. But the system exhibited a more powerful and complex wobble than an exoplanet would.

Sources indicate that âWe were really lucky to hear about this object when we had developed tools with which we could explain these motions,â stated Boven. âBut the real surprise came when we also detected the second radio-loud dwarf in the observations we did to confirm our model. It really allowed us to measure the system very precisely.â.

Measuring reflex motion accurately with the VLBI let the astronomers track the stars' paths, including the tiny wobbles, which in turn let them understand the mass of the stars with extreme precision.

In a recent development, this figure from the research shows the VLBI detections of both members of DG CVn, and their modeled motion across the sky. The dates mark the predicted positions of DG CVn B over time. The inset image shows recent observations when both sources were detected. Image Credit: Boven et al. 2026. A&A.

It has been revealed that "In our recent observations, we reliably detected both binary components," the authors write. "A unique and accurate determination of the 1647.647 Â± 0.027 day orbit, with a parallax distance of 18.1851 Â± 0.0033 pc (about 59 light years), is presented. The dynamical masses were estimated with a precision of 0.16% from the sampled posteriors.".

The pair of stars orbit each other every 4.511 years on an elongated elliptical orbit. When they're closest to one another, they're only separated by 0.59 astronomical units. DG CVn A is the more massive of the pair with 0.39 solar masses, while DG CVn B has 0.36 solar masses. The pair is close enough to measure their distance with parallax, which gives accurate measurements.

The red dwarfs and their radio emissions are central to this work. The stars are simply too close together from this distance to be separated in optical observations. But the VLBA can pinpoint their locations with extreme accuracy. All of this work let the researchers characterize the system in clear detail, following the motions of both stars through the sky separately.

âDG CVn is a beautiful example of what precise radio astrometry can reveal,â said Jay Blanchard, NSF National Radio Astronomy Observatory astronomer and study co-author. âBy following these two stars over many years, we can see their orbital motion directly and use that motion to determine properties that would otherwise be extremely difficult to measure.â.

Sources indicate that these accurate measurements also tell astronomers about their planetary systems. Planets form in protoplanetary disks around stars, and since these stars are so close together, that limits the size of their disks. Smaller disks mean smaller planets, so that limits the size of any exoplanets in the system. It's also extremely unlikely that any long-period planets are orbiting either star.

According to the researchers' estimates, an exoplanet in orbit around one of the stars could only be in a stable orbit if its orbital period was less than approximately 23 days. For a circumbinary planet orbiting both stars, the orbital period would have to be at least about 36 years. These approximations are also important, because they can refine the understanding of how exoplanets can form and survive in binary star systems.

Gaia's Data Release 4 is due in a couple of weeks, and it will include binary star parameters for the mission's complete survey. But that data alone won't be able to differentiate between binaries where both are low mass stars, and binaries where one might be a massive planet. But the VLBI will be able to address that. "Astrometric follow-up of selected detections with VLBI can help to differentiate between binary star systems and reflex motion due to large exoplanets (or even both)," the authors write.

Recent findings suggest that "We have presented a complete binary orbital solution with high accuracy based on VLBI astrometry of a binary that is difficult to resolve for optical telescopes on the ground or in orbit," the authors write. "The absolute astrometry provided by VLBI allowed the individual dynamical masses to be determined with high accuracy. These results show that VLBI is well suited for studying the orbits of radio-loud stars.".

According to recent reports, the results also show how powerful the combination of archival observations and latest observations can be. "The value of combining archival and recent VLBI astrometric observations has been demonstrated. It resulted in a highly accurate determination of the system composition, orbit, position, and distance," the authors write. "We present the first dynamical mass measurement of a binary containing a CPV star.".

According to recent reports, the VLBI network of radio dishes is about to have a growth spurt when the Square Kilometre Array and the Next Generation Very Large Array come online. That will improve the system's reach and precision.

According to recent reports, "In the future, we hope to make measurements precise enough to detect planets in orbit around such radio-loud dwarfs,â noted Huib van Langevelde, chief scientist a the Joint Institute for Very Long Baseline Interferometry and Leiden Observatory professor. âWe think that when the ngVLA and the SKA become part of the VLBI network, we can do even more precise measurements, for many more, more distant stars.â.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (818 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A dead star and its Sun-like companion have given astronomers an unexpected way to investigate mysterious radio pulses and detect stellar storms thousands of light-years away.
  • In a recent development, mysterious radio signals have been appearing across the Milky Way, switching on and off over minutes or hours.
  • Now, a newly discovered star system more than 5,000 light-years away is offering an important clue.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A dead star and its Sun-like companion have given astronomers an unexpected way to investigate mysterious radio pulses and detect stellar storms thousands of light-years away.

In a recent development, mysterious radio signals have been appearing across the Milky Way, switching on and off over minutes or hours. Astronomers have found only about a dozen of these unusual sources, and one question has been especially difficult to answer: What is actually producing the pulses?

Now, a newly discovered star system more than 5,000 light-years away is offering an important clue. Known as GPM J071507−114153, it contains a white dwarf, the dense core left behind after a star dies, orbiting a companion remarkably similar to our Sun. The white dwarf spins once every eight minutes.

The discovery is unusual because astronomers have never before detected these radio pulses from a white dwarf paired with a Sun-like star. Previously identified systems producing similar signals have typically involved much smaller, cooler stars known as red dwarfs.

These mysterious sources belong to a class called long-period transients (LPTs). Since researchers at the International Center for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR) first discovered one in 2021, around a dozen have been identified. Several contain a white dwarf and another star, although astronomers have struggled to determine which one produces the radio signals.

Scientists at the Curtin University node at the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR) have linked mysterious radio pulses to an unusual pairing of stars — a dead star that spins every eight minutes and a star similar to our own Sun. Credit: Natasha Hurley-Walker.

In the newly discovered system, scientists finally had enough information to narrow down the source.

“This is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion, so we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself,” remarked Dr Sam McSweeney, the study’s lead author and a commissioning scientist with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory.

McSweeney made the discovery while working as a researcher at the Curtin University node of ICRAR. To confirm and better understand the white dwarf’s movement, the team processed more than 100 hours of radio observations using computing resources at the Pawsey Supercomputing Research Center.

The radio pulses also revealed something unexpected about the white dwarf’s companion. Researchers detected evidence of stellar flares on the Sun-like star, similar to the activity associated with auroras here on Earth.

“As a bonus, we also saw the white dwarf moving behind a region with a strong magnetic field, most likely a ‘stellar prominence’, which is a large loop of plasma erupting from a star’s surface.”.

The observation suggests astronomers can use radio signals to investigate magnetic activity on distant stars, even when those stars are thousands of light-years away.

“It’s amazing that by using radio wavelengths we can detect the storms on a star over 5000 light-years away.”.

Both observations were described by Associate Professor Natasha Hurley-Walker, a co-author of the paper.

Recent findings suggest that finding such a rare system required several powerful telescopes working together. The researchers first identified its radio signals during a large survey of the Milky Way, then used additional observations to pinpoint its location.

Sources indicate that “We detected this system in a large survey using the MWA (Murchison Widefield Array) to scan the entire Milky Way visible from Australia. We then used the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa to determine its precise position,” remarked Associate Professor Hurley-Walker.

Recent findings suggest that once the radio source had been located, optical observations from the W.M. Keck Observatory on Maunakea, Hawaiʻi Island, confirmed its association with a G-type star, the same broad class as our Sun.

Industry observers note that the MWA, led by Curtin University, is located at Inyarrimanha Ilgari Bundara, the CSIRO Murchison Radio-Astronomy Observatory on Wajarri Yamaji Country in Western Australia. MeerKAT, meanwhile, was built and is operated by the South African Radio Astronomy Observatory in South Africa’s North Cape province.

Both facilities are precursors to the larger SKA telescopes now being developed, SKA-Low in Australia and SKA-Mid in South Africa. These future observatories are expected to provide more detailed observations of unusual radio sources and help astronomers identify additional systems that have so far escaped detection.

“If we are already making such discoveries with precursor telescopes, just imagine how many more star systems we will be able to find, and what a beautifully detailed view of their signals we will have, once the SKAO telescopes are completely built,” said Dr McSweeney.

Reference: “A long-period transient with a Sun-like companion” by Samuel J. McSweeney, Natasha Hurley-Walker, Arash Bahramian, Csanád Horváth, Nanda Rea, Antonio C. Rodriguez and Ingrid Pelisoli, 12 November 2026, Nature Astronomy. DOI: 10.1038/s41550-026-03016-z.

Are Uranus and Neptune Secretly "Rock Giants"? A Noble Gas Might Hold the Answer

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1036 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For decades, astronomers have divided the planets in the outer solar system into two distinct camps.
  • In a recent development, scientists are getting excited because there has been an ongoing debate that these distant worlds are actually covered in rock.
  • Understanding why the presence of one noble gas isotope leads to understanding whether rock is present or not requires a bit of a diversion into the world of bananas.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For decades, astronomers have divided the planets in the outer solar system into two distinct camps. Jupiter and Saturn were the âgas giantsâ made up primarily of hydrogen and helium. Uranus and Neptune were the âice giantsâ, and were much smaller but were packed with heavier elements. A newly introduced paper from Olivier Mousis of the Southwest Research Institute and his co-authors, available in The Planetary Science Journal, explores whether we can use an isotope of a noble gas - argon-40 - to determine whether there are hidden mountains of rock under the ice giantâs thick atmospheres.

In a recent development, scientists are getting excited because there has been an ongoing debate that these distant worlds are actually covered in rock. But we canât simply fly a probe out a few billion miles and drill down into their surfaces to determine that for ourselves. Instead, they decided to use proxies, such as the concentration of argon-40, as a rough measurement for how much rock there is below the atmosphere.

Understanding why the presence of one noble gas isotope leads to understanding whether rock is present or not requires a bit of a diversion into the world of bananas. Or at least, it gives me an excuse to talk about bananas in a planetary science article. Bananas are radioactive, and the thing causing their radioactivity is potassium-40 - a relatively unstable form of a very common element. When potassium-40 decays, it turns into argon-40, which, as a noble gas, hardly interacts with anything.

Fraser talks about how to proposal a mission to Uranus.

Industry observers note that most of this radioactive decay takes place in rocks containing potassium-40, rather than bananas, so one of the most common sources of argon-40 is literally rocks. After it is created, it bubbles up out of those rocks and escapes into its host planetâs atmosphere. In fact, it makes up around 1% of the air youâre breathing right now.

On the ice giants, this same process could hold - argon-40 could form inside a rocky surface, and then bubble up into the planetâs atmosphere over billions of years. So we should be able to send a probe to measure the concentration of argon-40 in their atmospheres, and that would serve as an effective proxy for the existence of rock under the atmosphere.

According to recent reports, thereâs just one catch - rocks arenât really the only source of argon-40. In fact, there was already plenty of it floating around in the protosolar nebula that the Sun and all the planets eventually formed out of. Therefore, Uranus and Neptune could have âtrappedâ this leftover argon-40 before they were even mature, causing argon-40 to eventually appear in their atmosphere, but not from rocky surfaces.

Fraser talks about efforts to go back to visit the ice giants of the solar system.

Recent findings suggest that according to the paper, the amount of argon collected by the early versions of Neptune and Uranus depends entirely on where they formed with regards to the âargon ice lineâ. This line, which happens around 23-35 Kelvin, the temperature that argon freezes into solid ice, or is trapped inside water ice, is the determining factor of how much primordial argon Neptune and Uranus had sucked up.

According to recent reports, unfortunately, thereâs still a lot of debate about where exactly in the solar system the ice giants formed. If they formed close to the Sun and eventually migrated back out to the edges of the solar system, they might not have captured much argon ice, and the majority of the argon in their atmospheres would be due to release from rocks. On the other hand, if the theories about them actively moving through the solar system soon after their creation are true, then they would likely have captured a large amount of argon-40, making it useless as an indicator of whether or not the planets have a rocky surface.

Luckily, there is a way to potentially solve this puzzle. Argon-40 has a lighter isotopic cousin, known as argon-36, which is non-radioactive, and doesnât form in decaying rocks. Measuring its level would act like a control group, allowing scientists to estimate how much of the argon present in the atmosphere would have been swallowed at birth, as we have other estimates of the ratio between argon-40 and argon-36 in the early solar system.

Industry observers note that itâs good these sorts of insights are coming out now, as there is right now a mission, Uranus Orbiter and Probe, which is in active development and planned to arrive in the system in the 2040s. That still gives us some time to finalize our theories about what we would expect to find there. And perhaps, once it does arrive, weâll be able to definitively answer whether or not the âIce giantsâ have a truly solid surface or not.

A Upcoming Light-Powered Quantum Processor Could Overcome a Major Computing Barrier

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (942 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new light-based processor suggests future quantum computers could tackle very different problems without being rebuilt, while laying the groundwork for more reliable calculations.
  • Light has enormous potential for quantum computing, but one of its greatest strengths is also a major obstacle.
  • Researchers from Imperial College London’s Department of Physics and collaborating institutions have developed a fresh approach that could help overcome this limitation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new light-based processor suggests future quantum computers could tackle very different problems without being rebuilt, while laying the groundwork for more reliable calculations.

Light has enormous potential for quantum computing, but one of its greatest strengths is also a major obstacle. Photons, the tiny particles that make up light, are excellent carriers of quantum information because they rarely interact with one another. Yet those interactions are essential for many of the calculations that quantum computers need to perform, making it difficult to build versatile machines using light alone.

Researchers from Imperial College London’s Department of Physics and collaborating institutions have developed a fresh approach that could help overcome this limitation. Their programmable quantum processor, called Clavina, combines different types of quantum operations in a single system, allowing it to tackle multiple computational tasks without requiring an entirely new hardware design.

The research, published in Nature Photonics, offers a promising direction for building more flexible light-based quantum computers, including systems that could eventually detect and correct their own errors.

Most photonic quantum processors are designed with a particular task in mind. Adapting them to solve another problem can require substantial changes to their hardware, limiting how easily the technology can evolve.

In a recent development, clavina takes inspiration from ordinary computers, which use specialized components to handle graphics, artificial intelligence, and other demanding tasks. Instead of relying on one fixed arrangement, the new processor uses a central control unit to direct information through a programmable optical network and specialized modules.

Recent findings suggest that the optical network handles linear operations, which manipulate light without requiring photons to interact. The additional modules provide nonlinear operations, expanding the kinds of calculations the system can perform. Because these components can be combined in different ways, researchers can change the processor’s functions without rebuilding it from scratch.

Dr. Shang Yu, the study’s lead author and a Marie Skłodowska-Curie Fellow at Imperial, stated, “We set out to build a photonic quantum processor that provides a step change in functionality over our previous designs. Our latest architecture ‘Clavina’ is scalable, modular and extensible, allowing different functional modules to be used depending on the computational task we wish to perform.”.

To test what this flexibility could achieve, the researchers put Clavina to work on two very different challenges.

The first involved simulating the Bose-Hubbard model, a well-known problem in condensed matter physics that describes how quantum particles interact. These calculations involve many-body interactions, where the behavior of multiple particles must be considered together. Such simulations are challenging even for other quantum computing technologies, including superconducting quantum computers.

Dr. Jinzhao Sun of Queen Mary University of London explained, “The versatility of our hardware enables us to integrate nonlinear operations and linear operations. We use these operations to perform simulations involving many-body interactions, which are also restricted on superconducting quantum computers.”.

The second demonstration addressed another major challenge facing quantum computing: keeping delicate quantum information safe from errors.

Quantum systems are vulnerable to noise and disturbances that can interfere with calculations. One possible solution involves creating specially structured quantum states that encode information in ways that make errors easier to detect and correct.

According to recent reports, among the most promising are Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states. Producing these states has been difficult for light-based systems because earlier approaches worked probabilistically, meaning researchers could not reliably generate the required states whenever they needed them.

Using Clavina, the team demonstrated a much more consistent method of generating GKP states. Although this does not mean they have built a fully error-correcting quantum computer, it addresses an notable obstacle to making error correction practical.

Industry observers note that dr. Raj Patel, a UKRI Future Leaders Fellow who leads Imperial’s photonic quantum computing program, said, “Our architecture allows the generation of exotic quantum states such as Schrödinger cat states and Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill states, which are valuable resources for fault-tolerant quantum computing. The nonlinear operations in our architecture provide a universal gate set at the physical level which is required for the future implementation of bosonic error-correcting codes.”.

A universal gate set provides the fundamental operations that can be combined to carry out different quantum computations. Having these capabilities available in one programmable processor could support future error-correction techniques that use specially encoded states of light.

The architecture also offers possibilities beyond the two demonstrations. By allowing researchers to change or introduce functional modules, Clavina could be adapted to different scientific problems as quantum computing systems become larger and more complex.

Co-author Ying Dong of China Jiliang University said, “Previously, researchers would have to build photonic hardware tailored to a specific task. The ability to switch in different functional modules in our architecture enables a single set of hardware to perform multiple functions without overhauling the design. Clavina can solve graph problems, simulate quantum systems or generate large entangled states and resource states for error correction.”.

Industry observers note that rather than developing a separate photonic processor for every new challenge, researchers could eventually build on the same adaptable foundation. Clavina’s demonstrations suggest that the ability to change what a quantum computer does may become just as valuable as increasing its computational power.

Alwehaibi, Shana H. Winston, Dayne Marcus Lopena, Zi-Cheng Zhang, Guang Yang, Runxia Tao, Mingti Zhou, Gerard J. Machado, Ying Dong, Roberto Bondesan, Vlatko Vedral, M. S. Kim, Ian A. Walmsley and Raj B. Patel, 31 July 2026, Nature Photonics. DOI: 10.1038/s41566-026-01962-8.
