The Simons Observatory is Online and Surveying the Cosmic Microwave Background

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1668 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the Simons Observatory in the Atacama Desert has begun its mission to survey the Cosmic Microwave Background.
  • In a recent development, we live in an age of large astronomical surveys, enabled by powerful computers and data handling methods.
  • There are automated surveys for transients like supernovae and asteroids, radio-sky surveys to spot objects obscured by thick dust, and massive surveys just getting started like the Vera Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope's three core surveys.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the Simons Observatory in the Atacama Desert has begun its mission to survey the Cosmic Microwave Background. Its goal is to detect undeniable evidence of the Big Bang and cosmic inflation. Can this unique survey succeed where others have failed?

In a recent development, we live in an age of large astronomical surveys, enabled by powerful computers and data handling methods. While powerful telescopes still perform detailed observations of individual targets, and always will, wide surveys have a power all their own. The ESA's Gaia mission, for example, has completed its survey of billions of stars and generated a massive amount of foundational data that researchers will draw on for decades to come.

There are automated surveys for transients like supernovae and asteroids, radio-sky surveys to spot objects obscured by thick dust, and massive surveys just getting started like the Vera Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope's three core surveys.

Sources indicate that but another Simons Observatory's survey hasn't garnered the same attention that some of the other have. The Simons Observatory (SO) consists of four telescopes working together: three small 0.5 meter aperture 'scopes in its Small Aperture Telescope (SAT) and one large 6-meter one in its Large Aperture Telescope (LAT).

The unusual configuration gives the SO the best chance to observe tiny details in the Universe's first observable light, the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB).

This image of the Cosmic Microwave Background is from the Simons Observatory, the newest and most powerful observatory to study the CMB. It's unique arrangement of three small and one large telescope increases its resolution by an order of magnitude over its predecessor, the Planck satellite. The Simons Observatory's main goal is to find the elusive evidence from the epoch of inflation, and thereby confirming the Big Bang model of cosmology. Image Credit: Simons Observatory.

It has been revealed that the stuff of the Universe was too opaque for light to travel through it at first. Photons were effectively scattered by the hot, dense plasma that permeated the Universe. Eventually conditions changed. The Universe expanded, the plasma cooled, and photons could travel. This was the recombination epoch and it occurred about 380,000 years after the Massive Bang.

Sources indicate that note that the name is historical and reflected our earlier understanding of the Universe. It wasn't actually a recombination, it was the first time that electrons and protons combined to form neutral hydrogen, and that's what made the cosmos transparent. Its name should probably be changed to the combination epoch.

But regardless of its name, the cosmic microwave background is the relic radiation from the Universe's first light, and it holds clues to the Universe, especially to the Substantial Bang theory of cosmology.

Industry observers note that other efforts have been made to map the CMB. NASA's Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP) and the ESA's Planck satellite both made the effort from orbit. Right now, the South Pole Telescope (SPT) and related facilities are doing the same.

The SPT made an important discovery. It detected for the first time what's called the B-mode polarization of the CMB. The B-mode is important because it was created by primordial gravitational waves generated during the epoch of inflation, the first moments of the Universe's inflation. So finding the B-mode was important evidence for the Big Bang theory.

The South Pole Telescope at the AmundsenâScott South Pole Station, Antarctica. The SPT is a 10-meter telescope that is credited with the first detection of the Cosmic Microwave Background's B-mode polarization. Image Credit: By Amble - Own work, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/9057466.

But there was a problem. Gravitational lensing can also create B-mode polarization, and it has nothing to do with the Big Bang or inflation. It's difficult to tell which source created the B-mode polarization the SPT detected. So its initial detection was put in doubt.

In a recent development, this is where the Simons Observatory comes into the picture. It's been calibrating its instruments for two years and is now getting down to business.

âTo have all the observatory motors humming, gears turning and data flowing makes me joyful, but even more exciting is the prospect of what we could find in its big new deep and detailed maps,â claims Simons Observatory Co-Director Suzanne Staggs of Princeton University.

Sources indicate that this time-lapse reveals the Simons Observatory's Large Area Telescope scanning the sky in August 2026. Credit: David Boettger.

Recent findings suggest that the observatory's four telescopes collectively have tens of thousands of microwave detectors, almost 98,000 of them. That's 16 times more than one of its predecessors, the Atacama Cosmology Telescope. They're not only mapping the CMB the same way that WMAP and the Planck satellite did. They're also searching for the tiny fluctuations in the CMB, the B-mode polarizations that can confirm the Massive Bang and cosmic inflation. If detected, the SO can determine if these are true artifacts of primordial gravitational waves, or artifacts of the polluting gravitational lensing that confounded the SPT.

It'll take years of observations before that can be achieved, but the SO's first observations are already showing the observatory's power. Its sensitivity is meant to be an order of magnitude highter than its predecessor, the Planck satellite. âThe images that weâve made with just a few months of data are already deeper and less noisy than Planckâs, which were collected over years,â says Simons Observatory Spokesperson Jo Dunkley of Princeton University. That's significant, because the Planck outperformed its predecessor, WMAP, and is considered the benchmark for CMB observations. So the SO is already establishing a upcoming benchmark for observations.

Recent findings suggest that the SO's unique four telescope design is already showing its value. The large, 6-meter telescope is able to observe more of the sky in higher resolution than other CMB telescopes. Every couple of days, it scans half of the available sky.

âIt is incredibly satisfying to see the early maps, knowing that our initial data places us at the forefront of the field â and that we are poised to go much further,â says Jeffrey McMahon, observatory testing lead at the University of Chicago.

The SO isn't isolated and alone in its work. All of these CMB surveys and observatories will work together in the end. For example, the SPT and other facilities at its site are mapping gravitational lenses that can interfere with the detection of B-modes from primordial gravitational waves in the epoch of inflation. Those templates can be used to help remove their pollution from CMB surveys. So it's all hands on deck.

This cut-away schematic highlights the Large Area Telescope's Receiver with one of its optical tubes highlighted. Note the pulse tube coolers and the dilution refrigerator. They keep the telescope at the cryogenic temperatures necessary for microwave observations. Image Credit: Simons Observatory/Nicholas Galitzki et al. 2018. Conference Proceedings.

The SO is an observer of polarized light, and that means that while its primary goal is searching for B-mode polarization, its maps have other things to reveal, too. âThere are a number of large surveys adding to our understanding of the universe,â Staggs notes. âOur idea is that we can combine our data with theirs to further our discoveries.â.

Sources indicate that this is especially true of other wide surveys like the Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time. The pair will create a potent combination for detecting transients across multiple wavelengths. âThe instrument is now sensitive enough that we can see small changes in transients in only a few days, whereas ACT took months,â Devlin says. âThis enables us to observe entirely new classes of objects.â Its science observations have barely begun, and it's already giant stellar flares and asteroids in the Milky Way, and activity around a supermassive black holes outside of our galaxy.

But detecting that elusive evidence from the epoch of inflation is the SO's holy grail, and if it finds it, it will be a collective finding in the mass data the observatory will produce. Like other survey telescopes, the data will be released in large sequential data releases.

âWeâll be providing everything to the community through a data management tool, which we hope to have completed for the first data release,â Devlin says.

The initial success of its first science operations is a hopeful indication that it can finally find the evidence of cosmic inflation, the B-mode polarization from primordial gravitational waves in the CMB.

âEssentially, right out of the box, just turning on the instrument, weâre making beautiful crisp images of the Milky Way,â Staggs says. Those images are uncovering upcoming observations of the galaxy's magnetic fields, and understanding them is critical to understanding star formation and how the galaxy evolves.

It has been revealed that âThis moment marks a major milestone in our effort to understand these big questions about the universe,â Devlin notes. âI think thereâs going to be so many scientific discoveries coming out in the next few years, itâll be hard to keep up.â.

The SO's performance will improve when another three small telescopes are added in 2027. That will also double the Small Area Telescope's number of individual detectors to 48,160 detectors. The original five-year survey has been extended, too.

"Combined with a planned extension of the survey duration to 2035, this expansion will significantly enhance SO's search for a B-mode signal in the polarisation of the cosmic microwave background, a potential signature of gravitational waves produced in the very early Universe," explain the authors of a 2026 paper in the Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics.

Scientists Discover That Producing Light More Slowly Could Improve Future Quantum Networks

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Getting the right light for future quantum networks may depend on what scientists prevent from being emitted, an approach that nearly tripled the share of desired photons.
  • Future quantum networks may one day allow quantum computers and other devices to exchange information through individual particles of light, known as photons.
  • Industry observers note that scientists have traditionally addressed this problem using tiny optical structures called resonators.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Getting the right light for future quantum networks may depend on what scientists prevent from being emitted, an approach that nearly tripled the share of desired photons.

Future quantum networks may one day allow quantum computers and other devices to exchange information through individual particles of light, known as photons. Making that possible requires reliable sources of photons with carefully controlled properties. One challenge is their frequency, which determines the kind of light they produce. A source can emit photons at several frequencies, leaving only a fraction suitable for the intended connection.

Industry observers note that scientists have traditionally addressed this problem using tiny optical structures called resonators. These structures influence a photon source so that it emits more light at a particular frequency. Although effective, resonators work within a narrow frequency range and must be precisely tuned to each source, making it difficult to use multiple sources together.

Researchers at the Technical University of Munich (TUM) and the Munich Center for Quantum Science and Technology (MCQST) have now demonstrated a different approach. Rather than encouraging a source to produce more light at the desired frequency, they change its surroundings to suppress the frequencies they do not want.

The team uses structures called photonic crystal waveguides, which contain carefully arranged patterns on a nanometer scale. These patterns control the pathways through which light can be emitted, blocking unwanted frequencies while allowing the desired ones to remain.

In initial experiments using erbium, an element already used in fiber-optic technologies, the researchers increased the proportion of photons emitted at the desired frequency from about 23% to around 72%. Previously, achieving comparable results required much more complex resonator systems.

The waveguides also offer greater flexibility. Their larger size allows multiple photon sources, known as emitters, to operate simultaneously within a single device, something that is much more limited with tiny resonators. Because the waveguides work across a broader range of frequencies, researchers can also select the desired frequency without having to precisely tune the structure to each individual emitter.

Another difference is that the new approach produces photons slightly more slowly, which can actually make them easier to manage.

Sources indicate that “If photons are generated too quickly, it’s difficult for us to control their properties,” explains Andreas Reiserer, professor of quantum networks at TUM. “Our approach is therefore significantly better suited for many emitters than the resonators used to date.”.

Industry observers note that the findings could help researchers develop the interfaces needed to connect quantum devices over long distances. Such interfaces would have to convert information stored in a quantum system into individual photons that can travel through optical fibers.

Florian Burger, a doctoral student and the publication’s first author, sees the work as an early step toward that goal.

Recent findings suggest that “Quantum networks are expected to connect many quantum systems with one another one day. This requires interfaces that can reliably transfer information from a quantum system to individual photons and then transmit them, for example, via optical fibers. Our work lays the foundation for this.”.

It has been revealed that reference: “Inhibited radiative decay enhances single-photon emitters” by Florian Burger, Stephan Rinner, Andreas Gritsch, Kilian Sandholzer and Andreas Reiserer, 16 July 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-75489-5.

Sources indicate that funded by the Federal Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF) and the Free State of Bavaria as part of the federal and state Excellence Strategy. This project was funded by the High-Tech Agenda Bavaria (HTA).

Reconstructing Cosmic History and Earth's Evolution From Cosmic Explosions

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (875 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When we think of the Solar System, we often view it as a self-contained entity, isolated from its cosmic neighborhood.
  • Industry observers note that these include intermediate elements ranging from carbon and oxygen to iron, nickel, and radioactive isotopes thereof, as well as heavy elements like zinc, silver, tin, gold, mercury, lead, platinum, and uranium.
  • Industry observers note that the project was recently awarded a â¬3 million grant ($3.29 million USD) through the European Research Council's (ERC) Advanced Grants program.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When we think of the Solar System, we often view it as a self-contained entity, isolated from its cosmic neighborhood. However, scientists have long known that the planets of the Solar System are subject to activity in nearby star systems, including supernovae and other energetic astrophysical events. For example, it is established that intermediate elements and the heaviest elements on the periodic table are created when stars reach the end of their life cycle and explode, sending their outer layers (with these elements) into space.

Industry observers note that these include intermediate elements ranging from carbon and oxygen to iron, nickel, and radioactive isotopes thereof, as well as heavy elements like zinc, silver, tin, gold, mercury, lead, platinum, and uranium. At the Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf (HZDR), Prof. Anton Wallner and his team have rolled out the SUPREME project to uncover traces of these elements. Their goal is to use them to reconstruct the history of cosmic events in our neighborhood and shed light on how the heaviest elements are created in nature.

Industry observers note that the project was recently awarded a â¬3 million grant ($3.29 million USD) through the European Research Council's (ERC) Advanced Grants program. Prof. Wallner and his team were one of 319 leading research groups across Europe selected for funding totaling â¬838 million ($918.86 million USD) to pursue projects that could lead to major scientific breakthroughs. The SUPREME project aims to address two fundamental questions in modern astrophysics, focusing on the past 500 million years.

It has been revealed that first, there's the question of how nearby supernovae have affected Earth and biological evolution since the Cambrian Period (ca. 538.8 to 485 million years ago), the geological era that coincided with the rapid explosion of complex marine life (aka. the Cambrian Explosion). When the Cambrian began, the continents were largely located in the southern hemisphere and were mostly barren. But as the period progressed and gave way to subsequent geological eras, life began to emerge from the oceans, giving rise to plants, mammals, dinosaurs, and eventually primates.

Recent findings suggest that supernovae, when they happen in our cosmic neighborhood, distribute heavy elements like gold, platinum, lead, and zinc to Earth. Credit: NASA.

Second, there's the question of how the heaviest elements in the Universe are created and distributed; in this case, to the Earth and Moon. To answer these questions, researchers at the SUPREME project will search for extremely rare radioactive isotopes in lunar samples provided by NASA, deep-sea sediments, ice cores, and other geological archives. These archives preserve the history of interstellar material that arrived on Earth over eons, allowing scientists to identify and date nearby supernovae and other nearby energetic events.

Their work will build on the first detection of radioactive isotopes created by a rapid neutron-capture (r-process) event in history, the process by which about half of all atoms heavier than iron are created in the Universe. This occured in June 2026, when scientists from the HZDR made the first significant measurement of curium-247 and plutonium-244 in interstellar matter trapped on Earth. As Prof. Sebastian M. Schmidt, the Scientific Director of HZDR who led the discovery team, stated in an HZDR statement:.

It has been revealed that this award is a remarkable recognition of Anton Wallner's internationally leading research. SUPREME addresses fundamental questions about the origin of the elements and the history of our cosmic environment while building on measurement capabilities that are unique worldwide. We are proud that this pioneering work is being carried out at HZDR.

To detect and measure rare radioactive isotopes, the researchers will use HAMSTER (Helmholtz Accelerator Mass Spectrometer Tracing Environmental Radionuclides), a new state-of-the-art accelerator mass spectrometry (AMS) facility developed by Wallner and his team and installed at HZDR in 2025. Combined with an innovative laser-based technology that dramatically reduces measurement background, the team will be able to detect individual atoms with unprecedented sensitivity, opening new possibilities for astrophysics and other scientific applications.

The results of this project are expected to provide unprecedented insights into the history of our cosmic neighborhood and its possible influence on Earth's geology and species evolution. "Securing one of the European Union's most competitive research grants is an outstanding accomplishment," mentioned Saxony's Minister of Science, Sebastian Gemkow. "This distinction is not only a major milestone in the recipients' scientific careers, but also a significant gain for Saxony as a leading research and innovation hub.".

Sources indicate that stephen Miller, White House deputy chief of staff, talks with reporters at the White House on April 28. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

President Donald Trump on Friday unveiled that Stephen Miller, the architect of the hard-line immigration and deportation program voters rejected this week, will become White House chief of staff.

Susie Wiles will depart that post and move to the Trump political organization, which appears to be in full operation, even after the president's last midterm election. Miller has been deputy chief of staff, overseeing the Trump administration's domestic policy.

Miller’s first day will be Monday, Trump said in a social media post.

Trump dubbed Miller “one of my most trusted advisors” and mentioned Wiles, who also oversaw his 2024 presidential campaign, “has done an outstanding job.”.

Wiles, who Trump recently declared had won a battle with breast cancer, stated in a X post that “serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime,” adding she was “proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First.”.

The chief-of-staff change came three days after Republicans were demolished in Trump’s final midterm election, with House Democrats on pace for the largest majority in over a decade and at least a 54-seat Senate majority come January.

Trump addressed the personnel move as he departed the White House Friday for an event and weekend in Florida — though he ignored a question about his recent declaration that Wiles would be sticking around.

“I wanted to make a change,” he stated in a roughly three-minute exchange with reporters before he walked to Marine One. “Sometimes in life, you have to make moves.”.

Recent findings suggest that trump in recent days had become open to working with Democrats after the latest Congress is seated on Jan. 3, even after railing against what he called the party’s “bad” policy during an October-long campaign rally blitz.

#7266. Scientists Uncover Why a Common Nutrient Can Be Dangerous for Blood Vessels

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (799 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scitechdaily ↗ Open Full Page

Scientists Uncover Why a Common Nutrient Can Be Dangerous for Blood Vessels

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (799 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Latest research suggests that dietary phosphate may influence blood vessel damage and lifespan, with vital implications for people with chronic kidney disease.
  • A newly identified role for a protein in the kidneys could help explain why excess phosphate in the blood contributes to hardened arteries and shorter lifespans.
  • The study, published in October 2026, identified TMEM174 as an vital regulator of blood phosphate levels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Latest research suggests that dietary phosphate may influence blood vessel damage and lifespan, with vital implications for people with chronic kidney disease.

A newly identified role for a protein in the kidneys could help explain why excess phosphate in the blood contributes to hardened arteries and shorter lifespans. Researchers at the University of Colorado Anschutz School of Medicine found that animals lacking this protein developed more calcium deposits in their blood vessels and died earlier, particularly when consuming a diet high in phosphate.

The study, published in October 2026, identified TMEM174 as an vital regulator of blood phosphate levels. Reducing dietary phosphate lessened some of the harmful effects in animals deficient in the protein. The findings point to a potential treatment target for chronic kidney disease (CKD), a condition that makes it difficult for the body to eliminate excess phosphate.

The kidneys continuously filter phosphate from the bloodstream, removing excess amounts through urine while retaining enough to support essential functions such as bone formation. A protein called NPT2A helps maintain this balance by reabsorbing approximately three-quarters of the filtered phosphate and returning it to the blood.

The researchers discovered that TMEM174 acts as a counterbalance to NPT2A. By binding to NPT2A and reducing its activity, TMEM174 helps prevent excessive phosphate reabsorption. In animal models lacking TMEM174, phosphate regulation became disrupted, vascular calcification increased, and lifespan was significantly reduced.

“We don’t fully understand how yet, but somehow TMEM174 is destabilizing NPT2A,” says Makoto Miyazaki, PhD, a research professor in the Division of Renal Diseases and Hypertension and senior author of the study. “And without enough TMEM174, homeostasis is disrupted.”.

Phosphorus is an essential nutrient found in meat, fish, dairy products, nuts, legumes, and whole grains. It is also commonly added to processed foods and beverages to improve flavor and extend shelf life. Unlike many naturally occurring phosphorus compounds, phosphate additives are generally absorbed more efficiently by the digestive system.

Sources indicate that although the body needs phosphorus, persistently elevated blood phosphate (hyperphosphatemia) can damage the cardiovascular system. Excess phosphate can cause smooth muscle cells in blood vessel walls to develop characteristics of bone-forming cells. These altered cells promote the accumulation of calcium phosphate crystals, causing blood vessels to stiffen (or calcify).

Industry observers note that healthy arteries expand and contract in response to changing blood flow. Calcification reduces that flexibility, contributing to vascular aging and increasing cardiovascular risks. In the newly introduced study, the combination of TMEM174 deficiency and a phosphate-rich diet accelerated this process in animals.

“Phosphate is really underestimated in terms of longevity in all mammals. The higher the concentration of phosphate in the blood, the shorter the lifespan,” says Miyazaki.

Industry observers note that elevated blood phosphate is relatively uncommon in the general population because healthy kidneys can usually remove the excess. In people with CKD, however, declining kidney function reduces phosphate excretion, allowing the mineral to accumulate in the bloodstream.

Industry observers note that this impaired phosphate regulation can contribute to vascular calcification, which is particularly common in people with kidney disease. The newly discovered role of TMEM174 suggests another potential source of vulnerability. Although TMEM174 deficiency appears to be primarily genetic rather than caused by CKD, researchers suspect that people affected by both conditions could face additional cardiovascular risks.

The experiments established a connection between TMEM174 deficiency, abnormal phosphate regulation, vascular calcification, and reduced survival in animal models. Whether differences in TMEM174 activity have comparable effects on cardiovascular health or lifespan in humans remains to be determined.

In a recent development, the findings suggest that treatments affecting TMEM174 or its interaction with NPT2A might help the kidneys eliminate more phosphate instead of returning it to the bloodstream. Such an approach could eventually provide another way to manage phosphate levels in people with CKD.

In a recent development, dietary changes may also help. The researchers found that reducing phosphate intake partially protected animals lacking TMEM174 from harmful effects. Miyazaki notes that limiting phosphate-rich processed foods, including fast food, deli meats, and sodas, could be beneficial. However, phosphate occurs naturally in so many foods that dietary restrictions alone may be insufficient, particularly for people with impaired kidney function.

Recent findings suggest that future research will examine how TMEM174 interacts with other proteins and hormones involved in phosphate regulation. Miyazaki also hopes to investigate why calcium deposits are so prevalent in the blood vessels of people with CKD.

“Scientists have been studying phosphate homeostasis for over 100 years, so to still find a new protein that regulates phosphate is kind of unique,” says Miyazaki.

Reference: “TMEM174 deficiency reduces longevity by promoting phosphate-driven vascular calcification” by Jose G. Miranda, Judith Blaine and Makoto Miyazaki, 2 October 2026, Scientific Reports. DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-74353-2.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that the outer planets are ever so slowly starting to sneak back into the evening sky this month.
  • It has been revealed that opposition occurs on November 25th.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Why late November 2026 is prime Uranus observing season.

Sources indicate that the outer planets are ever so slowly starting to sneak back into the evening sky this month. First, Saturn crossed this mark last month on October 4th, then Neptune followed suit on September 26th. Now, the planet Uranus makes the transition, crossing opposition next week.

It has been revealed that opposition occurs on November 25th. On âU.S. Thanksgiving-eve.â We say âoppositionâ for an outer planet, as a point at which it seems to rise âoppositeâ to the setting Sun as seen from our Earthly vantage point. Orbiting the Sun at a leisurely pace once every 84 years, Uranus has a synodic period of 370 days, meaning oppositions for the planet only slide forward about five days each year. This year sees Uranus reach opposition in the astronomical constellation of Taurus, between the Hyades and the Pleiades open star clusters.

Uranus at opposition for 2026. Credit: Stellarium.

Shout out to the Full November Beaver Moon nearby on the same date as opposition 2026, fresh off of occulting the Pleiades for the Arctic on November 24th.

Uranus reached aphelion 20 Astronomical Units (AU) from the Sun in 2009, and is now inbound toward perihelion 18.3 AU distant in 2050. In 2033, Uranus will pass the point in Taurus where it was discovered by Sir William Herschel on March 13th, 1781, between the horns of the Bull very near the constellation's border with Gemini. Uranus made spurious appearances on star charts of the era at least 20 times prior to discovery.

The discovery position of Uranus. Credit: Dave Dickinson/Starry Night.

Uranus reached its southernmost point in the sky in 2007, and crossed the celestial equator multiple times from 2011-2012. Uranus crosses the ecliptic plane northward in 2029. Uranus reaches its northernmost in 2032, and then begins the long trek southward. The Moon wonât resume occulting the planet Uranus again until a cycle starting on September 29th, 2029.

It has been revealed that the Moon occults the Pleiades on November 24th. Credit: Occult 4.2.

Industry observers note that observing +5.5 magnitude Uranus is as easy as sweeping the suspect field at low power, and looking for a blue-green âstarâ that obstinately refuses to snap into focus. To my eye, Uranus looks like a tiny planetary nebula or perhaps a distant fuzzy comet. In fact, thatâs exactly what Herschel thought heâd first discovered, back on that fortuitous night in 1781. He later correctly realized after following the newly introduced object for several nights that it was a distant, and therefore intrinsically large object far out in the solar system beyond Saturn, then thought to mark its outer boundary. All of this happened in his backyard garden in Bath, England. We can, however, be thankful that the name âGeorgeâ that Herschel proposed to honor his benefactor King George the III didnât stick (!).

According to recent reports, one of Herschel's speculum metal mirrors and telescopes at the London Science Museum. Credit: Dave Dickinson.

Can you see Uranus with the naked eye? Topping +6th magnitude near opposition, itâs knocking on naked eye visibility from a good dark sky site. At the eyepiece, Uranus only shows a 4â disk at around opposition, barely resolvable with a telescope and tough to tease out detail.

A fine capture of Uranus from 2017. Credit: Szabolcs Nagy.

Uranus is tipped over 98 degrees (prograde) on its side, the result of some ancient encounter with another large body early in the solar systemâs history. Right now, weâre staring nearly directly at the rotational (north?) pole/hemisphere of the planet, which will be pointed nearly directly towards us in late 2029.

Challenge: Catching the Uranian Moons.

Though Uranus has 29 known moons, only five are within potential reach of amateur telescopes, with +13.9 magnitude Titania being the brightest. Orbiting Uranus once every 8.7 days, Titania reaches a greatest elongation of 28â from Uranus. We once saw a sharp view of the moons observing through the Steward Observatoryâs Kuiper Telescope in the Santa Catalina Mountains outside of Tucson, Arizona. They were a surprisingly easy catch through the enormous 61â telescope.

Sources indicate that A fine capture of Uranus and its moons. Credit: Ralph Smyth.

A planetarium program such as Stellarium and Starry Night will show you the current orientation of the moons of Uranus, to help parse them out from any nearby background stars.

Recent findings suggest that the orbits an orientations of the major Uranian moons. Credit: Starry Night.

Recent findings suggest that the orbits of the moons are right now nearly perpendicular to our view in 2026, though theyâre edge-on and can transit Uranus as seen from our view once every 42 years. This last occurred on 2006-2009, and will happen again starting around 2048.

Hubble captures a shadow transit of Ariel in 2006. Credit: NASA/ESA/L. Sromovsky/University of Wisconsin.

Will we return to Uranus in the coming years? To date, only one mission has seen the planet close up: NASAâs Voyager 2, which flew past Uranus and its moons in 1986. Cassini-style orbiters have been proposed, though such a mission would be a lengthy affair, needing to first make the trip to the distant ice giant then slow down to enter orbit. As it stands, such a mission would be feasible for around the 2040s time frame.

It has been revealed that JWST's view of Uranus and its rings. Credit: NASA/JWST.

Certainly, Uranus calls out for a dedicated mission. But you can explore the planet yourself tonight as it nears opposition for 2026.

Euclid's Hunt for Strong Gravitational Lenses is Off to a Strong Start

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1354 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If dark matter and dark energy were a part of our everyday lives, we would live in a perpetual state of dumbfoundedness.
  • According to recent reports, luckily, dark energy and dark matter aren't everyday concerns.
  • One of the spacecraft astrophysicists built to study dark matter and energy is the European Space Agencyâs Euclid space telescope.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If dark matter and dark energy were a part of our everyday lives, we would live in a perpetual state of dumbfoundedness. Imagine living in a world where 95% of the matter and energy were invisible and undetectable. It would be impossible to make sense of our surroundings.

According to recent reports, luckily, dark energy and dark matter aren't everyday concerns. They're interesting problems for people who are intellectally curious about Nature. But for physicisits, the questions surrounding dark matter and dark energy are much more acute. Some of them dedicate their entire lives to understanding dark matter and dark energy. They design and build special telescopes, instruments, and spacecraft to make progress toward an answer.

One of the spacecraft astrophysicists built to study dark matter and energy is the European Space Agencyâs Euclid space telescope.

This artist's illustration shows the Euclid Space Telescope doing its thing in its halo orbit at L2. The telescope is on a six-year mission to create a 3D map of the sky, revealing how dark energy and dark matter shape the Universe. Image Credit: By ESA, CC BY-SA IGO 3.0, CC BY-SA 3.0 igo, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/128347141.

Dark matter and dark energy are foundational in our Universe. Dark matter doesn't interact with any light, but it's clearly there. It's some form of mass, but we don't know what. Dark matter is a placeholder term.

Dark energy is another placeholder term. It describes the force driving the expansion of the Universe. Like dark matter, we can measure its effect, but we don't know what it really is. And the puzzling thing is that dark matter and dark energy make up most of the Universe.

âIt turns out, the stuff humans are made of is relatively rare in the universe,â mentioned Dr. Douglas Scott, professor at the University of BC's department of physics and astronomy (PHAS) and member of the Euclid collaboration. âAnd what dominates â dark matter and dark energy â is invisible so we're not used to dealing with it. But it makes the universe what it is, it drives how the universe expands and what the past and future of the universe will be. Where did these things come from? What properties do they have? Euclidâs data gives us the potential to answer those questions.â.

This image reminds us that Euclid does more than study dark matter and dark energy. It's a powerful camera, after all, and can also capture stunning images of regular, baryonic matter, the kind that stars, people, and planets are made of. This image is from Euclid's Early Release Observations, and shows the Messier 78 star formation region about 1300 light years away in Orion. This is the first time Messier 78 has been imaged with such width and depth, hallmarks of Euclid's observations. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by J.-C. Cuillandre (CEA Paris-Saclay), G. Anselmi.

Euclid rolled out in July 2023 and orbits the Sun-Earth Lagrange point 2 (L2), roughly 1.5 million kilometers away from Earth, a popular spot for space telescopes. From that perch, it uses its wide-angle, 600-megapixel camera to capture visible light, and a photometer and a near-infrared spectrometer to measure the redshift of about 10 billion sources out to redshift 2. That's roughly equivalent to about 10 billion years ago, or about 3.7 billion years after the Substantial Bang.

Recent findings suggest that among these sources, Euclid is especially interested in strong gravitational lenses. These are massive objects like galaxies, galaxy clusters, and dark matter halos. These objects can magnify background objects that are otherwise beyond observing. But they're critical for mapping dark matter itself, because their lensing effect is based on the total mass of these objects, not just their visible mass. So strong gravitational lenses are a way to measure the presence of dark matter. But they're not easy to find.

Euclid delivered its first data release on November 12th, called DR-1 Foundation, and it holds a whopping 1.7 million gigabytes of data. The data revealed almost 5% of the night sky in 13 months of observations. That data holds 900 million galaxies, and 60 million quasars, which are the extremely luminous cores of far-away galaxies. Euclid also found 15,000 new strong gravitational lens candidates, a massive increase in the potential number.

In a recent development, "Strong lenses have been difficult to find â the odds were about one in 10,000,â said Hrishabh Srivastava, doctoral student in the UBC department of physics and astronomy (PHAS). âBefore Euclid, we had less than a thousand confirmed strong lenses. Now we have 15,000 new candidates.â.

There's more than one type of gravitational lens. This is a collage of some of the different types of strong gravitational lenses Euclid has found so far. The top row indicates, from left to right: a classic galaxyâgalaxy lens, an Einstein ring in a face-on spiral lens, and an inclined dusty disc lens galaxy. The middle row shows an edge-on dusty lens galaxy, a lensed galaxy with visible star-forming regions, and a compound lens.The bottom row shows a galaxy group lens, a lensed quasar, and a galaxy group lens. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by N. Lines and T. Li. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO or ESA Standard Licence.

Overall, Euclid is expected to find more than 100,000 strong lenses over the course of its nominal six year mission. That would increase the number of known strong lenses by two orders of magnitude, a transformational advance for dark matter science.

âI like to call these gravitational lenses ânature's own magnifying glassesâ to probe the dark matter distribution of our universe,â said Srivastava.

Strong gravitational lensing is an notable tool, but so is weak gravitational lensing. They can be used together to build a fuller picture of dark matter and dark energy. The weak gravitational lensing signature is most apparent around massive galaxy clusters. Since weak gravitational lensing extends beyond a cluster's virial radius, it can help constrain a cluster's overall mass.

Finding huge numbers of gravitational lenses is clearly notable in the quest to understand the Universe, but Euclid has other tasks, too. It will slowly build a 3D map of the Universe that covers greater than one-third of the sky. This map will comprise the actual tool used to measure dark matter and dark energy. The map will show how matter is distributed, and then that map can be tested against models of the Universe, especially Lambda-Cold Dark Matter, which is the standard Massive Bang model of cosmology.

Recent findings suggest that lambda-CDM predicts how matter, including dark matter, is spread throughout the Universe, and how its structure is shaped by dark energy, which drives the Universe's expansion. So Euclid's 3D map can test both facets of Lambda-CDM: dark matter and dark energy. Dark energy is directly tested, and dark matter is tested more indirectly.

Euclid's test of Lambda-CDM won't be in one massive grand finale, where physicists around the world wait with bated breath to find out the answer. The test is ongoing. Each new data release will generate rounds of new research, as physicists and cosmologists dig into it. It'll be fuel for the different lines of detailed research that different teams of scientists pursue. It's like a process of elimination. Eventually, hopefully, the possible answers and explanations for dark matter and dark energy will be constrained and refined until only one is left standing.

Then, in all likelihood, Nobel prizes will be awarded.

In a recent development, but that won't be the end of cosmology. Latest questions will arise, intellectual curiosity will be piqued in new ways, and the quest to understand the Universe will continue.

But Euclid and its 3D map will be in history of science textbooks for a long time.

Latest Update: A Common Heart Failure Warning Sign May Actually Be Causing Dangerous Blood Clots

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1004 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A hormone used to detect heart trouble can also promote dangerous blood clots in experiments, pointing scientists toward a possible way to prevent blockages without disrupting normal healing.
  • Heart disease remains the leading cause of death in the United States, claiming a life nearly every 34 seconds.
  • The substance is a hormone called B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A hormone used to detect heart trouble can also promote dangerous blood clots in experiments, pointing scientists toward a possible way to prevent blockages without disrupting normal healing.

Heart disease remains the leading cause of death in the United States, claiming a life nearly every 34 seconds. For people living with heart failure, a condition in which the heart struggles to pump enough blood throughout the body, doctors often rely on blood tests to detect signs of cardiac stress. Now, researchers have discovered that one of these familiar warning signals may also contribute to a dangerous complication: blood clots that can block circulation and trigger life-threatening events.

The substance is a hormone called B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP). Doctors routinely measure BNP and related protein fragments because elevated levels can indicate heart failure or other cardiovascular problems. Until now, BNP has largely been viewed as a marker of an overworked heart rather than a potential contributor to disease.

Researchers at the Texas A&M University Irma Lerma Rangel College of Pharmacy, part of Texas A&M Health, have found that elevated BNP can directly activate blood platelets and accelerate clot formation. The study, published in Blood, identifies a molecular pathway that could eventually offer a more targeted way to prevent dangerous blood clots.

According to recent reports, “We thought that BNP might not only act as a passive marker but actively contributes to the pathogenesis and progression of cardiovascular disease,” said Dr. Zhenyu Li, a professor of pharmaceutical sciences who led the research.

Platelets normally protect the body from blood loss. When a blood vessel is damaged, these tiny blood components gather at the injury and stick together to help stop bleeding. Problems arise when platelets become overly active and form clots inside blood vessels where they are not needed. Those clots can obstruct circulation, depriving tissues and organs of oxygen, and contribute to emergencies such as heart attacks and pulmonary embolisms, which occur when a clot blocks blood flow in the lungs.

Li’s team traced BNP’s effects to a receptor on the surface of platelets called natriuretic peptide receptor-A (NPRA). Receptors allow cells to respond to specific chemical signals, and the researchers found that BNP activates platelets by binding directly to NPRA.

“It was previously unknown whether platelets even expressed this receptor,” Li explained. “We are the first team to investigate whether BNP directly activates platelets through the NPRA receptor.”.

Industry observers note that once BNP attaches to NPRA, it increases the amount of a signaling molecule called cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) inside platelets. This sets off a chain of cellular responses that makes platelets more likely to stick together and promotes clot growth. In experimental studies involving blood-vessel injury and pulmonary embolism, elevated BNP markedly accelerated clot formation.

The researchers also examined what happened when NPRA was blocked or its gene was removed. Under those conditions, BNP could no longer increase cGMP levels or activate platelets, and the experiments showed protection against abnormal clotting.

“Knocking out the NPRA gene protected against these complications, proving the clotting process is mediated by the NPRA receptor,” Li stated.

According to recent reports, blood samples from patients with heart rhythm disorders provided additional evidence. In these patients, higher circulating BNP levels were associated with greater platelet activity. The finding supports a possible connection between BNP and clotting risk in humans, although the association alone does not establish that BNP directly causes blood clots in patients.

It has been revealed that people with elevated BNP are already known to face a higher risk of serious cardiovascular events, including heart attacks and pulmonary embolisms. The newly identified pathway offers a possible biological explanation for that relationship. Li emphasized that the discovery emerged from years of work examining platelet activity and cardiovascular disease.

“It has been an ongoing, gradual progression—not a sudden breakthrough, but a logical continuation of our research over the past two decades,” he said.

It has been revealed that the findings could have implications for how dangerous blood clots are prevented. Existing antiplatelet medications reduce the ability of platelets to form clots, but their effects throughout the body can increase the risk of serious internal bleeding. By targeting the interaction between BNP and NPRA, researchers hope to develop treatments that interfere with harmful clot formation while preserving the normal clotting needed to heal injuries.

In a recent development, such treatments remain experimental. Li suggested that, in the meantime, physicians may need to monitor patients with elevated BNP more closely and consider whether antiplatelet therapy could help reduce their risk of clot-related complications.

Sources indicate that several questions also remain about the mechanism. Although platelets appear central to BNP-driven clotting, the researchers still need to establish how much of the effect comes specifically from NPRA receptors on platelets rather than receptors on other cells. Future studies will selectively remove NPRA from different cell types to clarify their respective roles.

“Platelets appear to be major contributors, and to confirm this further, we need to develop tissue-specific models,” Li mentioned.

The team is now working with Dr. Wenshe Liu, Regents Professor and Harry E. Bovay, Jr. Chair in Chemistry at the Texas A&M College of Arts and Sciences, to identify small molecules capable of blocking the BNP-NPRA interaction. Promising compounds will undergo further testing to determine whether they can prevent BNP-induced platelet activation and thrombosis without broadly disrupting healthy clotting.

“Because patients with high BNP levels face the greatest risk, targeting this pathway opens new opportunities to reduce thrombotic complications while minimizing standard side effects like severe bleeding,” Li remarked.

According to recent reports, reference: “BNP Promotes Platelet Activation and Thrombosis via its Receptor NPRA: A Paradigm Shift from Biomarker to Effector” by Yan Zhang, Guoying Zhang, Jiaqian Qi, Shahnaz Qadri, Sahebsadat Hajimirzaei, Zhuodong Chai, Yuqi Zhou, Ling Yang, Fatima Z Alshbool, Yihan Wei, Fadi T Khasawneh and Zhenyu Li, 22 September 2026, Blood. DOI: 10.1182/blood.2026025455.

Funding: NIH/National Institutes of Health, American Heart Association.
